title: Need help resolving squad composition with random scenario system
question:
Using the random scenario system spreadsheet from files section we drew Japanese vs Russian playing scenario O. Not sure how to resolve Japanese and Russian squad composition? There are instructions on the back of Banzai rules and there is the scenario setup card in Vassal which give different suggestions. Scenario O on Vassal setup card and Banzai rules doesn't list the Russian side and if you look at scenario C the Japanese side is different.  

Edit: If you decide to use the scenario C squad compositions you then need to decide whether to use the Scenario C or O special rules? Probably simplest to just say it's scenario C instead of O and be done with it.
author: davidk64
consensus_answer:
Using the random scenario system spreadsheet from files section we drew Japanese vs Russian playing scenario O. Not sure how to resolve Japanese and Russian squad composition? There are instructions on the back of Banzai rules and there is the scenario setup card in Vassal which give different suggestions. Scenario O on Vassal setup card and Banzai rules doesn't list the Russian side and if you look at scenario C the Japanese side is different.  

If it is the spreadsheet I designed, I'm sorry missed that Russians cannot appear in O.   (I did catch there was no French match up.)

But you can do any of these things;
-  Redraw the scenario while still keeping the Jv.R nationality match up.
-   Simply play Scenario C, instead.  Yes, they C & O are both Pillbox scenarios but they have very different OOBs and mixing an Attacker from one against a Defender from the other would likely be extremely imbalanced. 
-  The selection system is more to suggest a random Scenario, not force the players to play an unsatisfying game;  whether due to imbalance, playing a scenario beyond the players experience level, playing a "bad" Scenario/nationality, etc.  Feel free to redraw any or all of the selection to get scenario both players will enjoy.

title: Lateral group transfer question
question:
In the General Vol 21 Number 1 scenario A series replay, on turn 5 the American plays a sideways movement card on his group C "as a Lateral Group Transfer". But given the German player only has groups at identity chit A and B isn't this illegal? Rule 17.7 first sentence says "... directly opposite an opposing group ..."

The rule states the player announces the intention to perform a lateral group transfer so presumably if the player doesn't make the announcement at the time of playing the movement card sideways he can't subsequently do so on a future turn (using that same played movement card) even if the necessary conditions still exist to make such a move? 

Where a game is played without aid of voice or text chat I guess you might agree that a lateral group transfer announcement was accompanied by putting down the new group identity chit in the adjacent column and taken away if the attempt failed.

I wonder whether having declared the intention to lateral group transfer a player can change their mind? 

Edit: Looking through past posts I see I have broached this issue before! See https://boardgamegeek.com/thread/1342845/article/35597336#35597336 where no conclusion was reached :)
author: davidk64
consensus_answer:
In the General Vol 21 Number 1 scenario A series replay, on turn 5 the American plays a sideways movement card on his group C "as a Lateral Group Transfer". But given the German player only has groups at identity chit A and B isn't this illegal? Rule 17.7 first sentence says "... directly opposite an opposing group ..."

No, it says "A group capable of movement can change its group identity and thereby its position directly opposing an enemy group...."  All it is saying if you move group from B to C, the directly opposing group would now be C--if it exists.  If the opponent  does not have a Group C, then there would be no directly opposing group to your Group C.  (Just like there would be if each side set up with a different number of groups at start.)

It is not stating a requirement, but a change of status of "directly opposing" groups.

The rule states the player announces the intention to perform a lateral group transfer so presumably if the player doesn't make the announcement at the time of playing the movement card sideways he can't subsequently do so on a future turn (using that same played movement card) even if the necessary conditions still exist to make such a move? 

Correct, if the intention to change a group's ID is not made when playing the movement cards, when group enters terrain, the same Group ID remains.  Very common if you want to get into better terrain.

Where a game is played without aid of voice or text chat I guess you might agree that a lateral group transfer announcement was accompanied by putting down the new group identity chit in the adjacent column and taken away if the attempt failed.

A common technique in ftf play is to place the new ID on the Movement card until new terrain is accepted or rejected (which would cancel the transfer).

I wonder whether having declared the intention to lateral group transfer a player can change their mind? 

I would say no per errata on Rule 5:  Movement cards not played directly to the discard pile cannot voluntarily be cancelled.  (Just like you can't rotate a Movement card from advancing to sideways because you change your mind about advancing.)

Edit: Looking through past posts I see I have broached this issue before! See https://boardgamegeek.com/thread/1342845/article/35597336#35597336 where no conclusion was reached :)

No big deal, that thread started 11 years ago and you added your question 5 years after that.

title: Prisoners/guarding (32)
question:
Taking a deep dive into rules I never see used in the games I've played of UF.  

From a re-formatted rule book that embeds the Q/A.  

32.12 & 16.42 By capturing a man and bringing him into a group, and
then stopping in suitable terrain, does the attacker satisfy the Relative
Range 5 requirement of the Victory Conditions, if, in so doing, it
eliminates the only Relative Range 5 enemy group?
A. Yes. Note, this rule is in effect to prevent a player from routing men
to avoid victory by the opponent.

---

I don't understand the answer.  Players can't rout men of their own volition that I know of.  I could see someone voluntarily panic one of their PCs to eliminate a RR5 situation.  Is that what it's talking about?
---

Prisoners, once taken, are placed
beneath the card of any one man in the capturing
group of the capturing player's choice. That man
may be pinned, wounded, or even unarmed but he
may not be the designated assistant crewman for any weapon.

---

It's not "that man may NOT be pinned"  Pinned PCs can actually do something?  The only thing is guarding?

--

If the designated assistant crewman is the only possible choice...

--

How is that possible?  Who is he crewing for if he's the only choice?

--

A player may change guards automatically as the sole Action of a group for that turn provided
the new guard is not currently pinned.

--

The 2nd paragraph says yes for pinned PCs as guards and the last says no.  I see there's a, very, slight difference in the initiation of the guard duty between the two but I don't see the point.
author: DiploGuy
consensus_answer:
Taking a deep dive into rules I never see used in the games I've played of UF.  

This is a rare situation.  It would only matter in a rear guard action scenarios ("X unpinmed men at RR5 (not Range Chit 4/5)") with all men in the group are pinned.

Prisoners, in general, are often forgotten about--I saw it once or twice in CC to get 5VP in a city fight.

From a re-formatted rule book that embeds the Q/A.  

32.12 & 16.42 By capturing a man and bringing him into a group, and
then stopping in suitable terrain, does the attacker satisfy the Relative
Range 5 requirement of the Victory Conditions, if, in so doing, it
eliminates the only Relative Range 5 enemy group?
A. Yes. Note, this rule is in effect to prevent a player from routing men
to avoid victory by the opponent.

---

I don't understand the answer.  Players can't rout men of their own volition that I know of.  I could see someone voluntarily panic one of their PCs to eliminate a RR5 situation.  Is that what it's talking about?

Yes.  You cannot simply rout a man.   You can voluntarily panic a pinned man. but there would be chance he dies rather than routs/captured at RR5.  Nor can you voluntarily rout unpinned men.

It is an attempt to prevent a spoil sport play when an Attacker reaches RR5 and only needs to reach good terrain or rally pinned men and the Defender voluntarily panics to eliminate that group.  At least the man could be captured (if he didn't KIA) preserving the justified win.  But obviously if he did KIA. this rule doesn't fix the problem.

At least it is VERY unlikely to come up:  It would be a late game desperation move by the defender who otherwise is not close to breaking his squad in Scenarios D or Q.

Prisoners, once taken, are placed
beneath the card of any one man in the capturing
group of the capturing player's choice. That man
may be pinned, wounded, or even unarmed but he
may not be the designated assistant crewman for any weapon.

---

It's not "that man may NOT be pinned"  Pinned PCs can actually do something?  The only thing is guarding?

Yes, that is what it says--even though it says should the guard be eliminated, his prisoners must be reassigned to an unpinned man.  (I have a feeling Courtney Allen and Don Greenwood may have been hemming and hawing on this rule.)

--

If the designated assistant crewman is the only possible choice...

--

How is that possible?  Who is he crewing for if he's the only choice?

Good, then this rule would NEVER come up!  (See what I wrote above!)

--

A player may change guards automatically as the sole Action of a group for that turn provided
the new guard is not currently pinned.

--

The 2nd paragraph says yes for pinned PCs as guards and the last says no.  I see there's a, very, slight difference in the initiation of the guard duty between the two but I don't see the point.  

Also, per errata, unpinned man must be in the capturing group in order to capture during a rout.

If you want to play with a house rule that says "Pinned men cannot be assigned to guard prisoners, but they can retain that role if later pinned", I don't think most opponents would object.  And that seems to fix the holes you found. (re: crewman and reassignment.)

As I said above, prisoners do not come up frequently:
-  You have get groups at RR5, which happens infrequently in the first place.
-  The players in that situation are usually more concerned with CC to eliminate the group or winning the scenario.
-  And unless the scenario is going to be determined by victory points (Only can happen in Scenarios A, B, G, J, M,  N.), the attacker would rather not take a prisoner at all--if only to avoid fp/To Hit penalties.  And rule 32.12 allows the "capturing" player to not take a prisoner if otherwise able, leaving the enemy man to rout instead.

It really seems like unnecessary chrome.  If it's a bunch of ELAN points for the campaign to take a prisoner (did privates really have any intel worth anything?) I see it might be worth the effort.  

Why not just say voluntary panic isn't allowed for groups at RR5?  Or.. it's a withdrawl if you do (campaign relevance).

Richard is the man...

You need an Up Front rules thing, he will have it right.

Yes, it is chrome.  I don't think it is unnecessary--prisoners were taken on occasion in WW2.

The main in game reason is to get 5 VP, but most scenarios are not decided by VP.  And you simply don't have reason to take prisoners in other scenarios, so you don't.

I don't play many campaigns, but I'm a bit surprised elan points are awarded for capturing a prisoner.  (CC KIAs are awarded 4 EP)

Why not just say voluntary panic isn't allowed for groups at RR5?  Or.. it's a withdrawl if you do (campaign relevance).  

There ARE legitimate, realistic reasons to Voluntarily Panic @RR5.  You have one man pinned in a group and the rest of the guys really need to move.  For example:  Rear guard Action, attacker at RR5 to one of your groups and you want to retreat before he reaches defendible terrain.

title: Confused about lateral flanking fire
question:
17.1 LATERAL FLANKING FIRE: Flanking Fire can originate at any Relative Range from a group whose last placed "Flank" Movement card was played sideways and remains in play at the end of the turn in which it was played

Does the flanking unit suffers from moving fire penalty? Does flanking stop once the flanking unit enters some terrain? 😕
author: pmiranda
consensus_answer:
17.1 LATERAL FLANKING FIRE: Flanking Fire can originate at any Relative Range from a group whose last placed "Flank" Movement card was played sideways and remains in play at the end of the turn in which it was played

Does the flanking unit suffers from moving fire penalty? Does flanking stop once the flanking unit enters some terrain? 😕

The moving penalty applies to the flanking group.  Play of terrain in the flanking group does not remove the flank condition

replies.body:
17.1 LATERAL FLANKING FIRE: Flanking Fire can originate at any Relative Range from a group whose last placed "Flank" Movement card was played sideways and remains in play at the end of the turn in which it was played

Does the flanking unit suffers from moving fire penalty? Does flanking stop once the flanking unit enters some terrain? 😕

The moving penalty applies to the flanking group.  Play of terrain in the flanking group does not remove the flank condition
I see, thanks!

You place the flank chit when either:
- You play a Flank Movement card in sideways mode.
-  You play a Movement card to advance to RR6 (i.e. as the rules put it, to RR4 by advancing from RR5.)
AND
***IF*** the Flanking group is adjacent to Flanked group and you also have a Front group (i.e. a group with the same ID as Flanked group)

You remove the Flank Fire chit:
-  When a Movement card or Wire card is placed on the FLANKING group (but importantly NOT a terrain card, which answers the OPs question--so long as the Flanking group is still moving, the Flank Fire effect is canceled by the moving fire effect.  This is how the Flanking group stops moving.)
-  When a Movement card (even a temporary one to remove Wire or unsuccessfully ford a Stream) or a terrain card is played on the FLANKED group.
-  If the FRONT group is eliminated or it transfers to a different ID chit.

The presence of a Flank Fire chit determines whether the Flanking group is entitled to doubled FP vs. the Flanked group.

-  When a Movement card (even a temporary one to remove Wire or unsuccessfully ford a Stream) or a terrain card is played on the FLANKED group.
-  If the FRONT group is eliminated or it transfers to a different ID chit.

The presence of a Flank Fire chit determines whether the Flanking group is entitled to doubled FP vs. the Flanked group.

Richard, I've always wondered about the "working rationale" behind both types of flanking. With natural flanking fire it makes sense to due to the firing angle after moving past the enemy group. And I get that the flanking group would have to be adjacent for the effectiveness due to proximity. And finally, having the flanked group opposed by a friendly group to create the "anvil" of the flank also makes sense. 
But the one that is kind of hard to mentally picture, is gaining flanking fire just because that moving group played a Movement card sideways. My best guess would be because the game is trying to simulate a fire advantage because the moving group is advancing to some portion of the battlefield that is giving it a temporary deadly fire defilade...or some such reason.

Richard, I've always wondered about the "working rationale" behind both types of flanking. With natural flanking fire it makes sense to due to the firing angle after moving past the enemy group. And I get that the flanking group would have to be adjacent for the effectiveness due to proximity. And finally, having the flanked group opposed by a friendly group to create the "anvil" of the flank also makes sense. 
But the one that is kind of hard to mentally picture, is gaining flanking fire just because that moving group played a Movement card sideways. My best guess would be because the game is trying to simulate a fire advantage because the moving group is advancing to some portion of the battlefield that is giving it a temporary deadly fire defilade...or some such reason. 

I don't know what the designer's rationale was for the Flank Movement cards, but I tend to picture it as some sort of advantageous fire position that is being abstracted, as the Terrain and Wire rules are.  

As for the game design reason, it prevents one side from just hunkering down entrenched in Woods for -3.   They'd be awfully hard to dislodge. The side attacking has some way to set up a large fire attack and the hankering group now has reason to leave.  This makes the game more dynamic.

From the Designer's Notes:
The concept of Flanking Fire is more than just fire from a position on the flank of an enemy unit. It could also be fire from a position which has achieved a more favorable LOS to the enemy group or has moved into a new firing position unobserved. The latter becomes especially true at the longer ranges.

title: AFV questions (stun effect, etc.)
question:
Background:  I have been playing Up Front for over 40 years, but I never liked AFV's and so avoided them.  Now I'm trying to use them more, and this has raised some questions that I didn't have to think about before.

Is a stunned, non-OT AFV forced to button up?  I think I had always assumed the answer was "yes", but re-reading the rules yesterday, I wasn't sure.  The clearest rule I can find is 28.45, which says, "A stun result flips any CE AFV card over to its Pinned/Button Up side."

Well, that is ambiguous.  It says it's only referring to CE AFVs, but then it mentions a Buttoned Up side, which a CE AFV does not have.  I think on the whole that I would find it odd that regular AFV's don't button up when stunned when OT AFV's do, but that's not much of a guide to go on.

I'd like to follow this up with a dumb question about boxed attacks.  I'm pretty sure I understand them, but they seem weird, so I just wanted to verify.  In brief:  when you shoot a boxed effect number against an AFV, you know exactly what's going to happen if you hit.  You simply add your boxed number to your relative range, and compare that to the defending AFV's numbers.  (There are exceptions for rifleman using inherent boxed FP at range 5 and for LATW.)  This feels weird to me because everything else in Up Front is accompanied by massive amounts of randomness, so for a hit's result to be absolutely known (with the possible exception of an immobilization or stun in case they have the same effect number) seems incongruous.  I just want to make sure I'm getting it right.
author: dcroxton
consensus_answer:
Couple of things - about getting AFVs to button up, one way for infantry to reduce the threat of an AFV is to fire at it with small arms, hoping to get a hit equal to or higher than its Morale value, which forces it to button up.  This is covered by 28.3:

An AFV card has two Armor defense values printed on each side of the card plus a Morale and CE Defense value on the front of the card. The Armor and Flank defense values represent the armored defense strength and is listed on both sides of the card; only attacks using solely boxed firepower or boxed "Effect Numbers" apply to this value. The MORALE and CE values are affected only by unboxed attack values.

This is how mortars can attack AFVs (and they have a small chance of damaging the vehicle as well [26.5]).  AT guns have the choice of firing AP - the process the OP referred to in his second question, which attacks the Armor/Flank values - or HE, which attacks the Morale value as above.  The HE attack is only possible, of course, when the vehicle is CE, or in the case of an OT vehicle if it is not already Pinned (except for one or two really weedy AFVs like the British Bren Carrier, which has a Panic value and can thus be attacked when Pinned).

And moving on to the OPs second question, you were right to feel that there should be a random element is resolving an AP hit - and there is!  25.4 says:

Once a hit has been obtained, the strength of that hit is determined by adding the To Hit Random Number on the RNC just drawn to the Effect Number listed on the ordnance card. (EXC: IG/AFV ordnance firing at an AFV target does not add the To Hit Random Number just drawn; instead it adds a number equal to the Relative Range between the firer and the target.)  The color of the RNC has no effect; all numbers are added. Having now determined the total strength of the attack (after modification for terrain and/or movement), it is resolved separately for each target in the defending group by drawing a new RNC and adding any black number or subtracting any red number drawn as per a normal fire attack [6.5]. 

So the Hit process establishes first whether a hit has been obtained, and secondly how damaging it is: for HE, the RNC on the To Hit card is used (provided a 0 would have hit, reflecting how close the HE round actually landed), and for AP a hit is a hit, but the RR is added to reflect increased penetration at closer ranges.  This gives you the base hit strength; then, in both cases, you draw an RNC for each target.  Firing at an AFV, of course, there is only one target, but you still draw an RNC.

So, a Panther (s7,i8,k9) rumbles up to RR4 to a plucky British 6-pdr (FE 3).  If the AT gun gets a hit, its base Hit Strength will be 3+4=7, and then it hopes the RNC will be at least 0, and preferably a black 2 or better to get a kill.

Don't forget, also, that unlike small arms and HE fire against an AFV, terrain does affect the resolution.  So if the AFV is in Brush, the Hit Strength is reduced by 1.  I suppose this reflects the possibility of the round being deflected or slowed by intervening obstacles.

Hope all that helps!  Oh, and Snipers are good, too.

replies.body:
Your question in interesting and I do not see it addressed in the rules--but I'll continue to look.

28.43 BUTTONED UP: Any other AFV whose Morale Defense value is equaled or exceeded by any attack becomes Buttoned Up when it is flipped over. An AFV which Buttons Up remains Buttoned Up for the duration of the scenario (barring play of a Hero card) whether it Buttons Up voluntarily or due to enemy fire. 

I don't recall if I ever ran into that situation. 

Anyone else?

A CE AFV has a buttoned up side on the back of the card. The OT AFVs have pinned sides.
You have answered your own question in 28.45
The difference is that a buttoned up AFV is not pinned, so as long as it is not stunned it can function normally albeit with reduced ratings.
A halftrack which is pinned ( it doesn't button up ) cannot do anything till it rallies.
Remember there is a morale and CE number on AFVs which determines pinning/buttoning up or worse a commander killed and also pinning and buttoning up.
Read 28.431 for the rule.
I also don't play with AFVs all that much as they are very powerful.
If you do play with AFVs pick light recon type vehicles.
Ah, my fault, I was mistaking CE for OT.  So it does cause them to button up.  Thank you.

Couple of things - about getting AFVs to button up, one way for infantry to reduce the threat of an AFV is to fire at it with small arms, hoping to get a hit equal to or higher than its Morale value, which forces it to button up.  This is covered by 28.3:

An AFV card has two Armor defense values printed on each side of the card plus a Morale and CE Defense value on the front of the card. The Armor and Flank defense values represent the armored defense strength and is listed on both sides of the card; only attacks using solely boxed firepower or boxed "Effect Numbers" apply to this value. The MORALE and CE values are affected only by unboxed attack values.

This is how mortars can attack AFVs (and they have a small chance of damaging the vehicle as well [26.5]).  AT guns have the choice of firing AP - the process the OP referred to in his second question, which attacks the Armor/Flank values - or HE, which attacks the Morale value as above.  The HE attack is only possible, of course, when the vehicle is CE, or in the case of an OT vehicle if it is not already Pinned (except for one or two really weedy AFVs like the British Bren Carrier, which has a Panic value and can thus be attacked when Pinned).

And moving on to the OPs second question, you were right to feel that there should be a random element is resolving an AP hit - and there is!  25.4 says:

Once a hit has been obtained, the strength of that hit is determined by adding the To Hit Random Number on the RNC just drawn to the Effect Number listed on the ordnance card. (EXC: IG/AFV ordnance firing at an AFV target does not add the To Hit Random Number just drawn; instead it adds a number equal to the Relative Range between the firer and the target.)  The color of the RNC has no effect; all numbers are added. Having now determined the total strength of the attack (after modification for terrain and/or movement), it is resolved separately for each target in the defending group by drawing a new RNC and adding any black number or subtracting any red number drawn as per a normal fire attack [6.5]. 

So the Hit process establishes first whether a hit has been obtained, and secondly how damaging it is: for HE, the RNC on the To Hit card is used (provided a 0 would have hit, reflecting how close the HE round actually landed), and for AP a hit is a hit, but the RR is added to reflect increased penetration at closer ranges.  This gives you the base hit strength; then, in both cases, you draw an RNC for each target.  Firing at an AFV, of course, there is only one target, but you still draw an RNC.

So, a Panther (s7,i8,k9) rumbles up to RR4 to a plucky British 6-pdr (FE 3).  If the AT gun gets a hit, its base Hit Strength will be 3+4=7, and then it hopes the RNC will be at least 0, and preferably a black 2 or better to get a kill.

Don't forget, also, that unlike small arms and HE fire against an AFV, terrain does affect the resolution.  So if the AFV is in Brush, the Hit Strength is reduced by 1.  I suppose this reflects the possibility of the round being deflected or slowed by intervening obstacles.

Hope all that helps!  Oh, and Snipers are good, too.
Thank you; I misunderstood that badly.  I am relieved, though, because this makes much more sense.

Background:  I have been playing Up Front for over 40 years, but I never liked AFV's and so avoided them.  Now I'm trying to use them more, and this has raised some questions that I didn't have to think about before.

Is a stunned, non-OT AFV forced to button up?  I think I had always assumed the answer was "yes", but re-reading the rules yesterday, I wasn't sure.  The clearest rule I can find is 28.45, which says, "A stun result flips any CE AFV card over to its Pinned/Button Up side."

That's your answer.  Yes, a stunned AFV flips over to the CE/Pinned side.

Well, that is ambiguous.  It says it's only referring to CE AFVs, but then it mentions a Buttoned Up side, which a CE AFV does not have.  I think on the whole that I would find it odd that regular AFV's don't button up when stunned when OT AFV's do, but that's not much of a guide to go on.

"CE" means not Buttoned up/pinned.  AH vocabulary is obtuse at times.

I'd like to follow this up with a dumb question about boxed attacks.  I'm pretty sure I understand them, but they seem weird, so I just wanted to verify.  In brief:  when you shoot a boxed effect number against an AFV, you know exactly what's going to happen if you hit.  You simply add your boxed number to your relative range, and compare that to the defending AFV's numbers.  (There are exceptions for rifleman using inherent boxed FP at range 5 and for LATW.)  This feels weird to me because everything else in Up Front is accompanied by massive amounts of randomness, so for a hit's result to be absolutely known (with the possible exception of an immobilization or stun in case they have the same effect number) seems incongruous.  I just want to make sure I'm getting it right.

You forgot you add another RNC (see 25.4) while resolving the attack after determining you got a hit.

The AFV/boxed ordnance rules don't come too frequently as there are no standard scenarios with AFV on AFV action and the only standard scenario with AT guns is the unbalanced, rarely played H.

question: Pretty self-explanatory. I agree it seems a bit odd, as WW2 radios tended to be rather temperamental and the spectacle of a squaddie stumbling along festooned with wires and carrying a battery pack while trying to raise the artillery operator seems ... odd.

Definitely. And remember the radio operator carries it, but it's the SL who's going to be holding the handset. Very hard to imagine it all happening on the move.

And when you look at what is explicitly allowed and disallowed while moving, Radio seems more at home in the latter collection of activities.

title: Rules don't explicitly tell you when you lose Natural Flanking Fire?
question:
I imagine it's as simple as you are no longer in the conditions for it and therefore don't have it.  The 17.4 section only refers to Flanking Fire.  It's specifying that specific rule.  Not the Natural one as far as I can tell.  

FF is lost when the flanking group plays a movement but that would be an odd condition for NFF since it wouldn't necessarily break the conditions needed for NFF.  I guess then can a group currently at NFF play, say, a lateral movement card, thereby not changing range chit, thereby maintaining the conditions for NFF and still enjoy the benefits of double fire power?  Which now has me remembering discussions on do you double first or halve first and if halve first do you still round down before doubling.... 

Wait a minute... upon further inspection... 17.3 (NFF) still speicifcally calls it Flanking Fire.  So the 17.4 losing conditions do apply to NFF?  Removing wire and failing to Ford a stream would make you lose NFF?  But how would one regain NFF as you're still in the exact same conditions to qualify for it?  But... the condition for NFF is moving forward to RR4 (chits 6) from RR5.  That seems to be it.  Moving forward.  So stopping at RR4 (6 on chits) you lose it as you no longer are moving? I know over thinking it but...
author: DiploGuy
consensus_answer:
Flanking is a complicated rule.

Gaining Natural Flanking is a result of moving from RR5 to "RR6" per 17.3.. (I prefer "RR6" to "RR4 but behind the target group".)

Losing any form of Flanking occurs under 17.4X, specifically:
-  Flanking group has a movement or Wire played on it.  (but not Terrain--needed to get doubled FP without 1/2FP for moving.)
-  Flanked group has terrain, even if rejected.
-  Flanked group has a Movement played on it, even temporarily to remove Wire or failed Ford attempt.
-  Front group eliminated or changes ID chit/completes a lateral group "transfer".

Gaining flanking (either naturally or via a Flank card) places a Flank Fire chit.  Losing Flanking removes the Flank Fire chit.  The presence of the ***chit*** determines doubled FP for flanking.

Once, natural flanking is lost  it would be difficult to regain. (retreat to RR5 and advance back to RR6) But, when in a natural Flanking position (i.e. RR6) (whether Flanking was lost or not), that group can Encircle on a later turn (if the Front group is at RR2 to the Flanked group), by playing a sideways Movement cards on the Flanking group.

And always double/halve all FP before rounding down.

title: Keeping Infiltrator status after a CC
question:
I think I understand the infiltration and the CC rules but one sentence has me puzzled under 20.73: "However, if he already has infiltrator status he may keep it to use in any subsequent CC or normal Fire attack against the infiltrated group only if he has defeated his last CC opponent by 3 or more in the resolution of their CC".

The bolded part is mine and is the one that is confusing me. I didn't see a situation where a CC attacker would not be infiltrated?
author: Marcon
consensus_answer:

The bolded part is mine and is the one that is confusing me. I didn't see a situation where a CC attacker would not be infiltrated?

You are correct, the attacker man in CC will be an infiltrator.  As pointed out above, a man in the defending group could be infiltrating the attacking group (or a different attacking group also at RR5), and rule covers those situations.

Keeping infiltration status would not apply to Banzai or Berserk, because in neither case is the man an infiltrator.  (20.91, 45.422)

title: Killed SL
question:
If your SL is killed or panics, you draw one less card "during that game turn". So if my opponent kills it during his turn (which I would expected is the most frequent case), the ASL will take over during my turn and I will not be penalized, right?

I just think it's weird that such a dramatic death does not entail a one-shot penalty.
author: Marcon
consensus_answer:
Unfortunately, I find no definition for Game Turn vs Player Turn, but the implication here is that 1 Game Turn = 2 consecutive Player Turns. Also, as you note, it would be weird if there was no penalty...so inflict the penalty.

4. SEQUENCE OF PLAY
4.1 The game begins with the player specified by the scenario taking his
play first. [In Design Your Own (henceforth referred to as DYO) scenarios
the player having spent less point on the construction of his force gets to
move first with ties resolved by RNC draw.] When he is finished, the
opposing player takes his turn. Player turns are then alternated until one
of the participants achieves his Victory Conditions as required by the
scenario in play or the Time Limit expires.

15.2 Should a player's SL be pinned at the end of his turn, or have just
been removed by a KIA or PANIC result during that game turn, that player
may only draw enough cards to restore the number of cards in his hand
[4.5] to one less than the number he is usually allotted.

P.S. We blew the dust off this recently to have two of us teach two others, and I noticed players (we two "veterans" included) had trouble remembering to short the hand by a card due to 15.2, so I had us park a regular card deck's JOKER under each SL to help us remember. If the SL was "15.2-ed", then that Joker was picked up into the SL-possessor's hand as a reminder that it was causing hand capacity problems. The card would get parked under the ASL if required. An additional bonus was that it also made it easier for the opponent to spot the SL's group, speeding the game up slightly during targetting choices.

That does make thematic sense but why do the rules say "during that game turn"? If my opponent fires on him and kills him, he dies during my opponent's turn and then my own turn starts, no?

As I understand it, the penalty would affect you on "your" turn. So, during the other player's turn, your SL is eliminated. Then, on your turn, you'd draw one less card. After that, things return to normal.

title: Snipers 14.5; We're supposed to "in lieu of discard" all of the cards before resolving any?
question:
14.5 If, in the course of a multi-card discard, two or more Sniper and/or
Minefield attacks are played on the same group resulting in the
elimination of the only target in that group, the discarding player may
alternate his selection of a target group for any discards yet to be
resolved.

The wording sure seems to suggest if, say, you're Russia and you go nuts with 4 "in lieu of discards" and it's 3 Snipers and a minefield you're supposed to pre-designate where each one is going.  If not then what's the point of this rule?  This also makes no sense if you first did the snipers and eliminated the only group that had a movement card on it therefore making your minefield discard ineligible.  So... what's this rule really talking about?
author: DiploGuy
consensus_answer:
14.5 If, in the course of a multi-card discard, two or more Sniper and/or
Minefield attacks are played on the same group resulting in the
elimination of the only target in that group, the discarding player may
alternate his selection of a target group for any discards yet to be
resolved.

The wording sure seems to suggest if, say, you're Russia and you go nuts with 4 "in lieu of discards" and it's 3 Snipers and a minefield you're supposed to pre-designate where each one is going.  If not then what's the point of this rule?  This also makes no sense if you first did the snipers and eliminated the only group that had a movement card on it therefore making your minefield discard ineligible.  So... what's this rule really talking about?

The point of the rule is you have only have the right to retarget a sniper or Minefield if it's target group ends up empty before resolution.  You cannot do that with other active discards (Terrain, Wire)

In a discard that includes wires & 2 snipers, you to predesignate where all three cards go.  Now, let's say you put them same single man group:
-  The wire will go on the group.
-  If the first sniper eliminates the group, you can retarget the 2nd sniper and the Wire (and any terrain or movement cards) will be sent to the discard pile.
-  If the second sniper eliminates the group, the Wire and any terrain or movement will go to the discard pile.

This rule prevents per errata (see 7.3 & 7.32) for example resolving a Sniper and NOW that a man is pinned, putting the Wire on that group.  Or the Sniper NOW eliminated the group, you could NOW send the Wire to a different group.

When you're discarding 4 cards, select the group(s) for your discards. This may be any number from 1 to 4 groups. The terrain will go on the group. The snipers will then fire.

If you happen to put both snipers on the same group, and the group is eliminated with the first sniper (discarding any terrain attached previously or just now), the second sniper (which has not yet fired) may then be moved to another group. title: 41.4 and Flanking Fire...how?
question:
We have only played two sessions using the Team  Play rules in section 41: both were 4 player affairs.

We remain unsure of how you can actually establish 41.4's permitted Flanking Fire between games.  
41.4 Fire between groups of different games is always conducted at
Relative Range 0 regardless of the range chits in play for the respective
groups. Overrun and infiltration are not allowed between forces of
different games. Sniper attacks and Flanking Fire are allowed between
forces of different games.

We are having trouble getting this to match up with the Letter ID requirements for 17.2:
17.2 A group can flank only an adjacent group whose ID letter directly
precedes or follows its own ID letter in the alphabet. [rest snipped]

The solution we come up with for a 4-player game is that you should extend things to consider these two pairs to be eligible for Flanking Fire:
[for this example, Left & Right are from the Axis perspective, which setup first in both games we played; this also ignores any Group E/Z stuff happening via reinforcements/inter-game transfers.]
Axis Group D (Left) is considered to "directly precede" Allied Group A (Right);
Allied Group A (Right) is considered to "directly follow" Axis Group D (Left).

Axis Group A (Right) is considered to "directly follow" Allied Group D (Left);
Allied Group D (Left) is considered to "directly precede" Axis Group D (Right).

We also presume that the flanked group still needs a group directly opposite it. 

How have others been playing it?
author: WBRP
consensus_answer:
That also seems like a possibility, although less fun from the perspective of inter-game interaction. 

The main problem I have with it is that the Group on the LOS Divider seems to immediately switch to the receiving player's fire control via 41.57, so this seems more like vanilla Flanking Fire within a single game instead of 41.4's Flanking Fire "between forces of different games." Also, I know what you are driving at with the "RR6", but I don't think Natural Flanking Fire may be established this way due to the wording in 17.3 referring to "forward" movement from Relative Range 5 to 4, and (i) the Group is always at Relative Range 0 before it is sent to the LOS Divider (and the entire time it is thereon), and (ii) 41.54 specifies that it must Retreat the turn before transferring. Note that, as far as I can tell, there is no Range Chit associated with the Group E(Z) while it is on the LOS Divider; it is in un-chitted RR0 limbo.

title: Does ordnance get any advantage from flanking fire?
question: ATR's mention that they are unusual in that they benefit from an improved to hit chance when they have flanking fire.  And, of course, fire vs. armour has a benefit when it is flanking.  What I haven't been able to find is whether regular ordnance (mortars, IG's, or tank main armament) gets any advantage from being in a flanking position vs. infantry.  Maybe I'm just overlooking it.  Implicitly, one might assume that its effect number number is doubled; or it might have no effect at all since nothing is specified.  I wass wondering if anyone could point to something in the rules that says definitively what should happen.
author: dcroxton
consensus_answer:
Yes, the errata clarifies mortars have no advantage when Flanking infantry targets.  (Actually, also the same vs. CE AFV targets.)

And AFV must use FLANK defense when they tagetted by AT ordnance fire by a Flanking group or if a sideways movement cards is in play on the AFV or is BOGGED or IMMOBILIZED (28.46) (Exception:  ATR provides it's TH# by +1 when flanking.  This is in addition to using the FLANK defense values.)

title: Clarification on split action cards and nationality markings
question:
Re-reading the rules, I noticed something that I think I "learned" incorrectly years ago, when there's two possible actions on a split action card.  The image serves to illustrate my question.   

Q:   Do nationality markings refer to everything on that side of the card?    In particular, when nationality markings are along the side of the card where it says Radio.  

The card on the left I had long interpreted to mean any nation could use it as a Rally card, but only the American or Russian player could use it for the Radio.  But re-reading the rules, now I think that only the American or Russian can use the card at all, for either Rally or Radio. 

The middle card same thing, the Russian can use Concealment, and the American or German can use it for Rally or Radio.

The right-hand card is easiest to understand, it's a Cower card for the Americans and a Rally card for the Germans or Russians.
author: Jobu88
consensus_answer:
If the card is a Split Action card with RADIO, then only the nationalities indicated on that side can use the card as RADIO or RALLY (because all RADIO cards are paired with rallies).

If the card is NOT  a split action card, but has nationality indicators next to RADIO, any nationality can use the card to Rally, but only the indicated nationalities can use the RADIO.

Also of course, Japanese use Russian Split Action, French use German and British use either German or American except for a RADIO which must be both German AND American.  Italian use no Split Actions (unless elite).

title: Flanking Fire and weapon malfunction
question:
This came up during a game tonight:  A group with a Flanking Fire bonus conducts an attack and the LMG malfunctions.   His firepower at the current relative range is 5.  But thanks to flanking fire he is contributing 10 firepower factors.   A malfunction decreases the attack by 1 for each 2 firepower factors or fraction thereof that the malfunctioned weapon was providing. 

Q:   In this case, is the attack reduced by 3 when the LMG malfunctions ( since the LMG has 5 FP at current range)  or is it reduced by 5 (since the LMG was doubled to 10 firepower for flanking fire?) .
author: Jobu88
consensus_answer:
I would say correct.  Although the rules and errata don't specifically say "(un)modified fp", I have to assume all modifications apply.  

It also does not matter if the weapon was *needed* to power the Fire card, the full penalty applies In the example in OP:  Group that is flanking has its LMG (provinding 10 FP) malfunctions, 5 Fire Strength will be lost, even if the Fire card was a 1 (1) and there were other rifles in the group which could power the card.

Also in all cases, each weapon is modified individually (including rounding down), so 5 moving men wirh bolt action rifles (with nominal 1 FP) would have total of 0 FP, because each rifle would be halved and then rounded down to 0 FP before adding the five of them up.

title: Does a group directly opposite to a Banzai declaration, that decreases its range chit, permit Banzai cancellation?
question:
Hello everyone,

Given this section of rule 45.43:
"The Japanese player has the option to cancel a 
Banzai attack only if the target group retreats or moves laterally out of range (i.e. the target group is no 
longer directly opposite or adjacent), "

Situation: A group declares Banzai on a directly opposite group at RR 1. The target group of the Banzai retrograde moves and decreases its range chit from 1 to 0.
Does the Banzai group have the option to cancel the Banzai? 

I am not sure if the "out of range" and parenthetical section applies to both parts of the "or"

Thanks,

John
author: Suulthanaur
consensus_answer:
No.  Simply retreating does not allow the Japanese to cancel Banzai.  But retreating (or moving laterally or having another group moving) to a positon where Banzai could not have been declared.  The "out of range" wording is really terrible.

Moving laterally is easy to explain.  Japanese Group A declares Banzai on American Group B.  Then the targetted American Group moves laterally moves to C--then the targeted group is now "out of range" (i.e. no longer directly opposite or adjacent.) so now the Japanese could cancel the Banzai.

As for retreating causing a Banzai group to be no longer eligible to be Banzaied, you have to check the errata.
Per the errata, 45.4 should have inserted after the third sentence, "However, Banzai may not be declared against an enemy group that is blocked at the time Banzai is declared."  
 It gives an example (modified slightly to make better example for this question).

AM:  A(3)  B(2)
JP:  A(0)  B(0)
The Japanese player cannot have Group A declare Banzai against American Group B, because direct movement of Japan A to American B to RR5 is not possible since it is blocked by American A.

What happens if a targetted group retreats into a blocked position, like this:

AM:  A(3)  B(3)
JP:  A(0)  B(0)

Japan A declares Banzai on American B, then Anerican B retreats to RC 2 and is now in a blocked position (like above).  Now, the Japanese Group A can cancel the Banzai, because now Banzaiing Japan group A is blocked from targetted American Group B by American Group A.

What happens if American A moves forward to RC4 after Japan A declared Banzai on American B in this position.  The same thing!  Banzai Japan A is blocked from tragetted American B by American A.

The sentence from Rule 45.43 quoted in the original question is incomplete.  In full it reads:
The Japanese player has the option to cancel a Banzai attack only if the target group retreats or moves laterally out of range (i.e. the target group is no longer directly opposite or adjacent),  or if another enemy moves in such a way as to block the access of the Banzai group to the declared target.

The missing text covers this third situation.

The Japanese are allowed to cancel a Banzai only if a position arises where it would not be legal to declare it.  This also prevents a Banzaiing group from attacking a different enemy group than the one it is targetting (which never mentioned in the rules or errata--given the blocking rules, obviously is not allowed.)

Hope this helps.

title: Scenario I: Partisans - Victory Conditions
question:
Here's an oddity.  I was playing Bruce Wigdor's UF program and the Germans had a small lead in VP.  They  had a 5-man group at R4 and played a forward Move.  The program instantly gave them the win - somewhat to my surprise.  I then checked the victory conditions, and sure enough it said "The German (Axis) player wins automatically if at least half of his force reaches range chit 5 and he has more Victory Points than the Partisan."  So far so good - the German doesn't have to be in cover for the win.

But here's the thing.  Rule 16.422 says "A unit in the act of movement cannot fulfill Victory Conditions."  In the many scenarios where you have to get x men into cover at range n, this means you can't have them in cover at range n-1, play a forward move, and claim the win immediately - you have to play a Terrain card at range n (and of course avoid being pinned or infiltrated).  But in the situation I described he is fulfilling the victory conditions - with a group in the act of movement.  On the face of it he should have to play a Terrain card (even Open Terrain) to take them out of Movement status.  Thoughts?
author: Barbarossa
consensus_answer:
So on that interpretation, when it says "A unit in the act of movement cannot fulfill Victory Conditions," it's referring to those Victory Conditions mentioned in 16.4:

Some scenarios require as part of their Victory Conditions that a certain number of unpinned men must reach a certain range chit or Relative Range position and occupy terrain "which will reduce the Fire Strength of an attack against them". 

and not Victory Conditions in general.  One could also observe that the neighbouring rules (16.421 and 16.423) cover Smoke and Gullies, which are only relevant for their terrain effects.  So yes, that suggestion certainly makes sense.

replies.body:

That rule seems to be preoccupied with explaining how one fulfills reaching a given range chit and occupying terrain that reduces fire strength against the group.  Note that the rule acknowledges that this applies to "some" scenarios.  So I would take 16.422 as limiting men that are moving within terrain that reduces the fire strength against them (and that are at the required range chit) from fulfilling the VP requirements.

For Scenario I, it explains the conditions for scoring VPs and doesn't restrict that to just non-moving men.

title: Can terrain be discarded on a Lateral Group Transfer?
question: Can terrain be discarded on a Lateral Group Transfer?
author: HuntedCity
consensus_answer:
Ok. So say it's just one man doing a lateral group transfer leaving a group that is in a building for a group in another building. My opponent drops a stream on my guy. Is he now alone in the stream? Does he become his own group? Is the group that he left now in a stream as well? What's going on here?

You seem to be confusing Lateral Group Transfer with Individual Transfer.  The rules are unnecessarily confusing with calling both very different actions "transfers".

Lateral Group Transfer (17.7) = lateral movement of a group from Group B to Group C (for example).  (This should be called "Lateral Movement".)  This is initiated by playing a Movement card in sideways mode while declaring the Lateral Movement.  (I generally put the new group marker on the movement card).  Prerequisite:  there can be no group ID in the location that you are going to (unless you are switching positions of two groups--which I won't get into here.)  On a later turn, the Transf...I mean Lateral Movement is completed by playing terrain on the group (The Group ID applies only now.)  The Lateral Movement is cancelled if terrain discarded by opponent is rejected or if open ground played under Wire that was played on the Laterally Moving group (as either would remove sideways Movement card.)

Individual Transfer (17.8) is transferring Individual men between groups.  First, the groups must be adjacent and at the same range chit and one or both groups must have an unpinned leader.  Then, one Movement card is played for each transferring man (more than one man can transfer.) and a Transfer chit on the man.  Transfer is completed when the receiving group uses an action to accept the transferring men (which can be placed in any position in their new group).  While transferring, they are "first men" resolved if either group is fired at, do not get any entrenchment TEM and an additional +2 TEM.  If a transferring man is pinned, its Transfer is cancelled and is returned to the sending group.  (During normal individual transfer, terrain cannot be discarded on the transferring man/men.  Both originating/destination groups will have terrain/OG in any  case.)

Group Creation (17.9) done by using Individual Transfer rules:
-  Group ID they are transferring to must be vacant.
-  Two or more men must be transferred at the same time to initiate Group Creation. 
-  If any of these men are pinned in the act of transferring, all transferring men are returned to their original group and Group Creation is cancelled.
-  Completed by playing a terrain card on the new group.  (Errata) If an opponent discards terrain on the new group, it can be accepted (thus completing Group Creation) or rejected.  If rejected, the transfer is cancelled and men returned to original group.

I VERY RARELY attempt group creation.

Hope this helps.

title: AFV overrun and encirclement......
question:
Just in the middle of playing scenario F , Infantry's Iron Fist.
I have the Soviet T 60 in group C opposite 4 German Infantry in Group C. The T 60 got to RR5 and has done an overrun. Afterwards I played a forward movement card and went through group C to RR4 behind it. Is German group C encircled? There is a Soviet group B.
I understand how the regular infantry encirclement works.
However since the AFV can actually go through an opposite group, unlike infantry, what is the purpose of the AFV going through?
author: petersolo1
consensus_answer:
No.  It is not encircled, which per 17.6 requires having a directly opposing group in front of the encircled group no further than RR2 (see 17.613)

Now, AH did not write the rules to cover situations where opposing groups with same ID actually get behind each other, as it so rarely happens (except in Scenario X, Surrounded, which has a special rule covering encirclements--have to be encircled from the same "force".)  So, now that the AFV has passed the target group, that encirclement probably could be obtained by moving the adjacent group at RR4 sideways, since it would fit the regular rules for encirclement in reverse.  (But that way lies madness!)

As for why advance through the enemy after an overrun?  You are not required to, but you might do it to get into position for victory points/conditions.  I'd be more likely to stay at RR5 and fire or overrun again until the enemy group is eliminated.

title: Why is one side of the setup a "hard wall" and other side not?
question:
Player 1 sets up groups A and B. Player 2 can create a group C (to the right of B), but nothing to the left of A. Seems a little arbitrary to allow player 1 to game the "edge of the map".

Or is my understanding incorrect?
author: ekted
consensus_answer: I think you would just get a bunch of degenerate cases without it. Germans set up A & B, then Soviets go A, Z, X, Y, and the game is just kind of odd. You want the squads to actually square up against each other, that’s the basic conceit of the game, so this is the easiest way to do it. I can imagine a set of complicated rules where the larger squad could offset slightly in various ways, but I just don’t think it buys you anything. In practice you can still do what you want do. If the Soviets set up as four groups the Germans will probably have to do lateral moves to cover the whole front and it gives you the same effect as if you had allowed a more free-ranging setup.

title: Malfed LMG breaks upon repair attempt. Is assistant freed from crew without an action for the group?
question:
Normally, an assistant crewman wanting to lose crew status takes the sole action for his group for the turn to accomplish that.

However, it seems clear to me that no action is needed if the principal crewman (the one with the LMG on his card) breaks the LMG while attempting to repair it. 

Rule 11.13 says "Once a man is designated as crew, he remains crew until he (or the weapon; 18.1)  is eliminated, attempts to infiltrate, or is designated as non-crew during his turn as the sole action of that group for the turn." (those italics are in the rulebook). Since the weapon was broken, I believe the crew counter comes off instantly - no action on a later turn required.

This happened to my opponent today. While he thought maybe an action was needed to remove the crew counter, I was sure that it did not require an action (and the wasted turn for that group). We played it my way, but he asked me to post the question here, so he can be sure. 

How do you play it?
author: gdnuke
consensus_answer: Is the weapon eliminated, or basically removed from play? I would think a broken weapon that is not repairable fits that definition no? Sometimes I find the Up Front rules just want to be read as is without over thinking them and when I read them that way they make more sense to me.

replies.body: Is the weapon eliminated, or basically removed from play? I would think a broken weapon that is not repairable fits that definition no? Sometimes I find the Up Front rules just want to be read as is without over thinking them and when I read them that way they make more sense to me.

You are correct.  The parenthetical clause covers it.

title: Wounded rules
question:
I thought i knew this game but maybe i do not. 
So If an attack gets the exact number equal to KIA value of an unpinned personality card (lets say an eight), then that card is not KIA is the wound column is equal to printed morale value. 
But also lets say you have a pinned card and attack it is equal to greater than the panic number so you check the rout number and the rnc rout column says it routs  instead fo panic but also the wound column matches the morale, that card does not panic, does not route but instead is wounded. Is that right?
author: vslimm
consensus_answer:
I thought i knew this game but maybe i do not. 

Don't worry.  Up Front has some of the worst rules ever.  It is still my favorite wargame.

So If an attack gets the exact number equal to KIA value of an unpinned personality card (lets say an eight), then that card is not KIA is the wound column is equal to printed morale value. 

If the final fire resolution number (i.e. including the RNC for the man) exactly equals the KIA # then you check RPC7w and if RPC7w equals the morale value of the man, the man will be wounded instead of KIA.  This happens whether the target man was pinned or not and he will retain his (un)pinned status.

But also lets say you have a pinned card and attack it is equal to greater than the panic number so you check the rout number and the rnc rout column says it routs  instead fo panic but also the wound column matches the morale, that card does not panic, does not route but instead is wounded. Is that right?

Not quite.  Rule 33.1 Wounds states that wounds "may possibly occur anytime an infantryman **routs** or otherwise be eliminated by a KIA result as a result of an RNC generating a final attack strength exactly equal to the lowest number required for KIA."  This would require a wound check on RPC7 when the pinned man routs as well.

To summarize:
On a pinned man:
- if the Fire Resolution number (FRN) > KIA, the man is dead.  No wound check is made.
-  if the FRN = KIA (usually 9), check for wound
-  if FRN < KIA but >= PANIC, first check RPC0r determine ROUT/KIA.

-  if RPC0r > Rout #, the man likely routs, but check for wound first.
- if RPC0r <= Rout #, the man is KIA. No wound check.

Note, this very rule came up at this year's WBC tournament.  So even experts screw up these rules.

replies.body:
So looking at the rules, I think I’ve been playing this incorrectly too! The example after 13.1 seems to pretty clearly spell out all the cases. If the personality card is unpinned and the result is exactly 8 (or 7 for a flamethrower), or of it’s pinned and the result is greater than or equal to the panic but less than or equal to 9, you check for wound. The rout result doesn’t have to result in a KIA - it just has to be triggered.

These days I actually don’t use the wound rules very often, they’re pretty deep in the programmed instructions and I find them fiddly for a low payoff, but if I started using them again that would definitely result in more wounds than the way I’ve always played (only if the final result is KIA on rout do you check for wound) which might make them more interesting.

title: Double Unbalanced Position?
question:
15.6 UNBALANCED POSITION: 
Should a player be reduced to one group, the opposing player at the end of his own turn may draw one additional card beyond that which he would otherwise be entitled to during each turn in which this condition persists.

As this rule is written, if both players are reduced to one group, then both  players may draw an additional card.

My thematic understanding of this (based on the name of the rule), is that the bonus card draw is intended to represent the advantage of outnumbering the opponent in groups.  Once this is equalized (i.e. both players down to one group), the situation is no longer "unbalanced" and therefore neither player should be entitled to an extra card. 
 However, the rule itself does not support this reading.  Thoughts?
author: R0B0T0
consensus_answer:
A)  It is very rare for this to happen without a broken squad on one side or the other.

B)  Rules as written would indicate both groups would receive an extra card.

C)  I see your point the because the apparent reason for the extra card is the side with multiple groups being able to outflank the solo opposing group easily.  Two opposing solo groups would not both gain such an advantage over each other.  And it could have been fixed by adding a simple clause:  "...so long as the condition persists or until both sides are reduced to one group."

(This brings up an interesting point:  Scenario J is designed to be played with 3 players.  Do both opponents get an extra card when a side is reduced to a single group?  Or does a player only get the extra card when ipponents are reduced to one group?  What if two are down to single group....does the remaining side receive two extra cards?  No, I don't want anyone to try to answer this.  There are good reasons no one plays this scenario.)

This isn't the only (or most egregious) time AH forgot an important detail in UF rules:

16.5. BROKEN SQUAD  a scenario ends when a player has lost more than half of their personality cards due to KIA and/or rout.  Reinforcements are not considered part of the force until they enter play."

Notice something missing....   like who won or lost!  (The immediately following example does state the player who suffers a broken squad loses.  But still.)

The rules should not include this provision.  Given the rules set as written, it would be a very extreme edge case where both players are reduced to one group and neither side has suffered a broken squad.  Rules (not just Up Front) shouldn't need to address extreme outliers.

However, given the situation postulated, both sides should benefit from the additional card.  Both sides are in a position to exploit the same vulnerability of their opponent, hence the extra card.  That vulnerability doesn't go away just because the opponent winds up in the same condition.
Whatever the ruling would be, it sounds like it would be an awesomely memorable play.

title: Looking for confirmation that cancelling a fire attack means no "fired last turn" modifier for observation attempt at night?
question:
Playing a night scenario. A fire attack card is played by German Group B for example. After the Russian plays a concealed card (or even if he doesn't, say if the German is moving a card through his hand) the German cancels the attack. I assume the attack is considered to have never happened, and the Russian does not get the +1 modifier to any observation attempt on German group B for it having "fired last turn" (38.3 bullet 4). 

Seems right and in accordance with the errata 38.3, which states that the observation modifier (38.3 bullet 3) for a group having undergone a previous fire attack from another group in the same turn will not be granted if that fire attack was cancelled. The errata basically says "cancelled means it never happened, except that the group did use its action for the turn."

question:
I've been pouring over the original rules, rewritten rules, summarized rules, and errata'd rules. But I swear I've see this ruling that I just can't find right now.
Many scenarios require a player to have a certain number of unpinned personality cards in, in specific range chits, in terrain that will reduce the fire strength of attacks made against them. But I swear I read that the group must not have a movement card over the terrain. Am I wrong in that?
So for instance in scenario A - if a group is in a Woods terrain, with their range chit at 3, and play a movement card to flip the chit to 4. Will that player win?
author: Townsie
consensus_answer:
16.422 A unit in the act of movement cannot fulfill victory conditions.

And as a consequence, if you are playing a scenario that depends on VPs (eg Scenario A) and have men in Terrain at a negative range chit, towards the end of the last deck play a Movement card to avoid the negative VPs!  (And play it Forward or Backward (if possible) in case your opponent drops a Marsh on you.)

title: Weapon Malfunction 19.11
question:
I've just recently started playing Up Front as a solitaire game. And I realize that weapon malfunction is probably the most contentious rules section. I've looked through the errata and some of the other posts here on this forum, but there's still a case that came up in my play session that I havn't been able to figure out.

19.11 says "If the firing group contains only one firing weapon with usable firepower factors, and a red RNC is drawn to resolve its attack that weapon automatically malfunctions..."

So, question no. 1: If I have a German group containing only a single personality card:  #4 with a Bolt-Action rifle. If this group fires and the RNC is a red 2, will Pvt. Schumacher's Mauser malfunction automatically?

Question no. 2: If this group instead was a German group consisting of two personality cards: #1 with a Machine Pistol which is assisting crew to #3 with an LMG. And the RNC is a red 2, will the Pfc. Schüssel's MG 34 automatically malfunction?
author: Townsie
consensus_answer:
I've just recently started playing Up Front as a solitaire game. And I realize that weapon malfunction is probably the most contentious rules section. I've looked through the errata and some of the other posts here on this forum, but there's still a case that came up in my play session that I havn't been able to figure out.

Yes.  Malfunction rules are some of the most confusing in the game.  Pretty much you have to follow the errata exclusively.

This is a legacy from Squad Leader's malfunction rules.  Roll the worst natural number and weapon breaks--but only weapons on separate counters were affected--not every rifle which were intrinsic to each squad counter.

19.11 says "If the firing group contains only one firing weapon with usable firepower factors, and a red RNC is drawn to resolve its attack that weapon automatically malfunctions..."

No, it says "Red 6 RNC", though technically that isn't correct.  It should be "Red RNC drawn that causes a malfunction."  This makes a difference with uncrewed machine guns (and Japanese and Italian LMGs) which have a malfunction number of x5-6.

Basically, that sentence is telling you no RPC is needed to determine which weapon broke--because there's only one.  The next clause of that rule states the attack terminates when this happens and no further men in the target group need be resolved.

So, question no. 1: If I have a German group containing only a single personality card:  #4 with a Bolt-Action rifle. If this group fires and the RNC is a red 2, will Pvt. Schumacher's Mauser malfunction automatically?

No, because the rifle breaks on a Red 6.  If it were Red 6, then the rifle would malfunction and it would end the attack.

Question no. 2: If this group instead was a German group consisting of two personality cards: #1 with a Machine Pistol which is assisting crew to #3 with an LMG. And the RNC is a red 2, will the Pfc. Schüssel's MG 34 automatically malfunction?

How many men are  is in this group?  I count three:
1)  a machine Pistol as a crewman for
2)  an LMG
3)  a rifleman

I am going to assume three men for this explanation.  (All unpinned)  I have my reasons.

If a Red 6 RNC is drawn, all three are considered firing and are subject to malfunction, an RPC(3) is drawn per 19.13 per errata:
-  On a 1, the crewman is affected, no malfunction occurs and the attack continues with -1 to Fire Strength for the remaining men for a momentary belt bobble.
-  On a 2, the LMG is affected.  The weapon malfs and the attack continues with the Fire Strength reduced by 1/2 the firepower (round up) provided by the LMG at this range for the remaining men.
-  On a 3, the rifle is affected.  However, at RR0 it provides no firepower (but it is STILL considered "firing") so the rifle malfunctions and there is no effect on fire strength on the attack.  At any other range, it is providing FP, the rifle Is malfed and the rest of the attack is resolved reducing the FS by 1/2 FP provided by the rifle (round up).

Now let's say the crewman and the rifleman were pinned (Only the LMG is unpinned.  STILL all three are considered "firing").  If a Red 6 RNC is drawn, all three could be affected, but if the RPC(3) chooses a pinned man (either the crewman or rifleman) then the weapon simply breaks with no effect on FS for the rest of the attack, because a pinned man was chosen.  If the LMG were selected, the normal penalties apply.

However, if a Red 5 RNC were drawn, the only weapon that could be affected is the now uncrewed LMG ( see 11.1).  (Uncrewed LMGs malf on x5-6.  The MP and rifle malf on x6.) In this case, no RPC is required and the LMG automatically breaks with the normal penalties.

Yes, it confusing.  Stick to the errata on all malfunction rules.

title: I don't understand the phrase "Remove the first x terrain cards to be discarded unused or as a RPC/RNC draw."
question:
Each scenario that I've seen include a phrase like this: "Remove the first four Woods to be discarded unused or as a RPC/RNC draw."
I can understand that in the city fight scenario - you'd expect less action among woods. But I'm not sure how to interpret this.
The way I've played it is that whenever a player discards a Woods card at the end of their round, we remove the card from the discard pile and we don't shuffle it into the action deck the next time we run out of cards. And whenever we see a Woods card as an RPC/RNC draw, we also put those cards aside.
But we can discard terrain cards to our opponents' groups, or we can play them to our own groups as regular. Is that the correct way of playing it?

As a followup, if I have a Woods terrain on my group, with a movement card on top of it. If I play, say, a Buildings and the Woods get put into the discard pile - does the card get removed from the deck? It's not strictly "discarded unused" is it?
author: Townsie
consensus_answer:
The way I've played it is that whenever a player discards a Woods card at the end of their round, we remove the card from the discard pile and we don't shuffle it into the action deck the next time we run out of cards. And whenever we see a Woods card as an RPC/RNC draw, we also put those cards aside.This is correct
But we can discard terrain cards to our opponents' groups, or we can play them to our own groups as regular. Is that the correct way of playing it?These cards are considered Cower cards [2.22] until the required number of this type of cards have been removed. The only way to playing them is face down as an Open Ground card. Once the required number type of cards have been retired of the game (by RNC/RPC or by discard), the remaining ones can be played normally. 
So following your example, until the four woods cards have been retired/set apart from the game no one can play a Wood card. Look at 16.1 and the example on it :geek_smile:

The only way to playing them is face down as an Open Ground card. Once the required number type of cards have been retired of the game (by RNC/RPC or by discard), the remaining ones can be played normally. 
So following your example, until the four woods cards have been retired/set apart from the game no one can play a Wood card. Look at 16.1 and the example on it :geek_smile:

Whenever a scenario says that a number of specified terrain cards are to be removed from play:
-  Anytime the specified card is drawn as an RPC/RNC, you do not place it the discard pile.  Lay it aside face up.
-  All specified cards are treated as Cower cards and cannot played as terrain (except as Open Ground) on either your or opposing groups. When such a card is discarded, again do not place it in the discard pile, reveal it and  lay it aside  face up.  (Mistakes are sometimes made, but usually the required number will be laid aside by the end of the first deck.  However, cards played as Open Ground remain hidden when they are discarded when their groups move to new terrain, so it is possible that a specified terrain card could legally be in  the discard pile.)
-  Once the specified number of terrain have been laid aside, any remaining terrain cards of that type are now valid and can be like any other terrain card and will be placed in  the discard pile normally for the rest of the game.  The cards previously laid aside remain out of play.

Some terrain cards are specified as Cower cards (particularly Pillbox and Minefield).  These cards are not removed from play when discarded.

As to your final question, it simply can't happen.

And the whole point is to model terrain:  City scenarios remove Woods, Rural scenarios remove Buildings, etc.  Most Jungle scenarios remove no cards (but there is no reason it couldn't be done--say setting aside Marsh to represent a relatively dense forest in Europe.)
Great answers, both of you. That they count as cower cards kind of made it all click for me - I didn't notice this clearly in the rules.

title: Relative Range.
question:
I don't get this.
If a group is at rage 5 (the closest), and the opposite group is at 5 (the closest), the chart at 5.6  says they are now at range 0-the greatest distance . Is this some disturbance in space/time? Furthermore...why do two opposite groups have different range chits at all? If the German group is at range 5 to the US group, isn't the US group at range 5 to the Ger group as well?
author: fortyfiverevolutions
consensus_answer:
I don't get this.
If a group is at rage 5 (the closest), and the opposite group is at 5 (the closest), the chart at 5.6  says they are now at range 0-the greatest distance . Is this some disturbance in space/time? Furthermore...why do two opposite groups have different range chits at all? If the German group is at range 5 to the US group, isn't the US group at range 5 to the Ger group as well?

I'm sure the professionals will also chime in, but I'll take a stab.

First, welcome to the wonderful rulebook that is Up Front.   Confusion when reading isn't unusual, so don't worry.

Trying to do this graphically:

When you set up Scenario A

AX RC   0   1   2   3   4   5
--------- G

AL RC    5   4   3   2   1   0
---------------------- G

The opposing groups are both at Range Chit 0.   The "distance" between them is 5, and to calculate relative range it's 5-5 = 0.

Now to the question posed

AX RC   0   1   2   3   4   5
----------------------- G

AL RC    5   4   3   2   1   0
--------- G

Both the Allied and Axis groups have moved 5 positions forward.  The distance between them again is 5, so the relative range is 5-5 = 0.

If only one group moved 5 positions forward, 

AX RC   0   1   2   3   4   5
--------- G

AL RC    5   4   3   2   1   0
--------- G

Then you wind up with Relative Range 5.  There are many combinations, and although the math is convoluted, it does work.

(I had to edit my original post as it did not like leading blanks on each line showing where a group "G" is located)

Hope that helps.

The important distinction to make is between ‘range’ and ‘relative range’. It is a ‘distance ‘ of 5 between your start line and your opponents start line. So if you move 5 forward and your opponent moves 5 forward, you have moved past each other and are now 5 apart. This is a good graphical representation of the ‘map’:
https://boardgamegeek.com/filepage/109374/range-board

So what helped me make sense of Range Chits and Relative Range was to think about Range Chits as ‘displacement’ - an indication of how far your group is from where they started (higher range chit = further distance from base); and Relative Range as a measure of ‘proximity’ to another group (high number = greater proximity).

Then there’s the idea that there are only five shared steps of range available to occupy between two groups with the same ID.

So if they both have a Range Chit of 0, my Group A and your Group A are at a Relative Range of 0. They share five ‘steps’ of space in front of them to advance into.
If my Group A is at Range Chit 2 and yours is a Range Chit 2, well then between us we’ve used up 4 of those 5 ‘chunks of space’ - we’re now at Relative Range 4. We’ve both displaced only a little way from our starting point but the proximity to each other is already getting pretty high.
If either group advances to Range Chit 3, we’ll be at Relative Range 5 to each other and nose-to-nose. No more advancing allowed because we’re each blocking the other’s way forward.

In your example of two groups with Range Chits of 5 …
1) If they both have the same group ID, there’s no way to have got into that position by simply advancing toward each other (there are other, fancy ways to end up there but we’re not talking about that at the moment); and
2) If they have different group IDs, then this would mean they have both advanced five range-steps forwards, unopposed, so have basically both reached the point where the other group started from .. so they’re back at Relative Range 0 to each other.

"Both the Allied and Axis groups have moved 5 positions forward. The distance between them again is 5, so the relative range is 5-5 = 0."
