title: Panic, rout and weapon acquistion
question:
I have two pinned germans, one armed with a rifle and one an LMG, each with a panic of 4 and rout >4.  Wouldn't you know it, they both draw an RNC of 5 with a 0r of 7, and they rout over to my opponent (which is ok, cause he is me.)

What happens to their weapons and who can acquire them?

(even after a few reads, i am not understanding panic vs rout, i keep confusing which is worse and their consequences.)

Thanks for the help.

EDIT: Victory points too.
author: scott_67
consensus_answer: 18.1 Weapon Loss - Rifle guy routs away with his weapon. Principal operator of the LMG leaves it behind. LMG can be acquired automatically by unpinned assistant crewman, as the group’s sole action (18.22). If he is gone, then follow 18.2.

replies.body: 18.1 Weapon Loss - Rifle guy routs away with his weapon. Principal operator of the LMG leaves it behind. LMG can be acquired automatically by unpinned assistant crewman, as the group’s sole action (18.22). If he is gone, then follow 18.2.

I have two pinned germans, one armed with a rifle and one an LMG, each with a panic of 4 and rout >4.  Wouldn't you know it, they both draw an RNC of 5 with a 0r of 7, and they rout over to my opponent (which is ok, cause he is me.)

What happens to their weapons and who can acquire them?

Correct, both men routed.  They each take their weapon with them (which the weapons cannot be acquired), with one major exception, if the man is the principle operator of a crew served weapon,the weapon remains for acquisition.

Men that are killed (Either Panic with Or=KIA),leave their weapon behind on the terrain card so they can be picked up (except in Marsh or Stream).  These weapons can be picked up by any man in the group as sole action for the group by drawing a Black RNC. (Exception: an assistant crewman automatically picks up his abandoned crewed weapon (no RNC required), but it still costs an action))

Note:  All dropped weapons are removed if a Movement or terrain card is played on the group (even if rejected or to remove wire). Movement cards played on an individual man (for transfer and avoiding a morale check) do not remove the dropped weapons. 

(even after a few reads, i am not understanding panic vs rout, i keep confusing which is worse and their consequences.)

"Panic" is when the result of the fire attack is greater or equal to than the a pinned man's Panic value, but less than his KIA value.   Then you check for ROUT vs. KIA using RPC0r (and wound if the man routs.)  

EDIT: Victory points too.

Casualty victory points are:
-  1VP for each opponent's man routed or wounded
-  2VP for each opponent's man killed or commander/crew KIA on AFV or infantry gun.
-  5VP for each prisoner held at the end of the game (But 0 if they escape)
-  6 VP for a killed infantry gun
-  10VP + anti armor (boxed) attack strength for a destroyed AFV.

Positional VP: Each unpinned man/infantry gun/(mobile) AFV in non-moving groups is worth VP equal their current range chit (Yes, groups that retreat score negative points.  Note the group does NOT have to be in terrain that has a negative TEM  (Exception: scenarios like City Fight or Jungle Meeting require the group must be in the specified terrain ), just not moving.)

I haven't played for a long time but what does the OP mean by "rout over to my opponent?"

Your opponent holds the removed personality cards (14.6).  So in this lonely solitaire game, they all went into the same pile.

Scott

title: Negative values for Fire power
question:
Hi guys, I have a question for you: 
When I use a Fire card can I have a negative value for Fire streght considering the modifiers?
Ex: 
Fire streght on the card used:2
Building terrain on enemy group: -3
I have -1 or 0?
author: Oblomov1
consensus_answer:
Can be the relative range negative?
Group A 0
Group D 0
RR 0 or -1?

No matter the distance it can't go below 0.  

Two ways to answer this: 
- If 2 groups are very far apart, like A vs. C or D is -1 RR at the start of the game. But in any such case negative RR is treated as RR0.

Range Chits can go <0, but one of the requirements is that the closest enemy group has to be RR1 or closer, so after retrograde movement, the group will not be further than RR0 from the closest enemy group.

title: Question: natural flanking vs. lateral flanking
question:
I finally got a copy of this game and am very excited to give it a try.  I am currently slogging through the rulebook, which has been tough but encouraging - it seems like a great system.

One thing confusing me is the flanking rules.  I know the rule on natural flanking has been clarified a bit in the errata and over on CSW (you can move sideways into a natural flank - you don't actually have to move from RR5 in the column adjacent to the enemy to RR4 behind the enemy in the column adjacent, as long as you end up in RR4 behind the enemy in the adjacent column one way or another).  While that did clear up some confusion, my remaining question is this:

Can one unit only naturally flank another unit from RR4 behind? In other words, if I am in RR4 adjacent and behind an enemy, if they move one range unit away from me, or if I move one range unit further away from them, such that we are now at RR3, do I lose my natural flank?

A strict reading of the rules would suggest so, but common sense tells me I should still be flanking that unit - just with a little less firepower.  

My thinking is that I do lose the flank, but I can regain it by lateral flanking? To do this I would have to have a flank movement card and play it sideways - is this correct?  Or of course I could move back to RR4 and regain the natural flank.

Can anyone confirm this?
Thanks in advance.
author: DougOSU
consensus_answer:
I finally got a copy of this game and am very excited to give it a try.  I am currently slogging through the rulebook, which has been tough but encouraging - it seems like a great system.

One thing confusing me is the flanking rules.  I know the rule on natural flanking has been clarified a bit in the errata and over on CSW (you can move sideways into a natural flank - you don't actually have to move from RR5 in the column adjacent to the enemy to RR4 behind the enemy in the column adjacent, as long as you end up in RR4 behind the enemy in the adjacent column one way or another).  While that did clear up some confusion, my remaining question is this:

First off, call "RR4 adjacent and behind an enemy" as "relative range 6".  for most situation that will be the case.  Much easier to understand.

The word forward is emphasized in Rule 17.3--coming in from any direction other than RR5 is not necessarily justifiable, but I think it is common  (Bruce Wigdor's Internet Up Front program apply the "Flanking is at RR6 from any way" interpretation.).  

But moving to natural flank from any position other than RR5 is EXTREMELY RARE.  I don't know if I have seen it 1000's of games.  Just achieving natural flanking is pretty rare.  It just doesn't come up, the attacking player is not going continue pressing forward after passing an adjacent group and/or isn't go way around in order get a natural flank.

Can one unit only naturally flank another unit from RR4 behind? In other words, if I am in RR4 adjacent and behind an enemy, if they move one range unit away from me, or if I move one range unit further away from them, such that we are now at RR3, do I lose my natural flank?

First, you lose the natural flank (or indeed ANY flank), when either the FLANKED group or FLANKING group has a movement card played on it (even to remove wire), the situation you describe cannot happen.  The Flank Fire chit would already be removed.

Second:  No, you cannot initiate natural flanking from RR7. 

A strict reading of the rules would suggest so, but common sense tells me I should still be flanking that unit - just with a little less firepower. 

No, because you lost flank status when either FLANKED group moved or FLANKING group moved. 

My thinking is that I do lose the flank, but I can regain it by lateral flanking? 

Yes, Lateral Flank using a FLANK movement card can be done from ANY relative range.  (Note, relative range is not mentioned in 17.1 & 17.2)

To do this I would have to have a flank movement card and play it sideways - is this correct?  

Yes, as usual for Lateral Flanking.

Or of course I could move back to RR4 and regain the natural flank.

Yes, but I don't think that will happen.  

Basically to initate flanking you need:
-  a FRONT group (i.e. same letter) as the potential FLANKED opposing group.
And either:
-  An adjacent FLANKING group having a FLANK movement card played on it in sideways mode.  (Lateral Flanking per 17.1)
-  An adjacent FLANKING group reaching RR6  (Natural Flanking per 17.3)

Hope this helps.  Flanking is one of the more confusing rules in the game.

One thing confusing me is the flanking rules.  I know the rule on natural flanking has been clarified a bit in the errata and over on CSW (you can move sideways into a natural flank - you don't actually have to move from RR5 in the column adjacent to the enemy to RR4 behind the enemy in the column adjacent, as long as you end up in RR4 behind the enemy in the adjacent column one way or another).  While that did clear up some confusion, my remaining question is this:

First off, call "RR4 adjacent and behind an enemy" as "relative range 6".  for most situation that will be the case.  Much easier to understand.

The word forward is emphasized in Rule 17.3--coming in from any direction other than RR5 is not necessarily justifiable, but I think it is common  (Bruce Wigdor's Internet Up Front program apply the "Flanking is at RR6 from any way" interpretation.).  

But moving to natural flank from any position other than RR5 is EXTREMELY RARE.  I don't know if I have seen it 1000's of games.  Just achieving natural flanking is pretty rare.  It just doesn't come up, the attacking player is not going continue pressing forward after passing an adjacent group and/or isn't go way around in order get a natural flank.

Can one unit only naturally flank another unit from RR4 behind? In other words, if I am in RR4 adjacent and behind an enemy, if they move one range unit away from me, or if I move one range unit further away from them, such that we are now at RR3, do I lose my natural flank?

First, you lose the natural flank (or indeed ANY flank), when either the FLANKED group or FLANKING group has a movement card played on it (even to remove wire), the situation you describe cannot happen.  The Flank Fire chit would already be removed.

Second:  No, you cannot initiate natural flanking from RR7. 

A strict reading of the rules would suggest so, but common sense tells me I should still be flanking that unit - just with a little less firepower. 

No, because you lost flank status when either FLANKED group moved or FLANKING group moved. 

My thinking is that I do lose the flank, but I can regain it by lateral flanking? 

Yes, Lateral Flank using a FLANK movement card can be done from ANY relative range.  (Note, relative range is not mentioned in 17.1 & 17.2)

To do this I would have to have a flank movement card and play it sideways - is this correct?  

Yes, as usual for Lateral Flanking.

Or of course I could move back to RR4 and regain the natural flank.

Yes, but I don't think that will happen.  

Basically to initate flanking you need:
-  a FRONT group (i.e. same letter) as the potential FLANKED opposing group.
And either:
-  An adjacent FLANKING group having a FLANK movement card played on it in sideways mode.  (Lateral Flanking per 17.1)
-  An adjacent FLANKING group reaching RR6  (Natural Flanking per 17.3)

Hope this helps.  Flanking is one of the more confusing rules in the game.

Thanks Richard! I'm glad I'm not the only one who finds it confusing...

Your thorough point-by-point answer is much appreciated.

title: Scenario K VCs
question:
I suppose squad break is in effect. Does it have to be achieved twice by Elite force to win (once per scenario segment)?

Thanks in advance.
author: Andrei Shlepov
consensus_answer:
I suppose squad break is in effect. Does it have to be achieved twice by Elite force to win (once per scenario segment)?

Yes, squad break is in effect.  

Winning a scenario segment can be achieved by victory conditions (4 men in one more non-infiltrated groups.....) or breaking the opposing squad.

Once the attacker (i.e. elite squad) completes either VC's or squad break, the game is reset as described in the scenario rules (Attacker forfeiting all men that were KIA'd, Defender receiving all men back. etc.) and the game continues.  The attacker has to complete VC's or opposing squad break a second time to win the scenario.

The defender (i.e. 2nd line squad) need achieve VC's or opposing squad break once to earn the victory.

However, (per published errata) Victory Points are not counted at the end of the final deck.  So, the Defender/2nd line squad will win by avoiding attacker victory conditions.

title: Movement cards over Smoke
question:
The rules say a Smoke card is removed when two Movement cards remain over it at the end of the turn. Do those Movement cards have to be played in uninterrupted succession for a Smoke card to be removed?

To illustrate the question: Smoke - Movement - Smoke - Movement. Is the first Smoke removed?
author: Andrei Shlepov
consensus_answer:
The rules say a Smoke card is removed when two Movement cards remain over it at the end of the turn. Do those Movement cards have to be played in uninterrupted succession for a Smoke card to be removed?

No

To illustrate the question: Smoke - Movement - Smoke - Movement. Is the first Smoke removed?

Correct.  However, the terrain card covered by 2 Movement cards remains in play, though the terrain is NOT counted if covered by 2 movement cards.  So the smoke which MODIFIES the terrain or virtual open ground (i.e. at the start of the game), would have no effect anyway.  So all this rule does is force discarding a card now that would not have an effect anyway even if left in play (unless forced back in multiple terrain rejections (rare) or puts only the Smoke card in the next deck if there is a reshuffle (minimal effect).)

title: Where's the rule that says transferring guy can be placed into any position within the group?
question:
The index doesn't list Transfer so I don't know where to look.  I'm pretty sure a guy transferring into a group can be put into any position.  I even think at that time you can totally rearrange the group order if you wanted to.

Also if the crew position is open can a transferring guy jump right into the crew position with no extra actions needed?
author: DiploGuy
consensus_answer:
The index doesn't list Transfer so I don't know where to look.

The rule that specified this was in the errata originally fromthe General:

17.8 When an individual transfer takes place, the group receiving the transfer can not be rearranged at that time (3.3). Where then do the transferring men go? Are the placed at the front of the group, at the back, or can they be placed anywhere they want, just so long as the rest of the group order is not changed?

A. They can be placed anywhere the owning player wants, just so long as the rest of the group order is not changed.
Example: Group A - 5, 7, 2, 10; Group B - 3, 8 (transferring), 11 can become:
Group A - (8, 5, 7, 2, 10) or (5, 8, 7, 2, 10) or (5, 7, 8, 2, 10) or (5, 7, 2, 8, 10) or (5, 7, 2, 10, 8).

  I'm pretty sure a guy transferring into a group can be put into any position.  

Correct

I even think at that time you can totally rearrange the group order if you wanted to.

That is specifically disallowed.

Also if the crew position is open can a transferring guy jump right into the crew position with no extra actions needed?

The transferring man can go to a position where they could become a crewman (i.e. adjacent to a crewable weapon), however it would still take an action to actually become the crewman, because it takes a sole action for that group to assign a crewman per 11.12.  (Note:  when assigning a crewman rule 11.11, which says the assigned crewman can be "moved" adjacent to the crewable weapon.)

title: Scenario E Qs
question:
1) Is 28.7 EX wrong? Looks like it supposes that the German halftrack's ARMOR k=2 and i=1 although it's 1 and 0, respectively.

2) If you got more than one berserk in a group, do they charge separately? Or do I have to draw pairs for all of them in advance? Could +3 additional attacker CCV bonus be applied in such a situation if they attack the same defender?

3) Is there a limit on overrun movement cards played in a sideways mode? Could I play several such cards on top of each over provided all other conditions fulfilled?

Many thanks in advance.
author: Andrei Shlepov
consensus_answer:
1) Is 28.7 EX wrong? Looks like it supposes that the German halftrack's ARMOR k=2 and i=1 although it's 1 and 0, respectively.

The example doesn't specify they are playing scenario E or exactly which AFV is being fired upon, except to say it is a German halftrack.  Both such vehicles (30 & 46) happen to have the same ARMOR values  i;s0/k1.  You are correct, nice catch!

2) If you got more than one berserk in a group, do they charge separately? Or do I have to draw pairs for all of them in advance? Could +3 additional attacker CCV bonus be applied in such a situation if they attack the same defender?

-  You draw all of RPC's in advance, (20.91) "After drawing an RPC to determine the defender(s) in a multi-man group..."  If multiple defenders are possible, there would have to be multiple attackers.
-  Yes, the +3 modification for multiple attackers still apples.  (At least there is no indication where it would not.)  For that matter, Concealment cards can be played on the Berserk man to aid in CC (as illogical as that may seem.)

3) Is there a limit on overrun movement cards played in a sideways mode? Could I play several such cards on top of each over provided all other conditions fulfilled?

No limit.  You do successive overrun attacks so long as there is an enemy group at RR5 to attack  (Of course, AFV cannot be immobilized, bogged and must have a working FT/MG.)  However, per 29.5, after an overrun, the AFV may play a Movement card to advance through a directly opposite enemy group (if that group has been overrun previously.)

Note, each overrun attack leave an additional sideways movement card in play on the AFV.  Any group with 2 or more movement cards in play on it is considered to be in open ground.

title: Just getting back into war games after a hiatus and I have a rules question...
question: When resolving a Sniper attack it looks to me that the RPC draw is made only after the RNC draw to determine if the attack was successful, if the Sniper misses then no RPC is drawn, correct?
author: Nazmainian
consensus_answer:
When resolving a Sniper attack it looks to me that the RPC draw is made only after the RNC draw to determine if the attack was successful, if the Sniper misses then no RPC is drawn, correct?

No.  Unless the target group is a single-card group, you first draw an RPC to see which card is the target.  Then you draw an RNC to determine the effect.

14.2     
Playing a Sniper card allows the player to attack one opposing card in a group of his choice regardless of the terrain occupied by that group. If the target group is a multi-Personnel card group, the card to be attacked in that group is determined by a RPC draw (see [14.6]). A Sniper may attack an AFV [28.431] only if its CE value side is face up.

14.3 RESOLUTION:     
A Sniper attack is resolved by drawing a RNC and comparing the number to the KIA & PIN values printed on the Sniper card. There is no significance to the color of the RNC drawn, nor are there any modifications. A "KIA" result removes the defender's Personality card from the game. A "Pinned" result flips his card to the Pinned side. If the defender is already pinned, the Personality Panics and must check for Rout [6.531]. Any other result is a Miss and has no effect. The Sniper card is placed in the Discard pile after resolution. 

This may be important if the player is trying to run the deck down.

title: Pinned OT AFV and Bog
question:
Suppose an open-topped AFV from scenario E is pinned, and then a Wire is discarded upon it. 

When checking for Bog, do I use the values on its CE side (because there are none on its pinned side; I'm using WGV cards just in case)?

Many thanks in advance.
author: Andrei Shlepov
consensus_answer:
Suppose an open-topped AFV from scenario E is pinned, and then a Wire is discarded upon it. 

When checking for Bog, do I use the values on its CE side (because there are none on its pinned side; I'm using WGV cards just in case)?

Many thanks in advance.

This is one of those questions that isn't adequately answered by the rules and errata.

Yes, use the "w" BOG value from the front of the card on OT AFV's--with the lack of any Bog values on the Pinned side, I would say go with the Front side values for ease of play.

Note: Non-OT AFV usually Bog values on both sides (and the values are one column worse (i.e. left) when buttoned up.) So maybe it should be similar with OT AFV's.

It likely doesn't come up often in play because people don't use their Wire cards on the odd chance of Bogging the AFV.  They seem more useful to play them on infantry groups--especially while they are moving with pinned men.

The WGV cards are identical except for errata corrections as the AH set, so that will not make a difference.

title: Moving Fire
question:
Need your thoughts.

Could an LMG (which DOES NOT require a crew) use moving fire?

12.13 to me indicates that the only LMG that can be used, is an LMG that has a crew.  If it is one of those no crew needed LMGs, it can't be used at all.

Thanks,
Doc
author: Dr Brian
consensus_answer:
Got from the modified rulebook which you can download here in BGG...from the Banzai rules section:

44.9 LMG: The Bren Gun is not considered a crew-served weapon; thus the absence of bracketed
firepower and malfunction values. A Hero card can be used to double the unbracketed firepower values
[10.45] of this weapon only if the Hero card is also a black RNC. This rule cannot be used for other
nationalities (EXC: Japanese).
..................................................................................................................................................................................
44.9 This rule states that the British and (via exception) Japanese non-crew served LMGs can only double its
firepower with the black RNC Hero card, thus implying that the American BAR can use either Hero card.
Specifically "This rule cannot be used for other nationalities (EXC:Japanese)." However, rule 50.6 (DESERT
WAR) states "Like all LMGs in the game which are not considered a crew-served weapon, a Hero card can be
used to double the LMG's firepower only if the Hero card is also a black RNC." Which rule is correct (as they
contradict each other), and how is the BAR handled?
A. Both are; nor do they contradict. The BAR is not considered to be an LMG. Either hero card may be used to
double its firepower.
CLARIFICATION:
The American BAR may use both Hero cards, and is not considered an LMG.
The British LMG may only use the Black Hero card.
The French LMG may only use the Black Hero card.
The German LMG may use both Hero cards, but doubles its bracketed value.
The Italian LMG may only use the Black Hero card.
The Japanese LMG may only use the Black Hero card.
The Russian LMG may use both Hero cards, but doubles its bracketed value.

It does not say anything that these CAN'T be used in moving fire, so common sense prevails and it should be able to move and fire..the restriction is only to which hero card can be used to double its firepower..

title: Natural Flanking Fire
question:
1) Do you place Flank Fire chit when attaining Natural Flanking Fire?

2) Do you lose Natural Flanking Fire when a Wire card is played on top of the flanking group?

Thanks in advance!
author: Andrei Shlepov
consensus_answer:
1) Do you place Flank Fire chit when attaining Natural Flanking Fire?

Yes.

2) Do you lose Natural Flanking Fire when a Wire card is played on top of the flanking group?

You lose Natural Flanking in all the same ways you lose Flanking when using a Flank Movement card:
-  Flanked group moves (even to remove wire) or enters terrain.
-  Flanking Group moves or placed in wire or rejects terrain.
-  The Front group moves away from its ID chit or is eliminated.

title: Mortars and Movement
question:
You can set up a mortar in a group on its own (with crew). In fact during initial set up you must form two to four groups, so just make your mortar team one of them.

There are also rules for transferring men from one group to another or even to start their own group.
consensus_answer:
I have only had the game for a week or so so I might be missing something obvious.

That is easy to do!

Am I correct that mortars must move with the group?  They can't set up at longer range and bombard while the  group moves up?  It seems strange that this would be the case but the rules seem to leave no question.  Unless the mortar is in a separate group and gets a flank fire card then the mortars must move all the way with the riflemen it seems.

They usually remain in the group they are in.  But there is nothing preventing setting the mortar and crewman (and occasionally a third man) as a separate group to fire away while your firebase and/or maneuver group advance.

To certain extent, mortars are more accurate at closer ranges up to RR3 or RR4--thus you may want to advance to get more hits and potentially better hits as the value of the To Hit RNC gets added to the effect of mortar.

Ok. Let's say I want to use the mortar in group A to soften up my objective in enemy group B and keep at a safe range. The only way to do this is with a flank card and fire from A to Enemy B?

No for several counts.

A)  It is not illegal to fire from Group A to Group B, C or D  (though the latter two situations increase the relative range  (see Rule 5.61) meaning you'll have less firepower or more difficult To Hit chance.

B)  Mortars (like all ordnance weapons except the ATR) gain no advantage of flanking position.

C)  All ordnance weapons can be fired with any Fire card.  Ordnance weapons do not have a FIREPOWER value and the number in the circle means nothing.  This makes them very handy--they can use "unusable" high valued Fire cards that clog your hand.

D)  If a group has both regular firepower and mortar, they cannot be used in the same Fire attack or can be combined in in any way to make a larger attack.  Splitting the mortar into a separate group allows attacks with the fire group and mortar on the same turn.

replies.body:
Yes, if a mortar team is part of another group then the whole group must move together.  That is why I usually set up a mortar team in its own group plus maybe another man or two if I can spare them to be replacements in case a member of the crew becomes a casualty.  Often I use the mortar group as a dump for low morale soldiers as mortar teams don't tend to move or come under direct fire very often - especially if you can move them into a gully.

You can, of course, also move individual soldiers between groups but that is a lot more expensive in terms of time and cards.

Steven,

Why the particular need for a Flank Card?

No rule book handy, but from what I recall, ordnance weapons fire fast and often since ANY Fire card can activate them for fire.

A Mortar at range 0 in Position A should be able to fire on Position B with no problem. 

So leave your mortar in Position A and move up the rest of your squad in Positions B - D. Use up all those big Fire cards to fire the mortar until the rest of your squad is in position to levy its own lethal fire...

Glad I could help, Steven!

Though the rulebook can be daunting, once you have it down, it's one of the best war-gaming experiences out there.

Cheers!

title: Doubling LMG Firepower with Hero cards
question:
I tried searching the threads and three(!) versions of the rules, but cannot come to a good conclusion on this - what is the correct procedure for doubling the firepower of a crewed weapon with bracketed firepower (such as an LMG) with a Hero card?  

The rules (orig rules: 10.45) seem to state that you always double the bracketed firepower value, but this makes no sense to me as the bracketed firepower is 1/2 the normal rounded up or down depending on the weapon. Thus, playing a hero on a fully-crewed weapon team will at best add a single firepower and at worst reduce it by 1 depending on how the values were rounded.

Rule 10.45 also states that if the FP for a soldier is already doubled, you triple the FP - so is a fully-crewed weapon considered 'already doubled' and you add the bracketed FP to the full FP to get the final value?

Ex: MG-34

Rng    FP   Hero FP  'Tripled'
 0    8     8        12   
 1    9    10        14
 2   10    10        15   
 3   11    12        17  
 4   12    12        18  
 5   13    14        20  

Using the 'triple' column makes the use of the hero card worthwhile for the MG-34 and seems to make the most sense, but I have not found a version of the rule book that I would interpret that way.  According to rule 10.45, the British Vickers Mark 1 actually drops in firepower at ranges 0, 2 and 4 through the use of a Hero card and that can't be right.

I just started playing Up Front over the past 2 weeks, so any input from you long time veterans would be appreciated.
author: The3Furies
consensus_answer:
I see I was being paged here  ;)

LMG/MMG's and Hero cards are kind of kluge of different rules, that can get confusing:
-  Crewable LMG's (G, R) and MMG's double the bracketed firepower per 10.45.  (Even the weapon is not fully crewed (pinned or no crewman--note most players in this situation use the Hero to rally the crewman in this case, so weapon far less likely to malfunction--usually the same amount of FP, but unbracketed malf numbers.)
-  Noncrewable LMG's (B, J, F, I) double their firepower only with Hero card with a BLACK RNC printed on it  (i.e. Card #30, YES; Card #151, NO) per 44.9 & 50.6.
-  BAR's (A) are not considered LMG's, so they double firepower on either Hero card.
-  AFV's:  Rule 28.421 states Hero card cannot be use to improve To Hit numbers or Firepower of AFV's.

The errata confirms that interpretation:

44.9 This rule states that the British and (via exception) Japanese non-crew served LMGs can only double its firepower with the black RNC Hero card, thus implying that the American BAR can use either Hero card. Specifically "This rule cannot be used for other nationalities (EXC: Japanese)." However, rule 50.6 (DESERT WAR) states "Like all LMGs in the game which are not considered a crew-served weapon, a Hero card can be used to double the LMG's firepower only if the Hero card is also a black RNC." Which rule is correct (as they contradict each other), and how is the BAR handled? 
A. Both are; nor do they contradict. The BAR is not considered to be an LMG. Either hero card may be used to double its firepower. 
CLARIFICATION:
The American BAR may use both Hero cards, and is not considered an LMG.
The British, French, Italian & Japanese LMG ‘s may only use the Black Hero card.
The German & Russian LMG’s may use both Hero cards, but doubles its bracketed value.

A realism argument can be made that if a Hero card played to double firepower of a man, the man is maneuvering within his general area (Remember:  The size of UF space is roughly the size of a football field) to get a better shot.  A weapon team wouldn't be mobile enough to take advantage such an advantage.  A weapon wielded by a single man could.

The real reason is more likely that AH thought doubling the unbracketed firepower of a machine gun was just too powerful when they were designing  Up Front.  When Banzai came out, they now had noncrewable LMG's so the Black Hero rule was put in as a compromise.

Also a weapon eligible for tripled FP:  Flank/Encircle/infiltration + Hero, triple whatever firepower it was eligible to double  (i.e. bracketed if it were a crewable LMG)  (Both Heros cannot be played on a single man to triple FP.

replies.body:
If the group is flanking (and therefore enjoying double firepower), playing a hero card on the LMG, I would play that you get to add the bracketed firepower of the LMG to the group.  

I'm not sure what other situation would cause the LMG to already have doubled firepower, other than playing 2 hero cards on it (which I've never seen happen)....but if this did happen, I would just take the bracketed value and triple it....so in your case at range 1, the tripled LMG would have 15 FP.

I hope that's correct.  Richard?

Dunno, I tend to think an equally if not more charitable reading of 10.45 -- at least insofar as it applies to an actively crewed MG -- would be to double the bracketed FP value of the machinegunner and to then add in the usual benefit for the weapon when it is actively crewed.  Conceptually, this could reflect grace under fire by the machinegunner or perhaps a willingness to increase his exposure slightly for greater effect, all without having to break off his crewed status and benefits.  The rules don't actually say the machinegunner forfeits the crewed bonus or runs off without the crewman, which you would think would sever any crewed status.

Interpreting the rule this way provides an effect for the hero card in this case just like it does in other cases while still not doubling the unbracketed FP or abandoning any crewed status. It would also have the odd effect that playing the hero card on a moving actively-crewed LMG would result in the same FP as playing the card on a stationary actively-crewed LMG.  An MMG can't be fired on the move even when fully crewed, so the notion that playing a hero card on an actively-crewed MMG in a stationary group conceptually represents that the principal has gone "off on his own" with an MMG and lost the crewed bonus seems suspect.

title: BOG?
question: On an AFV regarding a BOG, what does the number before the / represent? I know it's in relation to a Gully, Woods or Stream tertian. But what does it mean? How do I use it?
author: DarttiDare
consensus_answer:
That's what's confusing me. For the US #31 M3 HALFTRACK it reads... BOG:4/w7

I know the w7 is the w7 column on the bottom of a Action Card when on a wire. But what is the 4? is it column 4? 

Yes. 

Did you read this sentence?

You draw a card and check an RPC number at the bottom of the card to see if it is RED. The Bog numbers simply indicates particular RPC column checked: The w number for entering Wire and the other number when entering Gully, Stream or Woods.

For a 4/w7:  You check the 4 column on Stream, Gully or Woods,  
You check 7 on Wire.

Let's look a Tiger Tank:  German 36  4/w0:
You check the 4 column on Stream, Gully or Woods,  
You check the 0 column on Wire.

I think I know what your problem is here:  You ASS-U-ME the w on the AFV card and the w on the Action card next to RPC7 are the same.  They are not.

The letters on each Action card mean nothing when you check for bog--they are used for other reminders in the game:
2b -  Used as the starting RPC column when infiltrating a "Buttoned Up AFV"
4c -  Used as the starting RPC column when infiltrating a "Crew Exposed AFV"
5o - Used as the starting RPC column when infiltrating a "Open Topped AFV"
7w - Used to check for "Wounds"
0r - Used for checking for "rout"/KIA when a pinned man panics.

"25.6 TO HIT FREQUENCY: A To Hit frequency of "0-1" is reduced by one by treating it as a "0", a To Hit frequency of "0" is reduced by one by treating it as a "1", a To Hit frequency of "1" is reduced by one by treating it as a "2", etc. Similarly, a To Hit frequency of "3" is increased by one by treating it as a "2", a To Hit frequency of "1" is increased by one by treating it as a "0", and a To Hit frequency of "0" is increased by one by treating it as a "0-1", etc." 

How the hell can you reduce a number by going UP? I'm getting so sick of these rules! :cry:
author: DarttiDare
consensus_answer:
Here's what a frequency chart would look like from highest to lowest:

0-6  162
0-5  156
0-4  146
0-3  130
0-2  108
0-1   80
0     44
1     36
2     28
3     22
4     16
5     10 
6      6

So if the original to hit frequency is, for example, 0-2, and you need to add one to the frequency, it would now hit on 0-3. If the original to hit was only on 0 and you need to subtract one from the to hit, it now hits only on a 1. 

The way this works is there are more zeros than ones in the deck, more ones than twos, more twos than threes, etc.

Grant is absolutely correct--I added the number of cards in the deck for each range to above.

Any +1 To Hit (Acquisition) goes up the list, any -1 To Hit (Concealment, Smoke, Wire, etc.) goes down the list.

It should be noted:
-  If the ordnance weapon malfunctions, the weapon breaks and does not hit.  For example a weapon that breaks on x4-6 on a 0-4 To hit range, breaks on a Red 4. 
-  Normally color of RNC doesn't matter, but...  
If either firer is moving or target is moving (or Hull Down), Red To Hit RNC's are treated as a Miss.  If BOTH are moving, Red To Hit RNC's are treated as a Miss and the To Hit is reduced by -1.

- 25.4 & 25.43 often cause trip ups:  The number (either color) drawn on a successful To hit draws adds to the effect number of the weapon, BUT ONLY IF the weapon would hit on a Black 0  (i.e. its range is 0, 0-1, 0-2, etc.)  (Exceptions:  AT (boxed) ordnance from AFV's, IG's and ATR add the Relative Range, not the To Hit number if they hit.)

So a Russian Mortar at RR0, hits on 1 it's effect number is never modified--it will remain a 2.  

However at RR2 its To Hit Range is 0-2, it will have its Effect modified by +1 to 3 if a 1 was drawn or by +2 to 4 if a 2 was drawn on the To Hit draw.

The reasoning for this is that a single To Hit number indicates target that is hard to hit, any hit.  But if a range of numbers, it is possible to not only hit it, but hit right on the nose and do more damage.

2) The movement card has to have a Red RNC number on it.

title: Understanding a rejected Wire card right?
question:
Let me know if I'm understanding the rules right...

If I play a Wire card on my moving opponent's group and he rejects it, his movement card is placed sideways AND his chit range is taken back one? If so does this really just simply make him loose a step concerning movement? What would other benefits be? 

PS: I do know about him NOT qualifying for any flanking fire or lateral group transfers. 

Thanks in advance.
author: DarttiDare
consensus_answer:
Let me know if I'm understanding the rules right...

If I play a Wire card on my moving opponent's group and he rejects it, his movement card is placed sideways AND his chit range is taken back one? If so does this really just simply make him loose a step concerning movement? What would other benefits be? 

Let's start with this:  Wire cannot be rejected by an opponent.  Technically Wire is not a terrain card--so it can be discarded onto a moving or non-moving opposing group.  

If discarded onto a moving opposing group that group remains moving.  The opponent cannot play a terrain card (except Open Ground--which would stop the group from moving) on the group until the wire is removed.

What you describe is rejecting terrain.  When terrain is rejected, the last movement is modified:
-  If advancing or retreating, turn the Movement card sideways and the adjust the range chit to its previous value.
-  If the movement card was played sideways, remove it.  The group is no longer moving (if the final movement card was removed) and back in the original terrain.  Any advantage from that movement is also lost:  Flanking fire, group transfer, ford a stream.

Certain terrain cannot be rejected:  Stream, Minefield (non-desert), Marsh in a Jungle scenario, Soft Sand/Wadi in Desert scenario.

As to why does terrain get rejected is your opponent played a terrain you didn't want on the group to go into:   often a Marsh, sometimes you want to put them in a particular terrain like Buildings (see scenario B--City Fight) and your opponent offers you a Brush.  The effect on movement is the cost for rejecting the terrain.  

PS: I do know about him NOT qualifying for any flanking fire or lateral group transfers. 

As stated above, that group was moving sideways in both of those situations, the movement card was removed and any advantages were lost.

title: 28.72 Infantry protection when next to an AFV
question:
I have a question regarding rule 28.72. I had downloaded the rule reminder player aid. Here's the rule from the rulebook:

28.72 Similarly, friendly infantry in an adjacent group with the same range number as an AFV, may deduct one from the Fire Strength of all attacks against them (EXC: Snipers, Minefields) in addition to normal terrain modifications.

I've been reading this as applying to all types of AFVs (open topped, assault guns, regular tank). I've revisited the rule, and I'm wondering if this only applies to infantry next to open topped vehicles only based on the following:

(a) The first word "Similarly" indicates the rule extends from the previous 28.71, which can only apply to open topped AFVs (the only way infantry has an inherent boxed firepower factor).

(b) It's a sub-rule of rule 28.7 Infantry vs. Open Topped AFV.

Considering this, I thought I'd seek a clarification. Thanks. :)
author: davidlhsl
consensus_answer:
Rule says AFV ... and AFV has a definition, per Index and Glossary.  Clearly Clear (tm).

It is clearly clear the OP was confused--hence the question.

But when the are organized as follows:

28.7:  INFANTRY vs. OPEN TOPPED AFV:  Describes inherent boxed FP of 1 of infantry at RR5 vs. OT AFV's.

28.71:  Refers to the attacks specified in 28.7.

28.72:  Is a new general rule modifying any attack on infantry groups adjacent to any AFV.

Clearly 28.72 should a main rule (28.8 or 28.9--except those were eventually used.

Rules writing is HARD!

I should have added that another source of confusion is found in 28.71. It uses the term AFV and not just open topped. Since the rule indicates that it can reduce the strength of any inherent boxed firepower infantry attack (28.7) against that AFV, and since that can only happen with open topped AFVs, I didn't want to assume that AFV in 28.7 automatically applies to all AFVs. That, plus the other items listed, led me to seek clarification.

As much as the rulebook creates confusion, I've found that I can quickly find the relevant part of the rulebook when I need to remind myself of a rule during play. Rule 19 and other confusing items aside, it isn't as bad as other rulebooks I've read. Richard is correct -- Rules writing IS hard. :)

replies.body: I have always played with your original interpretation - that any AFV provides the defensive bonus to adjacent same-range infantry. I would say that if they meant for only OT AFVs to provide the bonus, they would've said so, instead of just saying "AFV".
I agree with Erich, and that is how I have played it too, as rule 28.72 states in the text AFV and not a specific type of vehicle.

(a) Infantry groups adjacent to any friendly AFV at the same range get -1 to FS of all attacks (exc. Snipers & Minefields) against it.

It really should not have been placed as a sub item (especially under a rule that applies only to Open Topped AFV's)--poor organization on AH's part.

title: Terrain capture from Stream
question:
Hi all. Going to run this delicate rules problem by the Group here and see what's Your take on it.

A Group is in an unforded Stream, at relative range to an enemy Group in buildings. One man of the Group sucessfully fords, infiltrates and subsequently infiltrates the enemy Group, killing the last enemy in CC.

Now, rule 20.8 says:Whenever the last man in a Group is eliminated while his Group is infiltrated, the Terrain card his Group occupied (including entrenchments)n is subject to capture by any Group currently infiltrating that Group.

While rule 8.53 says: A Stream can be left only by fording.

Which rule takes presedence? Fording has occured, yes, but only by one man. So how is this going to go down?

R. :)
author: stroar
consensus_answer:
This was with me ... and at times, one has to put on their ASL rules hat, and then see things clearly clear.

As Brent Pollock above posted, if this was ASL, it would be easy to solve.  The ASL Rule Book clearly states, when there is a conflict between rules, the higher order rule number takes precedence.  We don't have that luxury in UF.  Additionally, there is no official Q&A mechanism anymore, such as MMP who have the rights to ASL now.  So we are left with the rule book and ourselves.

Indeed Rule 8.53’s first sentence does state “A Stream can only be left by fording.”  The first sentence of 8.53 needs to be read in context with the rest of paragraph 8.53. title: Close Combat on Wire
question:
Just wanted to explore what happens when one of the involvees in Close Combat is on Wire: specifically, whether there is a -1 modifier to the CCV.

Firstly, how can this situation occur?  In four ways:

1) Most commonly, when the defender (ie the infiltrated group) is on Wire.

2) When the attacker infiltrates and then receives Wire while still infiltrating [13.36].

3) When the attackers are a Japanese Banzai group [45.423].  Note that this definitely states that the Banzai group, if on Wire, gets a -1 to CCV.

4) A Berserk man [20.91].  A clarification says: Berserk status allows CC in situations not normally allowed (i.e. vs. Pillbox or Minefield or from a Pillbox, Wire, Stream or Marsh). No infiltration check is made, and there is no modification made nor any check taken due to terrain or artificial terrain situations.

It’s worth noting that section 13.3 Wire talks about modifications to Fire Strength (or To Hit# for ordnance) but doesn’t mention modifications to CC.

So on the face of it we have no effect of Wire on CC except for Banzai men.

However, consider an argument from realism (I know, I know…), CC is combat at less than 50 yards, so includes close-range firefights and grenades as well as bayonet-and-knuckleduster stuff.  Wire is an abstraction of any condition that makes a group more vulnerable and/or less able to deliver fire; it seems to me perfectly justifiable to apply at least one of the modifiers to the CCV.

On that basis one could say that the references to Fire Strength in 13.32 should have included CCV; and that the exception for a Berserk attacker is reasonable because by definition he is unaware of his surroundings and thus ignoring any limitations imposed by Wire (look, he’s running around in a Minefield or battering at the slot of a Pillbox, so a few strands of wire aren’t going to inhibit him).

But what does the team think?
author: Barbarossa
consensus_answer:
I'm not playing Up Front for any realism aspect ... so I'd stay with the rules as written ... stay within what the game allows ... Anyone can come up with a number of arguments to support any position.

For example, to support the rules as written, I would say to myself once the act of CC initiates, be it through Infiltration, Human Wave, Berserk, Banzai, or whatever ... it doesn't matter where or what anyone was coming from, or even in previously.  That Wire is irrelevant now since they are now in the death throws of Close Combat, so let God sort it out now.

Doc

title: Basic movement question
question:
The rules say that if there are 2 movement cards on a group, then the group is considered to be in open ground. 

Is 2 the highest number of movement cards that a group can have played on it?  

Can someone choose to play 2 movement cards onto a group if they aren't in a terrain that requires it?

Many thanks for any assistance you can provide.
author: o0dano0o
consensus_answer:
The rules say that if there are 2 movement cards on a group, then the group is considered to be in open ground. 

Correct, once 2 movement cards are in play on group, the terrain is ignored--with the minor exception of a Gully.  In a Gully, the first movement card is "hidden" from opposing groups not on a Hill or at RR5.

Is 2 the highest number of movement cards that a group can have played on it?  
No.  Any number of movement cards may be on group, but only the last two count for defensive TEM. (I.e. +2)

Can someone choose to play 2 movement cards onto a group if they aren't in a terrain that requires it?

Yes--on separate turns.

Many thanks for any assistance you can provide.

consensus_answer:

Thinking in terms of what is being represented: the division of men into groups reflects pre-game command instructions of the form "you men form a team and go after this objective"; a leader is needed to update this and say "Private X, head over there and help those men." It makes sense to me that a leader could "order himself" to change groups.

One thing I always have to remember when reading wargame rules - especially rules written from the 70's and 80's is to take them VERY literally.  All the rule says I believe is that one of the groups must contain an SL or ASL (which it does).  It then gives some exceptions to that rule and unless there is an exception specifically stating that the ASL or SL cannot himself transfer then I cannot see why it couldn't be done.

My thoughts exactly. 
thank you Gents!

title: Entrenchment in woods
question: With mortar fire negate the entrenchment bonus along with the woods cover bonus?
author: caric
consensus_answer:
The -1 for entrenchment still counts:

36.2 An entrenchment entitles its group to deduct one from the Fire Strength of attacks against it in addition to the terrain effects of the Terrain card it currently occupies.

So the regular 0 TEM for Woods vs. Mortar/artillery has -1 added for the entrenchment.

replies.body:

The rules say something like "Woods terrain will not reduce blah, blah," which I take to mean that the *Woods* don't help but the Entrenchment still works.

Historically branches and trunks caused mortar and artillery rounds to burst above the ground, where the fragmentation was much deadlier than when a shell burst a foot underground. Thus Woods is not good cover, but if you are in the woods it's even more important to be in a hole, or what have you.

36.2 An entrenchment entitles its group to deduct one from the Fire Strength of attacks against it in addition to the terrain effects of the Terrain card it currently occupies.

title: AFV Questions
question:
Yes to both questions.

28.43 BUTTONED UP: 
Any other AFV whose Morale defense value is equaled or exceeded by any attack becomes Buttoned Up when it is flipped over. An AFV which Buttons Up remains Buttoned Up for the duration of the scenario (barring play of a Hero card) whether it Buttons Up voluntarily or due to enemy fire. A Buttoned Up AFV functions normally in all respects, but tends to have poorer accuracy, firepower, and mobility qualities as a consequence. An AFV starts CE. Should it wish to Button Up voluntarily, it must expend an Action doing so.   

28.431 COMMANDER KILLED: 

If the AFV's MORALE defense value is <= the final attack result number, the AFV merely Buttons Up or is Pinned as stated in [28.4]. If, however, the final attack result number is also >= the Crew Exposed (CE) value (or a Sniper KIA has occurred), the AFV commander has been killed and the AFV suffers other penalties in addition to being Pinned/Buttoned Up. Place a Commander Killed chit on the AFV card. Henceforth, that ordnance will have its To Hit frequency and Overrun strength reduced by one, and any non-ordnance attack it makes will suffer a reduction of one to its Fire Strength.   
28.4311 

An OT AFV may conceivably suffer a Commander Killed result more than once because when it is rallied it is again CE. Should such an AFV suffer a second Commander Killed result, flip the Commander Killed chit over to the "2 Crew Killed" side. Its To Hit frequency is reduced by two, and any non-ordnance attack it makes will suffer a reduction of two to its Fire Strength. If an OT AFV suffers a third Commander Killed result it is eliminated.
28.4312 
Each Commander Killed result on an AFV also serves as a one column shift to the left when checking for infiltration against an AFV.

14.31 VS AFV: 

A Sniper which scores a Pinned result on an AFV forces that AFV to Button Up [28.43] (or flip to its Pinned side in the case of an Open Topped AFV). A Sniper which scores a KIA result on an AFV not only forces that AFV to button up or flip to its Pinned side, but also places a Commander Killed chit on the AFV [28.431].

No, this flow chart chart at best confusing and is wrong.

You probably should calculate the needed To Hit number before drawing the RNC:
-  To Hit is spectrum that looks like this:

0-6   0-5  0-4   0-3   0-2   0-1   0   1   2   3   4   5   6
+1 means go one to the left, -1 go one to the right

-  Start at the To Hit # at the weapon's range.
+1 for the weapon has acquired the target.
-X for a concealed card played
-1 for each smoke (IN or OUT) or Wire (Out)
Only Black RNC will hit if either target or firer is moving or target is hull down.  (If target AND firer are moving (or target hull down and firer moving) the RNC must be Black and an additional -1 TH is applied.) 

Then draw the card to check the RNC.

The chart has the RNC drawn first.  If it red, checks firer or target moving and if not still applies the -1 TH which is wrong.  It should ask if "Either target or firer are moving?".  If Yes, then ask "Is the RNC Black?". if No, shunt that off to a Miss.

title: Things I Have Played Wrong For Years …
question:
…until I used Bruce Wigdor’s Up Front program.  I keep spotting mistakes in the program and I used to report them to Bruce, until I got wise.  Now I check the UF rulebook first, and four times out of five I find I was wrong instead.  Here are a couple of completely obvious things that I’ve got wrong any time these last thirty years:

1) You can’t reverse a Flank.  If you have a Flanked group and you play a Flank card sideways, yes it breaks the Flank but nooooo you don’t get to flank the flankers.  There it is in black and white [17.2]: A group cannot laterally flank a group which currently enjoys a Flanking Fire advantage over it.

(Note: there are obscure exceptions involving Natural Flanking, before Richard points this out.)

2) If you have a group on a Hill firing on an enemy group on another Hill, what’s the Fire modifier?  Zero you say, +1 cancels the -1.   Nope.  The attacking group doesn’t get Elevated Fire against the target because they’re on a Hill – but the target does get the -1 for the Hill.  So it’s -1. [Edit: Actually this is wrong and I was right all along - see below.]

[8.31] A group occupying a Hill may use Elevated Fire [6.41] to add one to the Fire Strength of any attack they make against any target group not occupying another Hill or a Pillbox.

(Note the Pillbox bit as well – that’s easy to miss.)

I found this out when my Panzerschreck (on a Hill) hit a T-34 (also on a Hill, after the retreating Russians despicably drew a black 6 for Random Reinforcements) with a black 0, and scored a black 1 for effect.  Yes! I thought, 4+1=5, immobilised!  But no, it was -1 for the Hill so I was thwarted.  I’d actually have been better off if the Panzerschreck hadn’t been on a Hill, because then the T-34 would have been Hull Down, but the black 0 would still have hit and the -1 for the Hill wouldn’t have counted … except that of course you can’t get an immobilise result if the AFV is Hull Down. (It would have been Stunned: [28.93]: A Hull Down AFV or IG cannot be immobilized; an immobilization result is treated as a stun result instead.)

Funny, I didn’t realise you could immobilise an IG ….

(In case you were wondering, I managed to win when Bernhoff, the last survivor of his 6-man group, snatched up the flamethrower and used a 1/5 Fire card to kill the one man I needed to get a break – possibly the worst Fire card ever used to win a scenario.)

title: Lateral Group Transfer & Individual Transfer Oddities
question:
Hi all

Had a game with my son last night (yay!) and he raised an interesting question about lateral transfers.

Basically he wondered why it was relatively simple to shift a whole group sideways but relatively hard (and super dangerous for the transferring soldier) to move single men between two groups.

Plus there's the thing where two entire groups can swap IDs by simultaneously moving past each other sideways...but if they want to merge into a single group they have to do it man by man..?

And then there's the other thing where a group consisting of a single guy  would suffer +1 to incoming fire when he's moving...but if that same soldier tried to transfer into another group he'd effectively get penalised for moving by...+2..?

I'm not arguing for house rules or anything of that sort, and I can see the gameplay requirement for this (you probably don't want single men leaping around the battlefield with gay abandon, or new groups forming or splitting up too simply and regularly). The thing is, most of Up Front's seeming weirdness actually makes perfect sense in its own terms but this area puzzles me. So I was wondering - is there something historical/practical that all this lateral movement funkiness might be simulating?

The other quirk is been relative range counting up. Would have Ben easy to do it the other way, but it is easy to resolve. It just looks funny.

The ill-fated kickstarter version was to have distance the following formula:

Distance = 5 - (Sum of Range Chits)
  Use Absolute value if >0  (i.e. |-1| = 1), 
  Adding 1 for lateral distance (i.e. more a single letter apart), 
  Max value of 5 for firing purposes

Advantages:
-  Makes 0 = close, 5 = far away.

Disadvantages:
Some game rules become really complicated:
-  Retrograde:  Moving to Distance >5 to nearest group is prohibited, etc.

-  Firing boxed ordnance from AFV/IG:  Currently add RR to effect.  under these rules you'd have to subtract it (also Boxed Effect Number of every weapon would need to be modified.)

-  Night scenarios:  Currently observation is done by drawing an RNC:  0-RR = sighted enemy and can fire at it.  With distance, it becomes 0 - (5-distance)

-  

The only silver lining about that KS failing is that it didn't allow them to screw up the rules like this. In the same vein, I'm happy to have the original cards with the weapons printed on them instead of the weapons as chits system.

title: Group Creation using Open Ground
question:
Here’s an obscure question – or rather a straightforward question where the answer is obscure.  During play, you can create a new group by making an Individual Transfer of two or more men simultaneously from an existing group, and subsequently putting them into terrain, either by playing a Terrain card on them or by accepting your opponent’s discard of a Terrain card.  The question is, can you create the new group by playing an inverted card as Open Ground?

At first sight one would say yes, of course, and this is how I’ve always played (on the rare occasions that this has arisen).  But playing Bruce Wigdor’s program recently I noticed that it doesn’t allow it – you have to play a “proper” Terrain card.  I was going to point this out as a bug, but I’ve several times reported bugs only to have Bruce point out kindly but firmly that I haven’t got the rules quite right, so I thought I’d check.  And on doing so, I began to wonder …

The relevant rule is 17.92:

The Group Creation is completed when the new group plays a Terrain card. If any transferring man is pinned prior to the play of a Terrain card on its group -- the transfer fails and the entire group is returned to the creating group. Otherwise, all rules for Individual Transfer apply.

OK, so an Open Ground card is a Terrain card, surely?  Let’s see what the rules say about playing Terrain cards; in 5.1 we have:

A Terrain card may be placed on any group (even one containing pinned Personality cards) provided it already has a Movement card of some type in place which is not already covered by another Terrain or Wire card.

So that’s the “proper” Terrain cards.  The use of Open Ground cards is covered in 8.1:

The back of every Action card depicts Open Ground. …  A player wishing to move into Open Ground may do so by playing any card face down on top of an already placed Movement card.

That covers normal movement, but in the Group Creation situation of course there isn’t an “already placed” Movement card.  So technically, I suppose, you can’t do it.  (And as usual, Bruce’s program accurately reflects the rules as written.)

From a realism point of view this doesn’t makes much sense – if you can start a group in Open Ground, or bring reinforcements into Open Ground, surely you should be able to create a new group in Open Ground.  You could make a case, perhaps, for saying that men would be unwilling to leave the perceived safety of an existing group unless there was some cover for them to leap into – although the rules would allow you to put them in a Stream.

So I think this is a case where the rules don’t quite say what they mean – shock, horror.  In framing 8.1 the writer forgot to allow for the obscure case we’re talking about.  But what does the Up Front world at large think?
author: Barbarossa
consensus_answer:
My opinion is that Open Ground is Terrain. Quite a few other rules talk about Open Ground in a way that is totally equivalent to other types of terrain (for example, modifications to infiltration, or ability to entrench), and note also that Minefields can be flipped over to become Open Ground when cleared (24.5), so I don't think 8.1 should be read as specifying the sole way inverted cards can come into play as Open Ground. (Noting, of course, that 3.6 specifically forbids playing inverted cards as Open Ground during initial terrain placement.) So if you want to transfer a couple of guys into Open Ground to form a new group, I say go for it (and pray the opponent's LMG doesn't immediately kill them).

Edit: checking the rulebook further, I see rule 7.3 on discarding terrain on the opponent's moving groups starts with "ny Terrain card other than Open Ground...", which in my mind bolsters the argument that Open Ground is Terrain and can be used in any situation calling for a Terrain card where Open Ground is not explicitly excepted.

title: Mortars
question:
Can a mortar do any damage to a AFV?

Yes, if you look at 26.5 Critical hits. 
If it draws a black hit then a black 6(or black 5 or 6 for Open top AFV)

Its like a real lucky hit.

Here's the whole rule:
26.5 CRITICAL HITS: A mortar can attack only the non-armored defence values of an AFV because it is
not a boxed (i.e. anti-armor) weapon. However, if a mortar scores a hit on an AFV with any black RNC
and then draws a black 6 RNC to resolve that attack (a black 5 or 6 RNC for an OT AFV) it has scored a
Critical Hit on that AFV instead of affecting the non-armored defence values of the AFV. A Critical Hit
achieved with a black 6 RNC immobilizes the target AFV. A Critical Hit achieved with a black 5 RNC
destroys an Open-Topped AFV.
consensus_answer: And of course it can cause the AFV to button up (or Pin if it's OT), and possibly get a Commander Killed result.

if he dies or panics, the charge can be picked up by someone else?

The rules don't explicitly state, but rather imply, that the demo charge must be assigned to a specific personality card.  correct?

21.1 SECONDARY WEAPONS: There are four types of secondary weapons: Demolition Charges [21.2], Panzerfausts [30.3], radios [40.0], and Anti-Tank Magnetic Mines [31.0]. Secondary weapons are represented by chits. Only unarmed men or those armed with a rifle, assault rifle, carbine, BAR, or machine pistol may carry a secondary weapon. No man may carry more than one secondary weapon.

if he dies or panics, the charge can be picked up by someone else?

Therefore half FS on a fire card, as well as the other effects of movement?

There more to flanking than this:
-  There has to be a front group (with same ID as the Flanked group)

Flank Fire chit is removed when:
-  FLANKING group has movement card played on it, has wire played on it or rejects terrain (thus removing the flank movement card.)  Key point not when terrain card is played on it .
-  When the Flanked group plays a movement card on its group (even to remove wire or failed ford of a Stream.) or a terrain card (even if rejected).
-  When the FRONT group is eliminated or transfers to change its Group ID.

title: Cards played as discard.
question:
When playing a card that must be played as a discard (wire, sniper, etc.), does the pplayer discard that card as part of his normal discard for his nationality, or does that single card play replace the normal discard procedure?

For example, if the Russian player discards a sniper, is he still allowed to discard the rest of his hand (or any part of it) as well?
author: PeteyWA
consensus_answer:
When playing a card that must be played as a discard (wire, sniper, etc.), does the pplayer discard that card as part of his normal discard for his nationality, or does that single card play replace the normal discard procedure?

For example, if the Russian player discards a sniper, is he still allowed to discard the rest of his hand (or any part of it) as well?

You can play a Sniper, Wire, terrain an opposing moving group and/or discard up to the number allowed by your nationality:  1 for German, French, 2 for British, Japanese, Italian, American, all for Russians.

In addition:
-  Russians may attempt entrenchment one or more times in lieu of a discard for each attempt.
-  Japanese may perform actions with movement cards and still discard 2 cards and show & discard cower cards (even if performing actions).

I am not entirely clear on this. So playing a Sniper or Terrain card on the opposing player is not considered a play by a group, it is considered a Discard? If so, as the US who has 2-Discards if no Action if played, I could Discard a Sniper on one group and a Wire card on another Group, THEN Discard two cards?

Nope. Discarding a sniper on one group and discarding a wire on another group would count as their two discards.

title: Victory condition
question:
I introduced the game to a friend today (talk about the blind guiding the blind... )

We were pushing on opposite sides of the groups, I moved Group A from the Gully in Range 3 to Range 4 and he moved from a woods in range 3 to Range 4. In my turn I didn't have a terrain card for the win, so I threw a wire to his units in range 4.

And he played a Wall. I gave him the victory, but did, he win? According to the rules I have seen he can play a terrain card below a Wire (no problem with that) and he wins if the card terrain plus (minus) the wire is above 1. But is it with the wall? The wall value is -2/-1 so with the +1 for the wire is -1/0 is this good enough?
author: abendoso
consensus_answer:
I introduced the game to a friend today (talk about the blind guiding the blind... )

And he played a Wall. I gave him the victory, but did, he win? According to the rules I have seen he can play a terrain card below a Wire (no problem with that) and he wins if the card terrain plus (minus) the wire is above 1. But is it with the wall? The wall value is -2/-1 so with the +1 for the wire is -1/0 is this good enough?

Several  problems here:
-  Terrain under wire:  Except for open ground, you cannot play terrain on a moving group in wire.  The play of the wall is illegal so long as the wire is there. (see 13.34 & 13.5)

-  Modifications to TEM for victory conditions:   Yes, Wire/Entrenchments count for determining "terrain that with reduce the Fire Strength  of an attack against them."  

In the case of a Wall, one wire on top of it does NOT completely nullify the reduction capability even if there is no directly opposite group.  Two wire cards on a wall would invalidate the Wall for this VC.  

Smoke does NOT count for this purpose--because breeze could blow it away.  (16.421)

These VC's have 5 parts:
-  X or more unpinned men.  (Pinned men don't count.)
-  in one of more groups  (They do not all have to be in the same group)
-  non-infiltrated (i.e. if a group is infiltrated the men in that group cannot count for the VC.)
-  at the proper Range Chit or Relative Range  (and not more)
-  In terrain that will reduce the fire effect of an attack against it.
All 5 parts have to exist to claim victory.

This means pinning some guys or infiltrating the group can be an effective last ditch way of staving off a loss.

replies.body:
I'm making some assumptions Antonio of your game (seems scen. A?)

-Two directly opposing groups (that is: two A group's) never can have a Relative Range of 6 (or more); the maximum is RR5. To advance beyond RR5, the opposing group must retreat or be destroyed.

-Never can be played a Terrain card below a Wire. The only exception it's the Open Ground Terrain

-In your example if a Wall plus a Wire is played on Range 4 is sufficient to achieve the victory conditions, BUT two Wires denies the victory.

title: Newbie questions calculating fire attacks and close combat
question:
Hi I have a couple of questions, I am a complete newbie and I am learning the game by playing solo against myself through all the scenarios so bear with me. (scenario C)

- Fire attack: I was in the middle of this situation. A group had played 2 movement cards, when it was hit by a Minefield. After much tolling they managed to play 2 sideways movement cards to exit the minefield, when they were attacked. What is modifier for the attack? I played a +2 for the 2 sideways movement cards and ignored the previous 2 movement cards. Is this correct?

- Close combat. One of my Russian units (in wire) got berserk and attack an opposing enemy unit. I randomly selected the defender in a 4 man group. Now, what is the modifier? Is it +9 (+3 per man that is not being attacked) or 0 (because the +3 only enters play when you attack a manned weapon)?
author: abendoso
consensus_answer:
Hi I have a couple of questions, I am a complete newbie and I am learning the game by playing solo against myself through all the scenarios so bear with me. (scenario C)

- Fire attack: I was in the middle of this situation. A group had played 2 movement cards, when it was hit by a Minefield. After much tolling they managed to play 2 sideways movement cards to exit the minefield, when they were attacked. What is modifier for the attack? I played a +2 for the 2 sideways movement cards and ignored the previous 2 movement cards. Is this correct?

2 {Points:
-  The minefield is a type of terrain--as soon as a group enters terrain, the previous movement cards and prior terrain are placed in the discard pile.  The movement/terain cards on the group would be:

Move
Move, Move
Minefield,
Minefield, Move
Minefield Move, Move.

So the prior movement cards were already gone before you were fired on.
-  Only the last two Movement or terrain cards count.  There can only be  movements cards OR (last movement card+last terrain) OR {Last terrain and no movement) + any Smoke or Wire cards vcan ever apply.

So correct, in your situation, the Defensive TEM would +2 since two movements cards are in play regardless of the terrain card below them (There is an exception for Gully)  

- Close combat. One of my Russian units (in wire) got berserk and attack an opposing enemy unit. I randomly selected the defender in a 4 man group. Now, what is the modifier? Is it +9 (+3 per man that is not being attacked) or 0 (because the +3 only enters play when you attack a manned weapon)?

The +3 modifier applies only:
-  When the attacking players has multiple men assigned to the same CC target.
-  When defending in CC, the the man selected is part of a multiman crew.
See 20.71 & 20.622.

Unless the Berserker was a attacking a crewed MG, the CC would be his PINNED value with no modification.

As soon as a terrain card is played on a group, previous movement cards are removed.  Since a minefield is terrain, you should have removed the previous movement cards.  

Note that Wire is not terrain.

For close combat, the +3 only applies for crewed weapons (that are crewed).  So, in this case, the modifier is 0

title: TEM are actually optional for the defender, who knew?
question:
Crazy how the rule nuances in this game never seem to run out.  If you read the terrain descriptions in the rules it clearly says the defenders MAY subtract their TEM from the fire attack.  The only must part is for negative modifiers for attackers.  Yeah even the +1 for attacks from a Hill are optional.  

Now, can you make a case for a situation where refusing your TEM would be an, at least, okay strategy?

I can only think of the defender wanting some men to get pinned in-order to use his rally card and keep his hand cycling.  Say he's the Americans and for group A he'll be laying a movement card, group B he'll be laying a terrain card and group C has no action he can use on them (they are already entrenched).  So perhaps he refuses the TEM for an attack on group C, hoping for pinned men, to use his rally card on.  That cycles 3 cards instead of 2.  Might be worth it during the final deck.
author: DiploGuy
consensus_answer:
Regarding this idea of declining a beneficial TEM in the hopes of pinning some men so that you can play a Rally card, never mind the risk and the gamey-ness of it, I can't find a rule that prevents you from playing a Rally card on a group with no pinned men. 

Actually, 4.23 states that one of the possible actions is to "reverse the status of pinned men", implying that if the Rally card won't unpin anyone it's not a permissible action. But that's implicit, not explicit. 

That issue was covered in the errata:
10.2 Can you play a Rally card on a group with no pinned men in order to get it out of your hand?
A. No.

I agree that refusing a beneficial TEM wouldn't ever make much sense. It's sort of like the rule where you don't have to draw back up to your full hand size. Though that one I can see being just slightly more useful. 

That I have done a few times.  Late in the third deck (maybe 5 cards left), I finally drew a movement card to advance to RC4 which would win the game and I already had good terrain  in hand.  My opponent was able to fire to burn the rest of the deck.    

Once I did it with no cards left in the final deck (The end technically does not happen until you attempt to draw a card) and my opponent was clever enough to not completely pass his turn  ;)  We laughed as we shook hands after that game.

replies.body: Intentionally refusing the TEM seems "gamey" to me and not in the spirit of Up Front.  But if there is a situation in which refusing the TEM might make sense from a "realism" or "historical" standpoint then.... I'm all game.   (sorry for the pun.  :shake:)

Being serious here--In all cases, "may" is used when the TEM helps the recipient.  "Must" or simple saying "Fire strength is reduced by 1" is used when it does not.  (Wire, stream, marsh, smoke) If taking the TEM helps you, you could choose not to do it, if there was some advantage in doing so.   But if the TEM penalizes, you can't avoid it.  It's same principle as refusing the penalty in the NFL.

In the end it is distinction without much difference because there seem to be no good reasons to not use a beneficial TEM.  The best purported use of such a tactic is increasing the chances of pin by a modest amount to play a single rally card.  If you are playing it that close to the vest, it can easily backfire:  Opponent has a second usable fire card and because you voluntarily avoided use of the TEM, now he has a chance to rout or kill some men, or encouraging a low fire strength attack that might have been cancelled is now performed because now there is a good enough chance to pin a man to deny you VP, etc.
