title: Groups disappearing -what to do?
question:
I am learning (slowly, very slowly) how to play this game and I came into a question that I am not sure how to resolve.

What happens when a group is only 1 unit big, or when a group has disappeared?

In my case, Russian Group B was hit hard (more on that later) by a German attack and ended up with 1 soldier left and the soldier was pinned (yes it was bad).

What happens to a 1 unit group? I played as if nothing happened but I remember reading something about groups being at least 2 units strong.

Afterwards the germans infiltrated and killed the Russian in Close Combat (I am learning so this was part of the learning process), they took the terrain (scenario B and the terrain was a building), and now I have a Russian Group A, and a Russian Group C. What should I do?

BTW, I am finding that this game is very bloody. An attack of 0 can easily pin a couple of guys (morale 2 or even 3), and routing them afterwards is very easy if they are moving, and you have to move in this game. I suppose that once I learn more rules things will change but I am mostly winning scenarios (against myself) by staying put and shooting everyone from afar.
author: abendoso
consensus_answer:
I am learning (slowly, very slowly) how to play this game and I came into a question that I am not sure how to resolve.

What happens when a group is only 1 unit big, or when a group has disappeared?

In my case, Russian Group B was hit hard (more on that later) by a German attack and ended up with 1 soldier left and the soldier was pinned (yes it was bad).

That sort of stuff happens.

What happens to a 1 unit group? I played as if nothing happened but I remember reading something about groups being at least 2 units strong.

One man in a group is still a group.  Only at the start of play or if a group is created by individual transfer during play does it have to be a minimum of 2 men.

Afterwards the germans infiltrated and killed the Russian in Close Combat (I am learning so this was part of the learning process), they took the terrain (scenario B and the terrain was a building), and now I have a Russian Group A, and a Russian Group C. What should I do?

Lack of a Group B is not a problem.  The Russian can "group transfer" (i.e. move sideways) either A or C to refill B, but they are not required to. 

All that happens when a group is eliminated is any terrain/movement card (unless the terrain is captured by the opponent) is discarded and the group ID & range chits are removed.

BTW, I am finding that this game is very bloody. An attack of 0 can easily pin a couple of guys (morale 2 or even 3),

A fire strength attack of 0 will pin a Morale 2 man about 1/4 of the time (~41/162), Morale 3 man about 1/6 of the time  (~27/162)  Morale 2 is a pretty weak guy.  

A Fire 0 attack against against a 6 man group might pin a man or not.  Placing the low morale guys where they are less likley to be targeted is a key part of the strategy of the game. 

 and routing them afterwards is very easy if they are moving, 
It should be noted that a group with pinned men can't have a movement  card played on it, even to remove wire.  (It is possible for there to be pinned men in a moving group, but they have to have started moving first and then were pinned by a later attack.) 

and you have to move in this game. I suppose that once I learn more rules things will change but I am mostly winning scenarios (against myself) by staying put and shooting everyone from afar.

You can't move willy-nilly, you have to prepare to move:
-  Don't advance without having a concealment and/or a rally card and a terrain card in your before playing the Move.
-  It is less risky to advance from good defensive terrain. 
-  Play a smoke on a group (if you can) before moving it.
-  Don't advance until your opponent's firebase has had some men pinned (particularly if the LMG is pinned)
-  If you are playing the Russian or Japanese or Italians who have no rifle FP at RR1, time your advance when the opposing firebase advances.

Of course late in the game, you may have no choice.

That being said, novice players tend to advance too rashly.  Three decks is quite a bit of time.

title: Italian LMG restricted by 46.4?
question:
I'm reading the old General article, Up On the African Front, which discusses Desert War and the author suggested ignoring rule 46.4 for the Italians so they can have two LMGs in one group.

So my question: is this how people generally play the Italians?  Is this how the rule is applied in Up Front tournaments?
author: arjisme
consensus_answer:
I'm reading the old General article, Up On the African Front, which discusses Desert War and the author suggested ignoring rule 46.4 for the Italians so they can have two LMGs in one group.

The rule does apply to all nationalities.  Some players start one LMG in a two man group and quickly transfer both to form a grandissimo firebase.

Kind of my opinion on the matter is that Italians have to get to RR2 in good order (That's the tricky part)  If they do they have so many guys that they'll have a shot.  I usually form two firebases, hoping for one to make it RR2 to do some damage.

So my question: is this how people generally play the Italians?  Is this how the rule is applied in Up Front tournaments?

In tournament, few people will play the Italians  (or outside of tournaments for that matter.)  If the tournament uses free choice of both players (like the WBC), few will agree to play an Italian scenario.  If it uses a back and forth system, they generally do not a player to pick the opponent's nationality.  In a tournament where the GM picks the scenarios, few GM's are so sadistic to force the Italians on everyone.  (Lest he get a revolt on his hands.)

title: Underlined names, availability, cards with special rules, Hull Down
question:
1. What is the significance of a card with an underlined name (such as Russian #38 SU-85)? I didn't think much of it until I read the errata file in the File section and it mentioned that some British cards should have their names underlined.

2. When a card specifies availability with only one date (a year or a month-year like Russian card #34 T34b, available 7/1941), does that mean it's available during that year or half-year only, or is it available beginning from that time until the end of the war?

3. Russian card #38 (the SU-85 again...you can see which cards I've been looking at today) has one special rule on the front (No Moving Fire Allowed) and two different special rules on the back (+1 TH vs Moving, +2 TH if Bogged/Immobilized). Do all three rules apply to the AFV regardless of CE/Buttoned Up status, or do they only apply to the CE/Buttoned Up status on the side of the card on which they're printed?

3b. If the SU-85 is Bogged, it gets a +2 TH. I assume this is supposed to be a penalty, which now makes it harder to hit a target, so I would add +2 to all the TH numbers at any given range. When the TH number is printed originally as a range (0-2), that turns it into a 2-4 required to hit, right?

4. Conceptually, what does Hull Down represent? I've read the rules and I'm still having a hard time visualizing what is happening to the AFV when it is Hull Down.
author: bigtex01
consensus_answer:
1. What is the significance of a card with an underlined name (such as Russian #38 SU-85)? I didn't think much of it until I read the errata file in the File section and it mentioned that some British cards should have their names underlined.

Underlined AFV's are assault guns which do not have a rotating turret.  (28.2)  In game terms, assault guns have -1 TH vs. moving target, -2TH when bogged or immobilized, and cannot fire when moving.

2. When a card specifies availability with only one date (a year or a month-year like Russian card #34 T34b, available 7/1941), does that mean it's available during that year or half-year only, or is it available beginning from that time until the end of the war?

It is available to the end of the war--but you probably should "phase out" early war equipment if you are designing an historically accurate late war scenario.

3. Russian card #38 (the SU-85 again...you can see which cards I've been looking at today) has one special rule on the front (No Moving Fire Allowed) and two different special rules on the back (+1 TH vs Moving, +2 TH if Bogged/Immobilized). Do all three rules apply to the AFV regardless of CE/Buttoned Up status, or do they only apply to the CE/Buttoned Up status on the side of the card on which they're printed?

The SU-85 is an assault gun.  All assault guns have those notes--with the except of the French 34 Char B1-bis 75mm Hull gun--which is treated as an assault gun.  Those rules apply whether buttoned up or not.  

3b. If the SU-85 is Bogged, it gets a +2 TH. I assume this is supposed to be a penalty, which now makes it harder to hit a target, so I would add +2 to all the TH numbers at any given range. When the TH number is printed originally as a range (0-2), that turns it into a 2-4 required to hit, right?

It is best to think of To Hit numbers in a spectrum, the left is better than the right:

0-6   0-5   0-4   0-3   0-2   0-1   0   1   2   3   4   5   6 

Bonuses and penalties are applied by moving left or right the appropriate number of steps.  (see 25.6)

AH was inconsistent with how it expressed TH bonus/penalties:
-  For acquisition, "+1TH" means to improve the TH number by moving to the left on the above chart.
-  For assault guns,  "+1TH" means to penalize you moving to the right.  (Which kind of makes sense in harder shots as TH1 is penalized to TH2.) 
-  Stream and Wire, "-1TH" means a penalty for firing a panzerfaust or fully crewed, non-moving, ordnance weapon (in Stream).
-  Concealment Cards/Smoke:  -1 means to make the shot harder, i.e. to the right.

Now that I think about it, I didn't catch that when I proofread the Banzai/Desert War cards  :gulp:.  At least it is obvious when penalty or bonus is to be applied.

4. Conceptually, what does Hull Down represent? I've read the rules and I'm still having a hard time visualizing what is happening to the AFV when it is Hull Down.

Some posted a nice chart showing the concept.  Essentially, the AFV is partially blocked so in game terms, a red TH is a miss.

replies.body:
I cannot really answer the other questions off the cuff but I can answer what "hull down" means.  Basically, "hull down" means that you can only see the top or the turret of a vehicle and the main body (or "hull") is hidden from view.  The term "hull up" means that the entire vehicle is seen.

Wikipedia has a great description of the concept here:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hull-down
https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/cc/Hull_down_tank_diagram.png

3b. If the SU-85 is Bogged, it gets a +2 TH. I assume this is supposed to be a penalty, which now makes it harder to hit a target, so I would add +2 to all the TH numbers at any given range. When the TH number is printed originally as a range (0-2), that turns it into a 2-4 required to hit, right?

That usage of +/- TH always bugged me (also see FLANK on the ATR), because I think of -x as reducing and +x as increasing. This is inconsistent with the other side of the Group ID counter where the counter shows +1 TH when it's acquired by ordnance.

As for (0-2) turning into (2-4), that's incorrect. Rule 25.6 deals with it, but gives you a couple of examples thinking that you'll pick it up.

You have to think of TH chances ranked as follows (from most likely to least likely to hit):

0-6
0-5
0-4
0-3
0-2
0-1
0
1
2
3
4
5
6

So if you have TH (0-2) and it's reduced by 2, then you move down 2 steps and get adjusted TH (0).

I knew I had seen the TH modification rules in the rulebook, but to be honest, with some of the rules consolidated in one section but others included as special cases of other rules, I start to forget what I saw where. I'm not complaining though--I doubt I could come up with a better way to organize the rules than they are (at least in the electronic formats I'm using). I'm just constantly impressed at the level of detail in this game that comes from a few decks of cards (even though there are a lot of side rules needed to implement all that detail).

I went back and looked at the Assault Guns rule section and wondered, "Why couldn't I find this, since I searched the pdf for 'underline'?"
It's because in the rulebook, it's called an "underscore." It's a little reminder that we may refer to the same things differently depending on where we grew up or where we live.

The Hull Down description and picture are perfect. I wish (for my own selfish reasons I suppose) that that picture had either been included in the rulebook or that I had thought of the possibility that Hull Down was a real-life term (and hence searched for it on Google) rather than just a term specific to this game. Live and learn. But understanding it conceptually now helps me put the rest of the rules in context.

Thank you all for your help (and thanks Richard for all the work you've done with the game aids and the rule clarifications over the years--it's been invaluable as I learn the game).

AH was inconsistent in other places in the rule book as well.  Like 17. Flanking Fire...  17.42 refers to the flanked group then 17.43 refers to the defending group.  Why switch what you're calling them?

AH was inconsistent in other places in the rule book as well.  Like 17. Flanking Fire...  17.42 refers to the flanked group then 17.43 refers to the defending group.  Why switch what you're calling them?    

No doubt.

Actually 17.43 is really bad in that term "defending" is often used as the side that defends in an attacker/defender scenario.  I don't think they meant that groups from attacking side aren't freed from Flank Fire when move.

I blame that sort of stuff on lack of word processors back in 1983.  (I'm sure Don and Courtney didn't)

Just one point about Hull Down: as Richard said, a red draw is a miss, effectively halving the chance of hitting.  But if the target is hit, it gets no modifier from the terrain.

This normally occurs when firing AP shot (boxed effect) at an AFV Armour/Flank defence, and it makes sense: the AFV's behind a wall, and if the shot goes over the wall and hits the upper part of the AFV there is no modifier for the wall.  

But it also applies when firing HE (unboxed effect).  This makes no difference when you're firing HE at AFV Morale/CE defence (which you do to try to get it to button up), since terrain never affects unboxed fire against AFVs, but it does matter if you are firing at a Hull Down Infantry Gun, where you can only use HE.  

We had this situation arise recently, and worked out that the rule is quite consistent: the IG is Hull Down on a Hill, say; you fire HE at it with half the chance to hit, but if you do hit, it doesn't get the -1 for the Hill.

title: individual Transfer, from a moving group?
question:
Brand new situation came up in a game I just played.  Can a soldier in a moving group transfer to another group?  If so would it be a +3, or possibly a +4, if the group he's moving from gets fired upon?

The rules do list the conditions in which you can't transfer and this isn't one of them.  So, currently I do believe it's allowed.
author: DiploGuy
consensus_answer:
Thank you.  In our situation he had a sideways card, on Group A, for fording the stream, then he laid a movement to back up, then wanted to transfer while still moving. So, that transfer would have suffered a +4 in this situation, wow.   

Yes, he'd have two movement cards in play on the group and the transferring men would have an additional +2. 

Important points, just the soldier(s) that are transferring get the extra +2, not every man in the group.  Also transferring men do not get the entrenchment -1 TEM if they are entering/leaving an entrenched group that is fired on.

title: Transfer Fire Bonus
question:
The rules say: "The transferred man is subject to a +2 modifier to the Fire Strength of all attacks against both groups as long as he bears the Transfer chit."

So is this saying that a fire attack against either group gets +2? Even the one that the man left? 

I'm just a bit confused by the wording of "the transferred man is subject" and then "both groups"; is it the group the man is in who suffers the +2 or both groups?
author: enzo622
consensus_answer:
No - what it means is that when either group is fired at, the man in question is one of the targets and he (only) gets an additional +2 Fire modifier.

So if Group A is entrenched in Woods and Group B is entrenched on a Hill under Wire, and Private Gormless transfers from A to B:

Fire against Group A is at -3, except for Gormless who is at 0 (Woods -2, entrench doesn't count for Transferring, +2 for Transferring).

Fire against Group B is at -1 (Hill -1, Entrench -1, Wire +1) except for Gormless, who is at +2 (Hill +1, Wire -1, entrench doesn't count, transferring +2).

Note also that the man transferring in or out is fired on first.
I think you mean "Hill -1, Wire +1" in Gormless' example B, but otherwise, I understand what you mean. Thanks.

title: The rules that most need refining?
question:
What are they, if any, in your mind?

I have two.

Weapon Malfunctions:
I don't see the need for all the exceptions.  I say whatever position you draw that persons weapon malfunctions, no matter what.  Now if it was a weapon that wasn't capable of contributing to the fire mission than the fire strength isn't modified.  If it is (even ones that currently have a 0 at the current range, the soldiers may be firing just ineffective) than the fire mission is modified in the usual way.

Inf./CC:
I'm fine with it being a two step process.  I just think it burns way too many cards.  

I'd like to come up with a way to determine Inf and CC matchups with just one card each.  I've been pondering the possibility but it would probably significantly change the odds, which I don't know if that's for the good.

Without putting too much thought into it here's possibly a way.  The number and the color are used to determine inf. The number in the initial starting position is the number of PCs that will inf. if a red number is scored.  Then you do the modifiers as usual.  Black, no PCs inf. while if red you do achieve inf. with the number of PCs equal to the number in the initial starting position.  You could further modify this by saying if the initial starting position is black then you subtract 1 from that number.  The idea being that the more PCs you attempt to Inf with the more likely you'll be spotted.  And since the further to the right you go the more likely you are to get a black number this makes inf with larger numbers more difficult.   

(I suppose I could play test this between both ways to see how big a difference in the odds it makes.)

As for CC matchups.  I don't see a problem with taking out the randomness.  Every odd count PC (1st guy, 3rd guy...) the defender gets to decide the assignment (they saw the guy coming in at just the right moment) and every even count PC (2nd guy, 4th guy...) the attacker chooses the assignment.

----------------

Thoughts on my ideas?  Or what are the rules you'd like to see refined?

-----------------
edit: My Inf. idea was confusing a rule.  You still would start at the column with the number in your opponents group.  Then run through the normal modifiers.  If it's a red number then you look at the column for the number of PCs attempting to infiltrate.  Then after possibly some more column shifts the number is how many get to go.  How you choose if their's a choice I don't know yet.

19.13     If the firing group contains more than one weapon with usable firepower factors, a RPC is immediately drawn to determine which weapon in the group actually malfunctions. All weapons in an attacking group (even those with a firepower of 0) are considered to be firing when the group attacks (EXC: flamethrowers, secondary weapons, ordnance, non-firing infiltrators, and the weapons of designated crewmen). If the RPC indicates a non-firing weapon has malfunctioned, there is no effect. If the RPC indicates a position occupied by a pinned man, there is no effect to the attack, but the pinned man's weapon does malfunction. If the RPC indicates a position occupied by a designated assistant crewman of a firing MG or a man whose weapon has no firepower at its current range, the malfunction is considered only momentary, and the fire against any remaining defenders in the defending group yet to be attacked is resolved with one less Fire Strength, but no weapon malfunctions. If the RPC indicates a position occupied by a firing weapon, that weapon malfunctions and combat vs. any remaining defenders not yet fired upon is resolved with one less Fire Strength for every two Firepower factors (or fraction thereof) previously contributed by the malfunctioned weapon. This reduction to the Fire Strength is made after any halving effects for Moving or Night Fire, and is made even if the firing group did not require that weapon's firepower in order to play the Fire card(s) used in the attack.

19.14     Although pinned men and those with already malfunctioned weapons are not considered to be firing, their weapons are always subject to malfunction (including flamethrower, ordnance, and the principal weapon of a designated crewman). A player cannot specify men as not firing solely to avoid the possibility of their weapons malfunctioning.

So, if zero firepower, it malfunctions, but you just lose one fire strength as a penalty.  No malfunction chit.

If pinned man, (they are scared so firing without purpose), they DO get a malfunction chit.

title: Need clarification on a CC rule...
question:
I understand that if my single PC goes in to close combat with a single PC in a group, and a crewed PC is chosen by my single Infiltrator for CC, that he gets a +3 toward CC and then, if successful, my PC has to immediately fight his crew member.
If my infiltrator successfully kills him and his crew member do I continue CC on the next member of the group that round or does it stop and I choose to continue on the following round if I want? I felt, from a realistic standpoint, that the other (this happen to happen in a pillbox) members of the group, would have seen me and went for me. So, I kept it going until my guy was killed. 
Was it correct to continue CC or should it have stopped after the two crew members were CC'd and killed? 
Also, was I only to give the attacked a +3 for his crew mate or for each one in the group?

Thanks!
Doug
author: caric
consensus_answer:
I understand that if my single PC goes in to close combat with a single PC in a group, and a crewed PC is chosen by my single Infiltrator for CC, that he gets a +3 toward CC and then, if successful, my PC has to immediately fight his crew member.

Close.  There is no +3 for CC defender--even on a crewed weapon.  (That +3 applies when 2 CC attackers target the same defender.)  But you would have to defeat the man selected by the RPC and then the crewman/primary operator of the weapon immediately in a second CC--unless both primary operator and crewman were attacked in CC on this turn.

If my infiltrator successfully kills him and his crew member do I continue CC on the next member of the group that round or does it stop and I choose to continue on the following round if I want? 

No--there are only 2 men on that particular crew (and really on any crewed weapon like an LMG, MMG, mortar, bazooka. etc.)  So two mena on the crew and then stop.

If there were 3 "virtual" men in the crew (as on a Infantry Gun (34.7)), you go the the third man and if you win all three CC's, then stop. 

Crew means only those manning a particular weapon--not the entire group. 

On the next turn you can continue with the Close combat process with that victorious man, but if that won by less than 3 on either, he would lose infiltration status, so that would have to re-infiltrate before attempting close combat again.

title: Squad Break = Loss?
question:
I was rereading the rules today and noted something odd about Rule 16.5  Broken Squad:

It reads in its entirety:

16.5 BROKEN SQUAD: A scenario always ends whenever a player has lost more than half of his Personality cards due to KIA and/or Rout. Reinforcements are not considered part of the force until they
actually enter play.

It just says "The scenario always ends..."  It does NOT says the player with a broken squad loses. 

Of course, I certainly think a player suffering a broken squad SHOULD lose immediately and his opponent, unless also suffering a broken squad, immediately gains the victory.  And I have never seen any Up Front player try to claim otherwise.  

But it just doesn't ACTUALLY say it in black & white.

Squad break causing an immediate loss is only mentioned in the example that immediately follows:

[EX: If a Russian player has 14 men and an AFV, he loses immediately upon loss of his 8th card. If a player has seven men and an IG, plus five men which will eventually enter as reinforcements [35.0], he
loses immediately upon loss of his 5th Personnel card prior to the entry of the reinforcements. After their arrival he loses only after having lost seven Personnel cards.]

It just goes to show rules writing is REALLY hard.  ;)
author: rri1
consensus_answer:
Seems that the rules are assuming that you've read rule 16.4 which is immediately preceding 16.5 (of course) which talks about counting the VP's at the end of a scenario in which victory conditions aren't reached.  16.5 goes on to say that in the case of a squad break, the scenario immediately ends and it assumes that you realize that you then revert to 16.4 (counting VP's) which in the case of a broken squad is going to result in a loss.

Two problems with this theory:
-  It is possible (and not particularly unlikely) that a player with more VP's could have a squad break. 

Example: In Scenario A:
Germans:  4 men at RC3 + 4 KIA's = 20 VP's
Americans:  8 men at RC1 + 5 KIA's + 1 rout = 19 VP's

-  And specifically per 16.4, VP's only apply at the end of a scenario "at the end of the time limit" and only those scenarios where the "which include a condition where one player wins by deny their opponent's Victory Conditions." 

On another side note:
16.4 is VP's  

16.41 states pinned men & bogged/immobilized/pinned AFV's don;t count for VP's.
  
Then, 16.42 is about what count as terrain "that reduces the Fire Strength of an attack against them" (which does NOT apply for VP calculation.)  This should have been listed before VP's and should specify that certain VP's may terminate the game immediately when achieved. 

Then they get around the incomplete Squad Break rule in 16.5

They pick the least important and least common way to win and list it first and put a higher subhead on it.  :shake:  

To be fair to Courtney and Don, in 1983 they probably didn't have a word processor to quickly make changes during the editing process.  :)

Yeah, I can see this isn't easy stuff to write.

Good luck!  You are setting yourself up for a big challenge!

I've played UF off/on (mostly off) for a couple of years now and while the game itself is a fairly simple one, the rules make it seem not so much so- and the rules has always been a source of contention among the players it appears in going back to old archives on CSW and such.

title: Infantry vs AFV (and also Flamethrowers, specifically)
question:
Hi folks

Had one of those moments where I've read the rules and gone "ah, yeah, fine I get that" but when it comes down to it, I realise that I really didn't quite get it at all... :)

So...infantry vs AFVs.
After some unpicking, here's what I think I understand - please correct or confirm, anyone who knows for certain:

1. Infantry vs AFVs...mostly not possible without an anti-tank weapon of some kind (bazooka, panzerfaust, ATMM etc).

2. However, if we're at RR5, and they try hard enough, then infantry *can* have an effect on Open Topped AFVs only.

3. At RR5, each unpinned, non-weapon-crew man, has an "inherent boxed firepower" of 1 vs OT AFVs.

4. This is NOT the same as an Effect number, it qualifies the group to use a Fire Card of an appropriate total firepower value.

5. To attack an OT AFV, you play a Fire Card requiring no more firepower than the group's total "inherent boxed firepower".

6. The Effect Number (in ordnance terms) of that attack is the Fire Strength of the fire card played (so it will often be less than than the total "inherent boxed firepower" of the group).

7. Then you draw an RNC, adding black numbers to the Fire Strength, subtracting red ones, and see what consequence that has, comparing the total to the AFV's armour values for either no effect, or an i/s/k result.

8. That same "boxed firepower" Fire Card also allows the group to perform an entirely separate, normal fire attack (drawing its own, separate, RNC card) vs the OT AFV's Morale/CE values before you resolve the attack against the AFV's armour. Bullets and grenades flying everywhere, basically.

There may be some adjustments for terrain in there too, or not, I can't recall and haven't looked it up at this point but...is that...about right...?

And then we have Flamethrowers...

Is a Flamethrower's boxed firepower value effectively equivalent to a really big "inherent boxed firepower"?

In other words: Is a flamethrower only able to attack OT AFVs as per the procedure above, or can it attack *any* AFV in this manner?

If there's a clarifying rule in the book somewhere I can't find it.
History is fairly silent on the effectiveness of man-portable FTs against tanks, so I'm thinking maybe it's OT AFVs only?

Thanks for the help

G
author: nyhteg
consensus_answer:
First, note that unboxed firepower can affect CE AFVs, possibly killing the commander or causing the AFV to button up.

That said, your statement of how things work with the inherent boxed firepower of infantry at RR5 is correct. Regarding flamethrowers: rule 22.5 explicitly says they can be used vs. the armored defense values of the AFV, but you are restricted to the (boxed) firepower of the flamethrower alone in the attack; rule 28.3 says that armored defense values are used in defense against attacks using solely boxed firepower values or Effect Numbers; and 28.4 says that "boxed firepower or Effect Number" attacks are "qualifying anti-armor" attacks that apply to the armored defense values. The OT status of the AFV is irrelevant - let 'er rip! The inherent boxed firepower of other types of infantry is a special case in which rule 28.7 applies; essentially, ordinary infantry have no boxed firepower outside the conditions of 28.7, but flamethrowers have it printed right there on their card.

title: Encirclement
question:
This section in the rules seems to have two rules contradicting each other, so I'm not sure if I am misinterpreting the meaning of "in front of".

17.62 says encirclement is broken when "...both encircling groups find themselves 'in front of' the encircled group. 

17.63 then says the encircling group can "'retreat' towards the encircled group... to reach RR5 and still maintain its encircling status".

But isn't RR5 considered 'in front of' the encircled group and thus violate 17.62?

Also I assume 17.6 means RR 2-5 when it says "... the adjacent enemy group must have an opposing group directly IN FRONT OF IT." 

Or did I get it all wrong and RR5 isn't considered "in front of" (and only RR1-4 are "in front of"?
author: abeheron
consensus_answer:
This section in the rules seems to have two rules contradicting each other, so I'm not sure if I am misinterpreting the meaning of "in front of".

17.62 says encirclement is broken when "...both encircling groups find themselves 'in front of' the encircled group. 

17.63 then says the encircling group can "'retreat' towards the encircled group... to reach RR5 and still maintain its encircling status".

But isn't RR5 considered 'in front of' the encircled group and thus violate 17.62?

No,  RR5 is considered to have both opposing groups in the same range.  (In an adjacent letter in this case.)  Though the rules seem imply that since you cannot move through a directly opposing group, at RR5 the groups are "just" in front of (or behind if the moving group arrived from RR6) each other.

Also I assume 17.6 means RR 2-5 when it says "... the adjacent enemy group must have an opposing group directly IN FRONT OF IT." 

If the groups are as follows:
American:         B
German:   A    B

The American Group B is encircles if and when German Group A makes a sideways move.

The encirclement would be broken if  (If American Group never moves in this example):
-  Either German group A or B is eliminated or laterally transfer away.
-  German Group A retreats to RC 1 (Placing it in front of the American group B)
-  German Group A advances to RC 6  (Placing it at RR1 to the American Group B)
-  German group B retreats to RC -2  (Placing it at RR1 to American Group B)
-  German group B cannot advance to RC 3 (due to the "no advance through an directly opposing group at RR5 rule.)

Note this makes it perfectly legal for either German Group A or B to continue the encirclement when they reach RR5.

If you think this rule is confusing normally, try it in scenario X-Surrounded!  :shake:

I understand your explanation, but I'm not sure I understand how German A is still 'behind' American B after retreating from RC3 to RC2, since when it was previously in RC2 it was considered 'in front' of American B.

Example:

Step1: 

American:         B
German:   A    B

German A here surely is 'in front of' American B...though not in an opposite group. I am also assuming that German B is also 'in front of' American B.

Step2:

American:         B
German:   A    B

Now German A has gone 'past' American B and is 'behind it', which is
what allows natural flanking or encirclement.

Step3:

American:         B
German:   A    B
 
Here German retreated back to RC2...how can it be it is suddenly still 'behind' American B, when at Step1 it was still considered 'in front of it'. - and the situation looks the same (concerning range chits...)

title: Japanese SNLF troops
question: Banzai 45.8 rule says that SNLF are Japanese second line troops. I'm guessin' why, considering that Advanced Squad Leader rulebook consider those troops roughly equivalent to the US Marine Corps. Just a thought.:)
author: 22GCT_Cook
consensus_answer:
SNLF are "Marines" in the sense they are part of the Navy, but their training and equipment was generally inferior to the Imperial Japanese Army.  (Unlike U.S. Marines)

Per the Designer Notes in Banzai:

Contrary to common belief, the SNLF were not superior to, or even equal to, normal troops.  Conversely , they exhibited a surprising lack of ability in infantry combat when encountering determined resistance.   In game terms, I have used then to represent almost any "second line" troops for convenience.  Take note as well, that there are no true elite troops listed for Japanese because there really weren't any.  Although there were units that performed exceedingly well in combat, that was due as much to circumstance or leadership as to organization.  The term "Samurai", which we use to classify elite units is merely a term of convenience; no such organized unit existed.

To a large extent, the names of elite and second line troops in Up Front for all nationalities are "terms of convenience".  Elite troops are used in scenarios for any experienced, highly trained, exceptional forces even if they aren't a part of of the "Guards", "Bersaglieri", "SS", "Airborne", etc.  (Note the Kickstarter edition, the name for the elite Germans was to be changed from "SS" to "Panzer Grenadier"--in large part due to SS troops not being superior, and often inferior, to regular Wehrmacht troops despite, or because of, their fanaticism.)  Likewise 2nd line troops, whether they are "conscripts", "Black shirts", "Volksgrenadiers", etc. are used for any troops with diminished effectiveness due to fatigue, replacements, etc.

I can never remember what the official names are and simply call then "Elite"______ or "second line" ______ troops :)

title: Ordnance vs AFVs, FIre Strength cards, and rule 28.31
question:
Rule 25.3 states that a Fire card of any value must be played for ordnance to make a To Hit attempt versus an AFV.  However, I'm a but confused by 28.31.

Rule 28.31 states, "If there are insufficient boxed firepower factors in a group to use a particular Fire card, the Armor and Flank defense values are not affected by an attack using that card."

So if my gun has a boxed firepower of 0 (such as the SdKfz231), I cannot make an attack against an armored target as no firepower card has a value of 0?

What am I missing here?
author: patch_bunny
consensus_answer:
Rule 25.3 states that a Fire card of any value must be played for ordnance to make a To Hit attempt versus an AFV.  However, I'm a but confused by 28.31.

Rule 28.31 states, "If there are insufficient boxed firepower factors in a group to use a particular Fire card, the Armor and Flank defense values are not affected by an attack using that card."

28.31 is not referring an ordnance attack--it is referring to a "boxed firepower" attack.  

Most firepower in unboxed (like with rifles/machine guns, etc. and thus per 28.31 does not apply vs. the ARMOR/FLANK defense values of the AFV's (Though they would apply vs. CE/Button UP/Pinned values of an AFV.)  Boxed firepower is only available with flamethrowers [22.5] and inherent boxed FP of 1 at RR5 by each personality card  vs. an OT AFV [28.7] 

28.31 is saying is if you have boxed firepower and you play a Fire card with Firepower number <= the amount of boxed firepower, you can apply the fire strength of the card (+/- RNC and TEM (if not a FT) -1 for adjacent infantry group) vs. the ARMOR or FLANK values of the defending AFV.

Boxed firepower attacks are quite rare.

So if my gun has a boxed firepower of 0 (such as the SdKfz231), I cannot make an attack against an armored target as no firepower card has a value of 0?

No, an ordnance weapon has a "effect number" not a firepower number.  

In this case, if you get a hit, the fire strength is the boxed effect number (in this case 0) + Relative Range (see 25.4) +/- TEM & RNC vs. the ARMOR or FLANK defense values.

title: Flanking fire from terrain
question:
Hi,
can answer me this.

Group A is Flanking Group b. Can I plain next a terrain card on Group A without losing Flanking status?

I know that if opponent plays terrain on Group b, the Flanking status is lost.

The idea is to shoot flanking fire from eg. building. 

-bsg77
author: bsg77
consensus_answer:
Hi,
can answer me this.

Group A is Flanking Group b. Can I plain next a terrain card on Group A without losing Flanking status?

Yes--that's the point because otherwise moving fire penalties would more or less cancel out the flanking fire bonus.

I know that if opponent plays terrain on Group b, the Flanking status is lost.

Flanking fire is lost when:
-  The FLANKING group has a Movement or wire card played on it or rejects terrain played by the opponent (thus removing the Flank Movement card or not reaching "RR6").
-  The FLANKED group has a movement card played on it (even to remove wire or ford a stream that does not stay on the card) or a terrain card  is played on it. (but not Wire--but that may not be advisable, but that is how I lost the WBC final this year.)
-  The FRONT group is eliminated either by losses or by transferring away.

The idea is to shoot flanking fire from eg. building. 

Sounds like a good idea to me!

title: Terrain bonuns fire (from) question
question:
If the last terrain or movement card played is a movement card but the card before is terrain, have I the circled terrain fire (from) bonus if I fire? From the wording of 7.1 and 7.2 it seems no, it seems that I have only the half fire strenght of moving fire (12.1) but I'm not sure.
Example: Stream (Hill) then Movement then fire with strenght 8
I will have fire strenght of 3 (5) or 4?
author: Beorne
consensus_answer:
I think this is covered in section 6.4:

6.4 FIRE STRENGTH: 
Once it has been determined that the Fire card(s) can be used, determine the final Fire Strength of the attack. If the attacking group is currently moving (has played a Movement card with no Terrain card yet placed over it), the Fire Strength of its Fire card(s) is halved [12.1]. 
6.41 

Modify the Fire Strength by adding any modifiers due to the attacker's position (see Wire [13.32], Stream [8.52], Marsh [8.41], Smoke [13.22], and Elevated Fire [8.31] for examples of Fire Strength modifications due to the attacker's position).
6.42 
Modify the resulting Fire Strength by adding any modifiers due to the terrain occupied by the defender, including any applicable Smoke and/or Wire cards.
6.43 
Modify the resulting Fire Strength by adding any modifiers caused by the movement status of the defending group.
6.44 
At this point, the defender may opt to play any Concealed card in his hand to further modify the Fire Strength of the attack. If he does so, the negative modifiers of the Concealed card are added to the Fire Strength to derive the final Fire Strength of the attack.

Where? It only lists all the possible modifiers without specifing the terrain plus movement fire (from) case.

Just add/subtract all of the terrain factors at the same time.  I am not trying to be rude here but it sounds like perhaps you are over complicating this?  All of the terrain environment modifiers (+ and -) should be added together at the same time but only AFTER the fire strength of the card has been halved due to the attacking group's movement is accounted for.

EDIT:  Perhaps breaking up the logic flow this way will help:
1) Determine the strength of the fire card(s) to be used in the attack.
1a) If attacking group is moving then halve the firepower of weapons that this applies to, use the bracketed values for crewed weapons that can still fire while moving, etc.  Determine if the fire card(s) can even be used in the attack at this point based on available firepower factors.
1b) If attacking group is moving then HALVE the fire strength of any/all fire cards used in the attack.
2) Process the attack like normally by accounting for attacker's and defender's terrain effect modifiers, use of a defender's concealed card, etc.

replies.body:
If the last terrain or movement card played is a movement card but the card before is terrain, have I the circled terrain fire (from) bonus if I fire? From the wording of 7.1 and 7.2 it seems no, it seems that I have only the half fire strenght of moving fire (12.1) but I'm not sure.
Example: Stream (Hill) then Movement then fire with strenght 8
I will have fire strength of 3 (5) or 4?

Per 12.1:  When moving the Fire Strength of ANY Fire CARD is halved before any other modification.  

If you are firing while moving, several things happen:
-  Firepower of bolt action rifles is halved (rounded down) and crewed weapons use bracketed FP (if they are allowed to fire at all).
-  The Fire Strength of EACH Fire card is halved.  (rounded down) (EXC:  Ordnance and some Flamethrower attacks)  That means if you used a Fire 3 & Fire 5 in one attack, the Fire strength before terrain effects is 3 (3/2-> 1 & 5/2-> 2),  not 4. 
-  Then any offensive or defensive terrain effects are added/subtracted.   (IF there is only one movement card on the group, attacking TEM would apply.)

So in your example playing a single Fire 8 card from a Hill while moving:  if 8/2 (Moving fire) + 1 (Hill) + Terrain of the Defending group (whatever that happens to be) + effects of any Wire or Smoke cards.

Better (shorter) answer:  Don't fire while moving (unless ABSOLUTELY necessary).

title: Questions on lateral group transfer
question:
From 17.7:
"A  group  capable  of movement  can  change  its  group  identity  and  thereby  its  position  directly opposite  an  opposing  group  by  announcing  a  Lateral  Group  Transfer  and playing  a  Movement  card  in  the  sideways  mode  (including  a  Ford  or Flank  card  thereby  possibly  fulfilling  double  purposes). "
What can be the double purpose of a flank card? Can one flank an enemy during lateral group transfer??? How?

Again from 17.7:
"A  group in  Marsh  may  change  identity  by  playing  only  one  Movement  card,  but still  requires  two  Movement  cards  to  exit  that  Marsh. ". Does this simply means that the card used to lateral group transfer bust be the second movement card played on the marsh?

Thanks, I'm no more used to AH's rukebooks ...
author: Beorne
consensus_answer:
For 17.7 flanking: if your group wants to change from A to B, it can (as long as B is empty), by playing a card in the sideways mode.

This is all that is required to change positions.

However, if you're in a stream, it would need to be a Ford card (as normal for any move from a Stream).  If you play a Flank card, not only do you change positions, but you'd also get flanking bonus.  Moving to an adjacent position on its own does not grant flanking bonus.  Note that flanking bonus due to the play of a flanking card is temporary and only lasts until your opponent or you plays a movement card (or your opponent goes to ground while moving).  This is different than positional flanking bonus.

So in the case the moving group will flank the group whith the newly acquired ID right?
When you play a flank card sideways you immediately declare who you are flanking, I don't think you can wait until you're in terrain to then choose who you're flanking.  So in the case where you're laterally transferring a group once you have moved into terrain and acquired a new ID chit either the group you were flanking is now right in front of you, so you lose your flank, or they are two Groups away making them no longer adjacent, which means you also lose your flank.  However, the double purpose of flanking and laterally transferring co-exist as long as you don't put that group into terrain- and take on its new group ID. 

For 17.7 Marsh.  Nope, it could be the first card played, but you're still in the Marsh until you play that second move card.

I thought that even in the case of two group switching position you have to play a new terrin to conclude the transfer. So now I think this is not needed: both retain tour old terrain right?
Thanks.

I'm pretty confident that you must have two movement cards in play to change terrain on a Marsh.  And you must put your group in terrain in-order to change the laterally moving group's ID.

title: Question Regarding Infiltration
question:
Just got this reprint on Drive Thru Cards and looking through some tutorials, had a question on infiltration.

If a man passes infiltration check and becomes infiltrator he can double his firepower and in doing so loses infiltrator status.  My question is, can that doubled firepower be used against any opposing groups or just the one he did the infiltration check against?

author: nd23rin
consensus_answer:
One never loses VP as a result of taking casualties. One gains VP from eliminating or routing the opponent's forces.

If a man is removed from the game due to Rout, that's 1VP for the opponent. If a man is removed from the game via Panic or KIA, that's 2VP for the opponent. This, along with all other aspects of calculating one's VP total, is covered in rule 16.4.

Removal due to Panic is considered KIA for VP purposes as indicated in rule 6.53. Also note that if you choose to eliminate one of your own men via Voluntary Panic, you must draw an RPC to determine whether they Panic or Rout for enemy VP purposes, as per rule 10.3.

Maybe this will help:

Movement [Sections 5, 7]
o	You may not move with one or more pinned men. 
o	You may play a movement card in front of a group to advance (increase the range chit by one), retreat (decrease by one) or move sideways (no change). Place the card in the appropriate facing. 
o	You would move sideways typically because of a terrain restriction (Marsh or Stream), to Flank, or for tactical reasons. 
o	You may not advance if the group opposite you is already at Relative Range 5. 
o	You may place a movement card while moving. 
o	If you have one movement card, you still apply the effects of any underlying terrain. If you have two or more movement cards, only the last two movement cards count. Any cards played earlier do not. [7.2] 
o	Each movement card played adds one to incoming fire strength. 
o	There are penalties for shooting while moving. See Fire while moving. 
Terrain [Section 7]
o	You may only play terrain on a group that has one (or more) movement cards in front of it. When you play a terrain, you remove (discard) all the movement cards and prior terrain. 
o	You may move into terrain with one or more pinned men. 
o	Any card may be played as "Open Terrain" (using the card back). Cower cards may be played as open terrain.

Firing ordnance (including an AFV's main armament) does not require you to discard a Fire card. Firing ordnance is an action for the group containing the ordnance and requires play of a Fire card of any strength. The firepower factor requirement and fire strength on the Fire card are ignored - instead, one follows the To Hit process to see if the fired round hits, and then resolves the attack against the targets if the process was successful, using the fire strength of the ordnance against the specific target type. So, firing ordnance can feel like "discarding a Fire card", but you're actually playing it as an action for the relevant group. That will affect one's discard capability in the usual way (Germans could still discard another card, other nationalities could not).

Once an opponent plays a terrain card on you (which is a discard for him), you then decide either to accept the terrain or reject it  (Exc:  The aforementioned Stream must be accepted).  If you reject it, rotate the movement card to sideways and adjust the range chit to what it would have been if the movement card had been played sideways.  If the movement card is already in sideways mode, it is removed entirely and the group would no longer be moving in its original terrain.

Play another movement card:  0 (Woods) +1 (Move) +1 (Move) = +2
Play another movement card:  0 (Woods) +0 (Move) +1 (move) +1(Move)= +2
Play a Hill on the group:  -1/(+1) (Hill)  All movement cards and the Woods are discarded.

In your example with the Gully and one movement card, you're still having the effects of the Gully, so you can only be attacked if RR5 or Hill and then you have the effects of both terrain and movement card.  If you play a second movement card on the Gully (or Marsh), you just have the effects of the two movement cards then right?

That was probably going to be my next question...

So normally, if you play a terrain card on a movement card, the movement card is removed and you have just the effects of the terrain card.

If you play a movement card on a terrain, you get the effects of both.  If you play an additional movement card, you get the effects of both movement cards but not the terrain.  You always look at the last two terrain/movement cards unless the last card was a terrain card.

So for the Marsh or Gully card which take a sideways movement card to 'get out of' before moving, when you have played the second movement card, you still just look at the last two movement cards and not the terrain card then right?

Marsh does require a movement card to be played sideways and then a second movement (in any direction) in order to exit.  Gullies do not--only one movement card is required to exit--very handy when approaching Range Chit 4!

For Marshes, you are correct--once the the second movement cad is in play, you only count the two movement cards as the defensive TEM.

In your example with the Gully and one movement card, you're still having the effects of the Gully, so you can only be attacked if RR5 or Hill and then you have the effects of both terrain and movement card.  If you play a second movement card on the Gully (or Marsh), you just have the effects of the two movement cards then right? 

Gullies have their own special feature--The group in a Gully even with one movement card on it can't be seen by the enemy except from a group on a Hill or RR5.  So a group is in a Gully  (TEM is expressed as "From Hill or RR5/Other terrain"):

Gully:  -2/NA  
First Movement:  -1/NA  (Group is still hidden from non-Hill enemy groups not at RR5)  (Note you could play a terrain at this point to exit the Gully.)
Second Movement:  +2/+1  (The first movement was hidden from non-Hill enemy groups not at RR5--so it is not counted for the TEM.)
Third Movement:  +2/+2

Don't worry about asking questions, the rules can be difficult to parse.

Ok, I think this clears up movement for me (until next time).

Thanks again!

title: BAR movement fire penalty?

Getting conflicting information from Greg's rewrite and the 2e rules...wondering if I missed an errata somewhere.

author: aram12
consensus_answer:
The first post in this thread:

http://boardgamegeek.com/thread/1008339/latest-3rd-edition-limited-edition-rulebook-posted

takes you to the draft version of the rulebook that was supposed to be released with the cursed Kickstarter project. I've printed it, placed it in my Up Front binder, and I've used it as a learning reference (particularly with those tricky AFV rules).

I had no idea whether it was a viable way of learning the rules.  I just dismissed it offhand because of the debacle that surrounds it.  

You have to ignore their rules for relative range, as they swapped the 0 (far) > 5 (closest) in the official game to 5 (far) > 0 (closest). That also has an impact in calculating ordnance attacks and another item that relies on RR that I can't think of off the top of my head. But I can easily translate this mentally and have no issues with it, but you do have to be aware of it.

They've also provided a way to go directly into close combat without first infiltrating. I've tested this, and it seems much riskier than the 2-step approach in the official rules. They do indicate you can still infiltrate, then enter close combat, with the exception of not requiring a morale check/move card discard. To play the official way, ignore the direct entry method, and add a note to infiltrators that they either have to pass a morale check or discard a movement card to go to CC.

Despite the fact they've made some tweaks to the rules (itemized at the end of the document),

Is the list of tweaks comprehensive?  Does it list all the changes, including the one's you've mentioned?  Because if not, I might as well be using the .96 rules as they both would have the same issue...undocumented changes/mistakes that have to be tracked and cross-referenced.

the rules are very useful to me as a learning reference, because it's much easier to read than the official rules. Once I've understood the part I'm learning, I can return to the annotated 2e rules that I also use and make clearer sense of it.

This.  That's exactly what I'm doing with the .96 rules.

There are also some additional rules that go beyond the official game that I'm tempted to try, particularly the weather rules. I also think some of the differences they've made are interesting to test, such as the aforementioned close combat procedure. But I need to focus on nailing the standard game before flying off into that realm.

I realize it seems counter-intuitive to learn from a resource that has differences that you have to adjust when you want to play officially. For me, the utility comes from clarity in getting the main points. I can then return to the more difficult rule book and make better sense of what I'm reading, because I now have a context in my head. I'm weird anyway, so this might not work for anyone else.

It may not work for your purpose, but it's at least something else you can try to see if it does.

Since you're also using the annotated 2e rules, make sure you download the scanned official 2e rulebook:

http://boardgamegeek.com/filepage/9395/front-rulespdf
(an even better scan is available for free at Wargame Vault)

Got it already.

And print the Index/Glossary page if you haven't already done so. It makes locating the rule you need to find during game play so much easier! 

This is my favorite play aid:

http://boardgamegeek.com/filepage/53639/comprehensive-front-player-aid

There another version of this with fancier graphics, but I prefer this because it has a lot of white space where I can write additional notes due to some useful information being missing from this. It's also missing info for Banzai/Desert War.

I've also found this incredibly helpful:

http://boardgamegeek.com/filepage/86049/player-actions

It contains a list of all the actions you can do during a turn. It's terrific for indicating which actions require a card, which actions allow you to rearrange the soldiers in your group, etc.

And all this stuff too.  It's great to know these aids are accurate.  Especially the comprehensive player aid...I mean, that's the WHOLE game right there...so easy to look up rules.  I'm curious what rules you've found missing from it.

Thanks for all the info...

 Rather than leave you to draw conclusions for yourself, I'm saying that rules written for "bolt action rifles" would not apply to BARs, and rules written for BARs would not apply to bolt action rifles.

Men firing BARs do not have their FPs reduced in any way due to their movement status, unlike bolt-action rifles or weapons with bracketed firepower factors. In this way they are like other single-man automatic and semi-automatic weapons (machine pistols, assault rifles, M1 rifles).

title: Movement stopped by concealment
question: Yes.
consensus_answer:
Enemy shoots at my moving group.
He calc's fire_strength, ect.
I play a Concealment card -1.
Combat is resolved no one in my group is pinned.

Question:
When it is my turn to take actions is my group still considered to be moving?

Once a movement card is played on a group, it always remains moving until the group has a "non-artificial" terrain card (i.e. Wire or Smoke) played on it (Exceptions:  moving sideways & rejects terrain or if the group is an AFV & is immobilized.)

I play a Concealment card -1.
Combat is resolved no one in my group is pinned.

Question:
When it is my turn to take actions is my group still considered to be moving?

Once a movement card is played on a group, it always remains moving until the group has a "non-artificial" terrain card (i.e. Wire or Smoke) played on it (Exceptions:  moving sideways & rejects terrain or if the group is an AFV & is immobilized.)

And just to be clear, your group would still be moving even if one or more men in it were pinned, at which point they can still have Terrain cards played or discarded on them - they just can't have additional Movement cards played on them.

title: Lateral Group Transfer (LGT) and Relative Range (RR)

3

author: aram12
consensus_answer:
do the rules outside of scenario X prohibit more than 2 groups sharing an ID?

Yes. Rule 17.7 on Lateral Group Transfer, second and third sentence: "In doing so, [a group] attempts to assume the identity of an adjacent, previously non-existant group. Such a group ID transfer can occur only if there is no other friendly group in that position at the start of the turn."

There is of course the exception later in the rule about groups swapping position. The rule also does not specifically forbid the situation where groups A and C both attempt to transfer to a previously-nonexistent group B slot, but I think the intent is clear. (In that case I would think groups A and C could both declare they were transferring to the B slot, but the first one to have terrain played on it and accepted becomes group B and the other one is now simply moving sideways in the usual way.)

replies.body: The rules and errata don't cover this situation with respect to groups of men (although Encirclement partially relates to it), however, rule 29.5 states that AFVs which make an Overrun attack on the group opposite them may then play movement cards to move through that group, which implies that said situation can exist.

And thus my confusion...

So...

3

2 -------     3

'b' has advanced to naturally flank 'A'

Then...

'A' performs LGT to become 'B'

----------(becomes B)
-----------3

--------        
2----------          3

And my brain explodes...

So what I see here is that 'a' can now RETREAT 1 and thus naturally flank 'A'...is that correct? i.e. the battlefield has "flipped"...

EDIT: OR...are 'A' and 'b' facing away from each other?

I have follow up questions, but I'll start simply because they become moot depending on the answer.

3

3

Can this exist?  Or any permutation where two "opposite" groups are at a range whose sum is greater than 5?

Short answer.  Yes.  See Scenario X:  Surrounded.  (More below)

Yes, 2 groups with different Group ID's can pass each other get to range chit total of 6 or more and then lateral transfer to then have the same ID.  (Though this is rare.  The rules only disallow groups at RR5 with same ID chit from further advancement (i.e. "going through") with the exception an AFV after an overrun.   

This happens all of the time in Scenario X:  Surrounded--where the attacking side splits his men into 2 "forces":  one starts at RC0 the other at RC10.  Encirclements/Natural flanking are only allowed in this scenario when accomplished using two groups from the same "force". 

This does create a few issues to consider with regards to encirclement and natural flanking--but they aren't really that hard to figure out (the "front" group would be at RR6 (or higher) and "Flanking/encircling" group have to be at RR4.  (To answer your second question is YES--the Flanking would have to retreat to RR4 to reflank.  Note this disallowed if the group is encircled.)

But this situation comes up so rarely it really not worth thinking about--it's a bit like asking what happens when when you are traveling at light speed and you turn on your headlights?

I've only been playing for a short time, but it seems that the situation would come up quite often...a solitary group moves to flank from RR5 to RR4, just like I detailed above...amoung all the other things that remove the natural flanking, an LGT does so as well...if you don't have wire, an LGT seems the best way to get out of flank.  As someone who has seen and played more games than I have, what am I missing here?

What you're missing is that only certain particular group arrangements allow this sort of thing to happen, and they don't arise all that often. For example, your initial example requires the capital-letter side to have no group B, which means either they have groups A and C (and maybe D), or just a solitary group A. In my experience, a situation where you have A and C but no B is rare (you usually want an A and B for effective concentration of fire), and if you have just an A and no other groups, you have worse problems to worry about than strange flanking situations and are likely going to lose the game soon (due to your opponent having a larger hand due to Unbalanced Position and due to you only being able to take one action a turn).

There are many reasons why your situation doesn't happen too frequently.

A)  A lateral transfer is not required to break the flank--any movement card, even to remove wire, break the flank.  You could move sideways (without transfer) or retreat.  Natural Flanking is INITIATED when the movement card is played to put the Flanking group at RR6.  A Flanking Chit is always removed (whether acquired naturally or through a Flank card) when the FLANKED group moves (even to remove wire), enters terrain or if the FLANKING group moves or is put in wire or if either the Flanking or Front groups are eliminated.

B)  Another reason is that if a group has reached lateral flanking, that means if there are enough men in it, you have no way from stopping it reaching the necessary RC for victory.   In Attack/Defender scenarios, the defender has little incentive to advance so rashly.   If it is VP only scenario, like City Fight, this gives up potentially a lot of VP. 

The moral here is always pay attention to Victory conditions.  If the outside group is a threat to win, you laterally transfer before your situation can come up. 

C)  Moving at RR5 to any group is highly dangerous--opposing groups will high firepower and you give yourself an additional +1 modifier.  You could get stuck in wire or a stream or abandoning good terrain for not so terrain.  Etc.  When groups try these sorts of things, they usually end up dead.  The other way to lose is get your squad broken.

I have played over 1000 games of Up Front, I doubt natural flanking has come up more than 10 times.

do the rules outside of scenario X prohibit more than 2 groups sharing an ID?

Yes. Rule 17.7 on Lateral Group Transfer, second and third sentence: "In doing so, [a group] attempts to assume the identity of an adjacent, previously non-existant group. Such a group ID transfer can occur only if there is no other friendly group in that position at the start of the turn."

title: Panic, KIA and Rout
question:
Ok, I think I know what happens in this situation, but I would like to get a consensus from the group:

Japanese PC #6 (Pvt Fujiyama) is pinned. His group is attacked and the Final Combat Number against him is a 5.

5 is > his Panic value of 4, so he's going to be removed from the game unless wounded.

Checking column 0r on the RNC (#6) gives a 6, which is less than the 7 needed for Fujiyama to rout. So no rout and no wound occurs.

However, 6 is greater than his Panic value of 4, so he's not considered KIA (per 6.53, which says that he's considered KIA only if the RPN is <= his Panic value).

What happens? It's clear from the first sentence of 6.53 that Fujiyama is removed from the game, but does he take his weapon with him, and does he really not earn VP because he didn't Rout or get KIA?

That just seems...weird...

This situation only occurs with the Japanese, right? And possibly with partisans?

Thanks!
author: Groo123
consensus_answer:
Yes, the procedure you listed is the way I was taught and always played. However, in teaching the game to some others the situation with Fujiyama came up and we managed to overlook 45.32.

However, in reading the rules closely, my opponent pointed out the wording of 6.53, specifically the bit about the PC is only considered KIA if the 0r RPN is <= the PC's Panic value. The Japanese seemed an exception, but clearly are not. In the case where a PC's Panic is 1 less than his Rout, which I think would > the PC's Panic and < his Rout.

I agree that the steps you listed are the way to play. That's how I've always played and seen the game played, but having a new player point this out--and having carefully reread the relevant rule sections--made me wonder if

a) the developer really intended for there to be a case where a PC is removed but isn't counted as KIA or Routed (which would be just weird...)

b) it's just another case where the rules don't (quite) mean what they say

My vote is for B. 

Anyway, thanks for taking the time to respond. Much appreciated. Now back to more playing and less worrying about the rules. ;-)

Use the following procedure when a fire attack value is generated against a pinned man:

1. Is the value less than the man's Panic value? Yes: nothing happens. No: go to 2.
2. Is the value greater than or equal to the man's KIA value? Yes: he is KIA. No: go to 3.
2. Is the "0r" column value greater than the man's Rout value? Yes: he routs (or is wounded if 7w equals his printed Morale). No: He is considered KIA (or is wounded if the fire attack value exactly equalled his Panic value and 7w equals his printed Morale).

Ignore the parenthetical statements about wounding if you aren't playing with those rules.

This procedure leaves no cases uncovered. A removed man will always be considered KIA or routed.

title: Lateral Group Transfer Qs
question:
I'm just getting into Up Front and have played a couple times through the very abbreviated game--up through Rule 16. A couple things in Lateral Group Transfer have me stumped.

1) This question comes from the Up Front play-through published in the old Avalon Hill General, Vol. 21, #1. Because a developer of the game was playing, I assume this must be a legal move. But it sure seems as though it goes specifically against the stated rule.

On Turn #6 the German player begins his turn with two groups in play, Group A and Group B. He plays two Movement cards to shift both groups laterally in the same turn. (B begins movement to Group C; A begins movement to Group B) Is that possible? Clearly Group B can move laterally to C, but I thought Group A couldn't move because Group B existed at the start of the turn.

One way I can read this move as consistent with the rule is that the completion of the lateral movement (i.e., getting terrain and switching group ID) is what can occur only when moving into an empty slot. Is that a correct interpretation?

2) How on earth does Lateral Group Transfer and the Marsh card work? If a group begins in a marsh and plays a lateral movement, can it on the next turn "stay" in that marsh but switch ID chits (so no new terrain is required)? Or does it have to play two lateral moves and also new terrain to complete its move?

I don't know that it matters, but I have 1st edition rules. Thanks for any input!
author: ACK ACK
consensus_answer:
17.7 is oddly worded.  "...In doing so, it attempts to assume the identity of an adjacent, previously non-existant group.  Such a group ID transfer can occur only if there is no other friendly group in that position at the start of the turn."

But then that rule goes on to explain how two groups could simultaneously exchange positions, thereby assuming the identity of a previously existing group and one that started the turn in that very group.  

So what were they trying to say by "previously non-existant group" as the next sentence takes away the "just currently vacant" interpretation?

True, the way the rule is written doesn't seem to allow this.  The only alternative would be to use this sequence of actions over three turns to transfer both groups:
-  Initiate transfer with B to C.
-  Complete B's transfer which becomes C.  Then initiate A's transfer.
-  Complete A's transfer to B.

It seems needlessly picayune to require this.

The first movement card required to exit a marsh cannot be used to initiate a lateral transfer.  The second movement card can be--since you could advance, retreat or MOVE SIDEWAYS only with second card.

I recently played Delayed Action.  In this one you need 5 unpinned guys/in terrain/reduce fire/at RR5 to win as the attacker.  I setup a Group in D to be the one that achieves this goal.  What I found interesting is Group D can never be at RR5 to Group B right?  Or if I were to move to Range Chit 6 with B at RC0, is that then RR5 to each other?

Not knowing that, instead at RC5, I laterally transferred to Group C.  And there's a significant benefit to this.  The defending group never gets a shot at RR5 because the group transfer doesn't happen until it's put into terrain.  Furthermore, it doesn't appear you have to announce which way you're transferring.  Of course a Group D can only go to C.  But Group C without any B or D can announce a transfer without saying which way it's going, so it appears.

I just found this to be a significant strategy that the defender doesn't get a RR5 shot off before you are able to place your terrain and win.
Defender should have shifted a group to protect his flank  that your attacker was  turning ...

If the field looks like this:

German:.....A-B-C
American:..A-B

Can german move their C to D?
Yes
So why does the first sentence of 17.7 include "... directly opposite an opposing group ..."

I think it is a poorly written rule.  Groups can clearly exist w/o an opposing group directly opposite them.  I see no reason why a lateral group transfer should be limited to moving only into a position that is still directly opposite an enemy group.

I wondered if the intention was that it's okay to move TO a position that has no directly opposing group but it's not okay to move FROM a position where there is no directly opposing group? Possible rationale being that if you have AB opposite AB then you want the B's to have the option of trying to flank and then encircle each other but if you have AB opposite ABC then C moving to D to reduce RR is akin to running away from the battlefield? The problem with this interpretation is that with AB opposite AB, after one B moved to C the other one wouldn't be able to follow and that surely couldn't be intended. This would be fixed if it said you can group lateral transfer if there is either a group directly opposite before AND/OR after you move.

My read is/has been that it is just a highlight of how to maneuver away from a blocking opponent, not a requirement to be blocked first.  Read it the context of following all the preceding limitations rules and this is a maneuver that can overcome them.

My understanding is that the following would happen:

Situation: Marsh / sideways move / forward move

Terrain rejection #1: forward move changes to sideways, reduce range chit

Situation: Marsh / sideways move / sideways move

Terrain rejection #2: topmost sideways move removed, no change to range chit

Nope.  It is possible, however unlikely, through repeated rejection of terrain to be placed back in the original terrain.  

All old terrain and movement cards are only removed from a group and placed in the discarded when a new permanent terrain card is placed on the group.  (Exception: placing n open terrain card on a moving group in wire does NOT remove the wire, but does remove the movement card(s) and old permanent terrain.) 

Only the top two movement cards card (or the top movement and permanent terrain card) + any artificial terrain (i.e. Smoke & Wire) ARE COUNTED for determining TEM's.  So a group moving (+1) from Smoky (-1) woods (-2) gets placed in a Wire (+1), the net defensive TEM is -1.  Or a group with 2 (or 17) movement cards on it has a defensive TEM of +2.

Here's a situation I couldn't find in the rulebook:

French group A is range marker 1
German group A is range marker 4

French plays red RNC Movement card to go to chit 0
Germans moves to chit 5

However, this situation is not likely to happen in an actual game.  
-  Not much reason for the French to retreat here--the Germans are either already at the range they need for victory in N@4 or the retreat will allow them to advance to range they need in an N@5.  In a VP scenario, this simply gives away VP.

This only makes any sense in a rear guard/delaying action type or Ambush scenario.  In which case, if the French are given any terrain that they can reject, they will almost certainly accept it.  

It did come up in a game. Scen C. The French were retreating back to range chit zero, beside their pillbox group.

title: Removing a minefield question
question:
A 4 man group stumbles into a minefield. One man is pinned. You decide to try remove it:

"24.5 REMOVAL:  If the group in the Minefield contains any unpinned man, he may attempt to clear a path through the Minefield  without playing a movement card  and thereby remove the Minefield card by drawing a black RNC > the Fire Strength of the Minefield. The attempt to remove the Minefield card counts as that group's only allowed action for the turn. If successful, the Minefield card is flipped over to represent Open Ground. However, if a red 5 or red 6 RNC is drawn, that man must undergo Minefield attack as per [24.31]"

Do you predesignate which of the unpinned men is undertaking the removal attempt (and therefore risking the red 5/6 attack) or do you just use a RPC check among the 3 unpinned men if you draw a red 5/6?

I can see it either way. The rule points you to 24.31 which includes the RPC procedure. However, the use of "he" in the phrase "he may attempt" makes it sound predesignated.

-Grant
author: sushidog
consensus_answer:
I vaguely recall a house rule where we allowed all unpinned men to try to clear and granting a "bonus" for each soldier after the first and using an rpc if the minefield attacked to determine which soldier took the check.

I remember it working for us but we were toying with the idea of also increasing the chance for the minefield to attack but never got that tested before my life changed and I stopped playing games as often as I like.
