title: Trouble with Move/Terrain/Range Rules
question:
I'm having a bit of trouble with the basic move/terrain/range rules and am hoping I can get clarifications. A few scenarios:

A group is in brush (-1) and has a move played on it (+1). Am I correct that the defensive fire modifier is 0? Is the group still considered to be in the brush, only moving? If I play another move on them, I believe that means they have left the brush and are in open ground, but still moving. What is the defensive modifier now, +1?

A group is in a gully where they cannot be fired upon (some exceptions) and has a move played on it. Units still cannot fire on it (again there are exceptions). If another move card is played on them, they are still considered to be in the gully, but can now be fired upon at... -2 (gully) and +1 (move)? If they play a 3rd move, are they now in the open? What is the defensive fire modifier?

Scenario A requires units to be at "Range Chit 4" to win. I get it that if they have 4 moves played on them they will be there, but what if the opposing group is at range 2? Does that mean they cannot push to 4 without eliminating or otherwise pushing the enemy back to range 1 (since the max range is 5)?

Thanks for your clarifications.
author: MikeWhit
consensus_answer:
I'm having a bit of trouble with the basic move/terrain/range rules and am hoping I can get clarifications. A few scenarios:

A group is in brush (-1) and has a move played on it (+1). Am I correct that the defensive fire modifier is 0? Is the group still considered to be in the brush, only moving? If I play another move on them, I believe that means they have left the brush and are in open ground, but still moving. What is the defensive modifier now, +1?

Basically, only the last two movement and/or "permanent" terrain cards are counted for terrain effect modifiers.  Everything in your example is correct except  terrain/move/move you only consider the two movement cards so it's a +2.  Terrain/move/move/move is also +2.

Also note technically, you do not discard movement or terrain until you enter new permanent terrain  *found in the errata) as it is possible to reject terrain multiple times and be forced back into the original terrain. 

A group is in a gully where they cannot be fired upon (some exceptions) and has a move played on it. Units still cannot fire on it (again there are exceptions). If another move card is played on them, they are still considered to be in the gully, but can now be fired upon at... -2 (gully) and +1 (move)? If they play a 3rd move, are they now in the open? What is the defensive fire modifier?

Nope.  Gullies are confusing, but the effect is NOT as as you describe:
The the firing group is  not on a Hill or at RR5, Gullies "hide" the first movement card played and  work as follows:
-  No move: can't be fired on
-  1 move:  can't be fired on (also moving group can now go into new terrain.  There is no exception that prevents terrain being played on a moving group in a gully.)
-  2 movements:  +1  (The terrain has no effect, but first move is considered to be "hidden" from the firer.  It is an exception to the "only last 2 movement/terrain cards count")
-  3 movements:  +2  (as per the "last two movement/terrain cards count" rule.)

If the firer is on a hill or at RR5, the defender gets a -2 TEM and there is no hidden movements, treat like any other terrain situation.  (Only last 2 movement/terrain count, etc.)

Scenario A requires units to be at "Range Chit 4" to win. I get it that if they have 4 moves played on them they will be there, but what if the opposing group is at range 2? Does that mean they cannot push to 4 without eliminating or otherwise pushing the enemy back to range 1 (since the max range is 5)?

You are ignoring one possibility-lateral movement (called "Group transfer" in the rules.)  This allows you move laterally changing Grouip B to Group C by declaring the start of the transfer when you play a sideways movement card and the completing the transfer when playing terrain on the group.  

This would allow bypassing an enemy group to reach range chit 4.

author: DiploGuy
consensus_answer:
I played this scenario for the first time last night and am a bit confused by the victory conditions.

So are many other people  ;-)

First it says the German's must get to range chit 5 with half of his forces, that must mean counting from the start of the game and not recalculating every time he loses a soldier right.

It probably should say 5 men.  But if you play it with DYO, it could be a different number.

It says victory points are only awarded for casualties.  A casualty is being wounded or killed in military terms.  Does this scenario mean that as well?  I think it's trying to say you don't get points for panic or rout, only for KIA (and possibly wounds as well). 

Nope--casualties also includes desertion (i.e. rout) or missing (i.e. voluntary panic/rout) or men captured.
 
Casualty VP's are:
-  1VP per rout or wounded opponent, 
-  2VP per KIA, 
-  5VP per prisoner 

It also, though poorly worded, seems to say only the Partisans get aggressive action points.

That is correct.  The partisans can gain points for advancing and will lose points for retreating to negative range chits.  The Germans do not.

title: Question about rule 13.23 Smoke
question:
13.23. Smoke does not prevent a Terrain card from being played on a previously placed Movement card, it merely adds to the defensive value of the last played Terrain card beneath it in that group.

I have trouble understanding the above rule. I thought only open ground can be played beneath a smoke card and any terrain played above a smoke card will cancel it?
author: raintree
consensus_answer:
But if it discard the smoke beneath it, why would it adds to the defensive value of the last played terrain card?

And what is there to stop me from moving range 0 to range 5 in the cover of smoke simply by playing move, open ground, move, open ground.

I think you have a bit of a misunderstanding here - new cards aren't played or discarded beneath smoke cards which are already on the table. A terrain card played on a group which has smoke present is played above the smoke, and immediately gets rid of the smoke cards. You can't play a card beneath a smoke card which is already present on the table.

To move from 0 to 5 under cover of a single smoke card as you describe in the second paragraph therefore isn't possible. 

13.23. Smoke does not prevent a Terrain card from being played on a previously placed Movement card, it merely adds to the defensive value of the last played Terrain card beneath it in that group.

I have trouble understanding the above rule. I thought only open ground can be played beneath a smoke card and any terrain played above a smoke card will cancel it?

Referring to 'the last played terrain card beneath it' does not mean you can play a terrain card beneath previously placed smoke. It just refers to terrain cards which were present before the smoke card was played. I think this is the crux of your misunderstanding here.

Regarding 'only open ground can be played beneath a terrain card'. Any terrain card can be played on top of a smoke card, providing there is a movement card already present.

The rule says two things:
1. Smoke does not prevent a Terrain card from being played on a previously placed Movement card. For example, you could place Smoke, then move and then could place terrain.  Smoke does not prevent being able to place terrain.

2. Smoke adds to the defensive value of the last played Terrain card beneath it in that group.  So, the presence of Smoke provides a defensive benefit.  I don't like the way this part of the rule is worded though.  If I place two Movement cards in a row, then the defensive value of the terrain beneath those two cards is no longer applied.  But the Smoke benefit is still applied.  Or have I been playing that wrong all these years?

I think you have a bit of a misunderstanding here - new cards aren't played or discarded beneath smoke cards which are already on the table. A terrain card played on a group which has smoke present is played above the smoke, and immediately gets rid of the smoke cards. You can't play a card beneath a smoke card which is already present on the table.

To move from 0 to 5 under cover of a single smoke card as you describe in the second paragraph therefore isn't possible. 

13.23. Smoke does not prevent a Terrain card from being played on a previously placed Movement card, it merely adds to the defensive value of the last played Terrain card beneath it in that group.

Just got done playing an intense battle of V. Ambush.  I won with 7 cards left by way of CC.  I had to eliminated 14 Japanese soldiers due to their 75% squad break rule and the reinforcements he got during the game.

author: raintree

You're right:

17.9 Once play begins, a new group can be created only by the arrival of reinforcements [35.0] or splitting an existing group by individual transfer.

You can create any new group (except E and Z) if the spot is empty. Creation is done by simultaneously transferring two men from ONE other group. title: What exactly is a 'turn'?
question:
If I pin my opponent's SL and he rallys him on his turn does he still receive 1 less card?

If I fire and a breeze card appears can my opponent play smoke on his turn?
author: Sitnam
consensus_answer:
If I pin my opponent's SL and he rallys him on his turn does he still receive 1 less card?

No.  If a player's SL (or ASL if the SL is eliminated) is pinned when he draws cards, he draws one fewer card.  If my opponent pins my SL and I rally him on the very next turn, I draw my full allotment of cards.

Also on the player's next turn after his SL is eliminated, a player always draws one fewer card--whether or not the ASL is punned.

If I fire and a breeze card appears can my opponent play smoke on his turn?
Yes.  Breeze only applies on the turn it was drawn.

A turn is one player's assigned of actions and ends with refilling his hand.

Later in the thread:
I suppose if it's near the end of the third deck and you already have the card or cards you need to win a sudden death victory. 

Actually you can always choose not refill your hand.  And you might choose to do so if you think the final deck will run out as you suggest.  No need to worry about whether SL/ASL is pinned or not.

title: Wounded men exchanging weapons?
question:
Just played U. Armor, I Japan my opponent British.  I got smoked.  Anyways something came up I've never experienced and the rules weren't clear enough.

PFC Yoruba (LMG) ended up getting wounded.  The resulting 1/2 FP penalty for the LMG is significant.  So I wanted to give it to an unwounded soldier but couldn't find the right procedure.
 
33.6 PORTAGE says a wounded man may not carry both a primary and secondary weapon, he must abandon one.  Do you think this rule still applies if he only has a primary weapon?  The rule further says that the abandoned weapon is acquired under the normal acquisition rules.  It doesn't specify the abandoning rule though.  Would you say it's an action to abandon a weapon?  

There is the weapon exchange rule at 18.21, which does allow a wounded man to automatically (as an action, no RNC needed) give his secondary weapon to  a man.  And it implies that a wounded man may voluntarily exchange his weapon however an unwounded man isn't allowed to, so who could the wounded man be exchanging with?  

I guess what I'm asking then is can a wounded man abandon his primary weapon.  Then an unwounded man could attempt to acquire it.  This would be a way around the exchanging procedure.

If what I'm asking isn't possible, shouldn't it be?  Your LMG gunner is wounded, isn't it normal for another soldier to take over the use of the powerful weapon?
author: DiploGuy
consensus_answer:
Hey Mark. Good to finally hear from you...:)
I think you may be able to have the Ass gunner take over the gun. You could then have the wound guy be an Ass. gunner at no detriment.
I believe that is how I have played it. 

Yeah I know, I went away for a bit...

Yeah the crew guy I believe can take possession of the gun from the wounded guy.  But the LMG I was using wasn't a crewed weapon.  

For the 2nd Edition only: 

18.21 & 33.3 To clarify these two rules:  

 A pinned man can never be involved in a weapon exchange.  

 Weapon exchanges of primary weapons must involve at least one wounded man.  

 Weapon exchanges of secondary weapons need not involve a wounded man.  

I wonder how you're seeing it that clearly in the rules.  

18.21 Weapon Exchange:...Primary weapons of pinned and unwounded men cannot be voluntarily exchanged." 

This rule implies that primary weapons may be exchanged.  For if that wasn't the case the rule would read "...primary weapons may not be exchanged..."  So who's left out in the list of who cannot voluntarily exchange?  Wounded men.  Well who can they exchange with then if an unwounded or pinned man can't do it?  So I'm thinking the wounded man needs to abandon it first.  The portage rule does allow for abandoning a weapon, but it seems to be in only the case where the man has both a primary and secondary weapon.

There is one way around all of this though.  Voluntary panic.  You just gotta wait for your wounded guy to get pinned so you can panic him and have his weapon picked up.

title: Ordnance firing + action for the group?
question: Multiple ordnances may fire from the same group separately on the same turn with multiple fire cards.  If the group fires normally for its action May ordnance still fire from the same group?
author: Sitnam
consensus_answer:
No.

25.2 A group may not make an ordnance attack in addition to a normal firepower attack, nor may two or more ordnance weapons combine to make a single attack. Therefore, an AFV which would otherwise be capable of both a normal firepower attack and an ordnance attack may use only one type of attack per turn. However, two different pieces of ordnance in the same group could each fire in the same turn at the same target as one Action, but each would require play of its own Fire card and would resolve its own To Hit attempt (and the effect of any hit obtained) separately. 

In practice, even two ordnance weapons in the same group at the same target should never come up.  All putting both in the same group would do is restrict firing the second weapon to the same target only if you have second fire card.
 It wasn't clear in the abridged version of the rules provided here.  It's odd to me to allow any number of ordinance to fire separately with fire cards but not let nonordnance fire separately in addition.  But if that's the rule, that's the rule.  Thank you.

title: Only two ASL?
question:
I'm working my way through the scenarios solo to learn the rules and scenario D calls for the Germans in a defensive posture to begin with no SL and two ASL.  Since there is no SL and ASL dynamic I take it if one is lost or panicked the opposing player doesn't get an additional card draw at the end of their turn since neither is the head of the squad.

Is that correct?

Following on from your query, there may be a misapprehension about the effect of NCO casualties.  If a player's current SL is pinned, his hand size is reduced until the SL is rallied (the status of the ASL is immaterial at this point) [15.2].  If the SL is killed or panics, the hand is reduced by one for one complete turn and then reverts to normal provided the ASL is able to take over (ie is still alive and not pinned).  If the ASL is killed or panics the one-card reduction becomes permanent. [15.4]

The increase in hand size by one card comes if your opponent is reduced to a single group. [15.6]  Whether he has lost SL or ASL doesn't affect this.

title: Does anyone understand the following rule?
question:
25.43 The Random Number on the to hit RNC is never added to the effect number of a hit if a black 0 RNC would not also have resulted in that hit.

I think it means that if the target were moving and only red RNC hits count then the number drawn is not added. I think...
author: Aaronplays
consensus_answer:
25.43 The Random Number on the to hit RNC is never added to the effect number of a hit if a black 0 RNC would not also have resulted in that hit.

As explained above:
If the To Hit # is expressed as 0-N, if you get a hit you add the number drawn to the effect--which may mean you hit the bullseye (i.e. drawing an N), rather than just hitting the target (Drawing a 0).

If the To Hit # is expressed as N, the best you can do is just hit thge target.

I think it means that if the target were moving and only red RNC hits count then the number drawn is not added. I think...

When there is a moving target (or moving firer, it they can fire while moving), only Black To Hit RNC's can cause a hit.  Red RNC's always miss in moving target/firing ordnance attacks.  (Moving target and moving firer reduces the To Hit by 1 step (i.e. 0-2 --> 0-1 --> 0 -->  1 --> 2) as well as causing Red RNC's to be misses.)

replies.body:
Normally the RNC is added to the Effect Number for the Final Effect Number to be applied. 

Eff Number: 5

Conditions dictate I need a Red or Black RNC of 0 through 2 to Hit.

I draw a TH RNC of a Red 1.

Hit!

Eff Number 5 +1 Red RNC is 6 for a final Effect Number.  Then resolve against the target.

----------------

Eff Number: 5

Conditions dictate I need a Black or Red RNC of 0 through 2 to Hit, then my opponent plays a concealment -3 driving the TH frequency down.

0-2
0-1
0
1

Now I need a hard 1 RNC, (Black RNC if the tgt is moving or hull down)

I draw a TH RNC of a Red 1.

Hit!

Eff Number 5, but a RNC 0 would not have got me a hit.  I needed a hard 1.  So Effect Number 5 +0 because the RNC 1 does not qualify. Final effect number is 5. 

Then resolve against the target

If this rule didn't exist, there would be a paradox in which a more difficult shot would be less likely to hit, but when it did hit, it would cause a stronger hit than if the concealment card hadn't been played.

It makes sense when you play it, like everything else in this superlative game!

As I think the previous answers will have illustrated, the idea is that if it's a difficult shot - eg a straight "2" to hit - the best you can do is get the basic damage - Hit Strength 5 in the example quoted.

If, however, it's an easier shot - eg "0-2" to hit - you may get a better result (dropping the HE round very close to the target).  So if you hit with a "0" it's the basic damage, but if you hit with a "1" you do a bit better and get an extra 1 to the Hit Strength.  Even better if you hit with a "2".

In the extreme case where it's a "0-5" to hit and you hit with a "5", you can do a LOT of damage!

title: Sandstorms and Victory Conditions
question:
I was playing a game with Bruce Wigdor using his Internet Up Front program.  The program randomly selects a scenario including desert/night/jungle rules.  This time the program selected scenario U:  Armor, me as the attacking Germans vs. Bruce's defending British, using Desert rules.

The scenario went very well for me after two decks the board looked like this:
British:                  B: 1 man (RC0,OG)     C: 4 men (R0, Oasis/Ent)
German:  A: 2 men (RC1)   B: 6 men (RC3,Wadi)   C: AFV (R2 OG)

Starting the third deck, a Red 6 is drawn and the dreaded sandstorm hits.  The question is who wins.

The victory conditions for Scenario U say in full:
The first player to have at least four unpinned Personality cards in one or more non-infiltrated groups at Range Chit 4 or 5 occupying any Terrain which will reduce the Fire Strength of an attack against them is the winner. If neither player accomplishes this by the time limit, the defending player wins.

Note:  Also Scenarios E, F & T also having similar wording as U.  "If neither player accomplishes the victory condition by the time limit, the defender wins." 

The rules for sandstorms read in full:
52.4 SANDSTORMS: Violent windstorms in the desert were fairly common and brought all fighting to a halt due to reduced visibility and clogged weapons.  Whenever a sandstorm occurs, the scenario immediately ends and is decided by points scored up to that point. Players must check for sandstorms at the end of each deck by drawing a RNC. If the RNC is a red 6, the scenario ends at that point.

Very clear reading of these rules:  
-  The game did not end by time limit, the automatic defender VC does not apply.
-  The sandstorm rule clearly says when sandstorms occur determine the victor by VP's.  The attacking Germans are leading by 28-0 at the time.   

(Also obviously the Germans are only one British elimination from a squad break or advancing group B one more space forward and placing into good defensive terrain for a victory.  Deus ex Machina to the extreme.)

I found no reference in the errata compiled by Andy Maly (http://www.boardgamegeek.com/filepage/70811/up-front-errata) or checking all of the game end and victory condition rules in section 16 that would in any way contradict that interpretation.  

The program awarded the victory to the defending British  and I have no reason to doubt that was Bruce's honest interpretation of the rules.  (Also until I looked the rules up, I would have said the same thing.)   And he certainly feels it is most realistic way to interpret how victory should be determined when a sandstorm occurs.  

But the way the rules are written, I see no way to interpret them so the defender wins this scenario.

Though clearly, this dispute means is between a win or a loss from both sides, I mainly want to find out what other player's opinion on this situation.  And in how these rules should be interpreted in the future.

My personal opinion is the sandstorm rule is capricious, unfair, and totally arbitrary and mainly added for humor value.  If rule like the sandstorm "saved" a game where I was losing extremely badly with no other way to way to avoid the loss, I would be embarrassed.  I would take no pride in such a "victory".  (I "won" a game of Hannibal on a 3000-1 series of die rolls--soured me on the game forever.)  Sandstorms really should not be applied in "serious" (i.e. tournament or league) play. 

Addendum:  A thornier issue applies when the victory conditions state "Defender wins by avoiding Attacker victory conditions" which occurs in many attacker vs. defender scenarios (C, G, H, I, L, O, P, Q, R, S, V, W, X)  

Clearly there is contradiction:  The sandstorm rules simply that Victory Points are to be counted when the sandstorm occurs.  
Basically was this meant to:
-  replace the regular victory conditions of the scenario 
OR 
-  augment the existing victory conditions so the "Defender wins by avoid attackers VC's" still applies?

Other issues:  Scenario D states the attacking must complete their either of VC's "by scenario end"  (Certainly it would play out same as above.)  Scenario K, the Attacking Elite player must win both segments and the errata specifically removes Victory Points as a consideration.  This works out to the same as "DwbaAVC's"

I certainly understand consistency would be desirable, but I don't know which way is correct.
author: rri1
consensus_answer:
I believe that Bruce programmed it correctly.

52.4 states: Whenever a sandstorm occurs, the scenario immediately ends and is decided by points scored up to that point.

Referring to 16.4, Victory Points

Should a scenario end due to time limit  and the Victory Conditions for that scenario do not include the condition that one player wins by denying the opponent's Victory Conditions, the winner is decided by the side having the most Victory Points.

The scenario did end due to time limit.
The scenario does include the condition that one player wins by denying the opponent's Victory conditions.

If end and not conditional then VP, else conditional.

replies.body:
I feel for both of you!  I have three comments:

1) Yes, the Sandstorm rule is a dispute waiting to happen and I would ignore it.  However, ...

2) I suppose it does reflect a feature of the desert campaign, and one that in general would work to the defenders' advantage.  In reality, if a sandstorm blew up I guess any offensive activity would have to cease, and so realistically a sandstorm would give the defender an auto victory.  VPs would only apply in scenarios where there is no attacker/defender (it would be bizarre to adjudicate a Pillbox scenario on VPs, for example).  But,...

3) I agree that the RaW give the win to the Germans in the case quoted.

Is it possible to argue that the other Desert rules favour either the attacker or defender, and that the Sandstorm rule acts as a balancer for the defender?  I don't see Terrain rules as favouring either side markedly (no Streams, but fewer Woods), and the increased malfunction perhaps hits the defender harder (although in practice it's worse for the Italians whichever role they take).

So my take would be, if you have to use the Sandstorms, only use the VP in the non-attacker scenarios.  But that would have to be a house rule.

Interesting problem.

First of all: yes, the sandstorm rule is lame and probably, as you say, added just for fun. I believe it has been removed from the rules in the 3rd Edition.

Apart from that, let's look at the problem from a little different angle: In reality, which side would the occurence of a sandstorm benefit the most in an attacker/defender situation?
My guess is it would benefit the defenders since they sort of know where they are and have the objective of just hanging in there. The attackers have a different objective which demands more manoevering and activity, all of which are made near impossible by a sandstorm.

Going by victory points to decide who wins when a sandstorm occurs in an attacker/defender scenario would actually benefit the attacker as they likely have more aggressive action VPs.

So, I actually think the system's ruling was OK in this case, though I fully understand your frustration over having lost since you'd most likely have bagged this one pretty soon if the game went on without the sandstorm.

One way could possibly be to count VPs, but only those for KIAs and routs. Then the decisive point would be who has inflicted most losses on the opponent when the game ends due to a sandstorm.

It didn't make sense that an attacker would get credit for a win having done absolutely nothing but, say, moving a 2 man group D to relative range 1 before a sandstorm occurred at the start of the 3rd deck.

Andy replied that a sandstorm should be treated as if the 3rd deck had just expired.  So victory points decide patrols, and the defender wins attacker/defense matchups.  I have no idea why this did not make it into the FAQ/errata, but I remember asking the question and then programming after the answer.

Which is more intuitive: the idea that, because of the threat of sandstorm, that the attackers must hurry to meet their victory conditions sooner, or that the defenders should advance to meet the attackers' superior force on equal terms even though they are outnumbered.  I can imagine "hurry up, we've got to get this done, we've got our orders," but not "let's charge this superior force in case a sandstorm forces them to call off their attack?"

I have no problem with the sandstorm rule, and I have no problem winning with it.  Heaven knows I've lost a lot of games because of a red 6 on a repair attempt.  This is hardly different.  

However, I think everyone is right that the rule did not receive the full attention of those who wrote it.  My feeling is that it was tested with patrol scenarios, and then they copied the rules into Desert War without actually thinking about the attack/defense implications.

Remember that the Desert War rules state at the beginning that the French may indeed be worse than the Italians.  How well tested could Desert War have been if they published it with this clearly incorrect statement?

There's a similar situation with the victory conditions for Scenario K (Elite Troops on the Attack).  The rules say the attacker must win both segments.  Technically, this means that, if the second segment ends after the 4th deck, the game goes to VPs to decide the match.  However, this means that an attacker could take almost the full 4 decks to win the first segment, losing half his men in the process, and then advance to range chit 1 in the final few cards of the game to win it.  Not only is this counterintuitive, but the attackers were doing much better than the defender using this interpretation.  This is another example of where the victory conditions, taken literally, produce a bad result.  I don't remember if Andy ruled on this one or if the league voted to change things, but now we demand that the attacker win the 2nd segment by squad break conditions, or by getting 4 at 4.

I'm not sure if Richard mentioned this, but I was the defender who stands to gain by this win.  However, anybody who knows me knows that this has nothing to do with the side for which I'm arguing.  I am well known for arguing for interpretations that hurt me when they come up in a game.  In fact, as I was doing so once at the WBCs, Don Chappel came up to me and said, "Bruce, you really need to take 'yes' for an answer sometimes."

If Andy decides to reverse his ruling, I will forfeit the match and award the win to Richard.  But I don't think that's the way it should go.

author: gamecat_uk
consensus_answer:
Yeah I can see this, although it would be great to have a mini board as well but I suppose once your used to it's comes like second nature.

First off - welcome to the world of UF. I am the person responsible for writing the rules in this edition so I am very interested in the areas of the rulebook that give you trouble. Please keep the comments coming.

A couple of comments on your other posts:
1.) Game-board - Not having a game-board, even for just tracking Group locations is one of the things that separates UF from all of the other war games out there. The actual battlefield is an abstraction of the real world and creates a unique environment where even the player himself has no idea what is in store right around the corner. 

Another reason why UF doesn't have a game-board is, at least in my opinion, it creates an indirect impression of specific terrain placement. Meaning, if a Group goes through a certain square on the tracking board and was in Brush, and then another Group goes through the same square and finds Woods - it confuses the player. If you retreat back to a previous square, using a board, one would think that it would always be the same terrain. But in the game, this is not always the case.

Thus the lack of a board really helps abstract the game from a set environment where the player can look down from God's point of view and plan their course of movement (see ASL and most other wargames). In UF, the Group and the player never really know what lies ahead... and this makes for a very fun game.

2.) Illustrations in the rulebook - At this time, I have not gone through the rulebook and marked where each image is going to be placed. I have a general idea - but it is something that I will be doing in the near future. I am currently working on proofing the Terrain Decks and other minor adjustments/proofs to the rulebooks. After these are complete, I'll be digging into the layout and marking it up for the layout team to really transform it into the final product.

The Fire cards and the differences between Fire Strength and Firepower will be easily identified when everything is complete. Also, at the beginning of the rulebook will be a series of cards with all of the parts/sections all labeled out for easy reference for newer players.

Anyways, hope this helps you out a bit to understand the "why" certain things are done the way they are.

Take care
TB

If you retreat back to a previous square, using a board, one would think that it would always be the same terrain. But in the game, this is not always the case.

Thus the lack of a board really helps abstract the game from a set environment where the player can look down from God's point of view and plan their course of movement (see ASL and most other wargames). In UF, the Group and the player never really know what lies ahead... and this makes for a very fun game.

title: Changing positions and crewing, 1 or 2 actions?
question:
If you change positions to crew for a weapon does that take 1 or 2 actions?

Imagine a situation where your LMG ends up being the only one left in a group.  You then successfully transfer in two men.  On the enemies turn they fire and pin the man right next to the LMG.  Now on your turn can you move the non-pinned man next to the LMG and crew it in the same turn?
author: DiploGuy
consensus_answer:
OK, let's walk through it.  :)

The LMG is uncrewed.  The player wants to crew the weapon.  How is this done?  Rule 11.12 explains it:  "The player may start the game with an assistant already designated as crew, or he may designate one during his turn as the sole action of that group for that turn (4.25)."

So, you assign a crewman by designating one man to be the crewman.

How to designate a crewman? See rule 11.11: "The man chosen as the assistant must be so designated by placing the two cards next to each other within their group and placing a "crew" counter so that it overlaps both cards."

So the act of designating a crewman involves placing the two cards together.

Rule 11.12 also includes a reference to rule 4.25.  The later rule allows you to "alter the composition of the group by performing [...] change crew assignments [...]."  In other words, taking the one action of designating a crewman will result in an altered group composition.

replies.body: Yes, crew assignment allows the needed reorder in the same action.
It has been a while since I read the rules, but as I recall it crewing is an action all by itself. This means two actions (two turns).

No, it is one action.

See rules 4.25, 11.11 and 11.12.  Rule 4.25 says you may alter the composition of the group by performing one of the following actions: weapon repair attempt, weapon acquistion attempt, change crew assignments, place smoke, attempt to entrench, attempt individual transfer, remove wire or remove mines.

Rule 11.11 says the man chosen as the assistant is designated by placing the two cards together and putting a crew chit on the assistant.

Rule 11.12 covers designating a crewman when one hasn't already been assigned.  It says the player can designate a crewman as the sole action of the group during his turn.

The OP asked about a case where the LMG is not yet crewed.  He can designate the unpinned man as assistant crewman and does so by putting the two cards next to each other and placing a crew chit.

I am not trying to be argumentative, but the rules you quoted do not support your assertion.

The LMG was not crewed. It is an action to crew a weapon (11.12). 4.25 says ONE action (emphasis mine) and moving guys around and assigning a crew are two separate actions.

So, rearranging men in a group is an action. Crewing the weapon is an action. One action per group per turn.

Lt (probably British): Urm, Perkins it seems to be rather wet all of the sudden
Perkins: Yes sir, we, um, seem to have wandered in to a stream
Lt: Fine, every one back up
Perkins: well sir, that would work in theory and we do currently hold four movement cards all with red RNC's but none of them are a ford so we have to try for a black draw 
(four red draws later)
Lt: Perkins, how in the Hades did we get to the middle of this stream with no one noticing?

Hated this rule since I learned how it really worked at my first Avaloncon and the dangers of teaching myself the game and then teaching everyone I played where reinforced.
author: ChandlerB
consensus_answer:
And the "stream" is one of those great moments in UF; it's Do or Die time. Makes the blood rush trying to extract those lads from a particularly sticky wicket they've gotten themselves embroiled in. Forward under fire? Attempt to retreat abit and approach from another path? Or find a flank to cross? 

And it also makes you think twice about moving to that great cover you see later in the game. Wondering if your enemy has been "shorting" his hand abit, laying in a trap for your crossing to seen terrain. Has he been playing out his hand fully, or could he be holding on you? 

A stream card is one that almost always make you think twice about the value of using up one of your valueable spots in your hand (unless of course you're the US or French, with really abit more space normally) to hold incase of being able to use later for devistating effects. Too early it's just a speed bump, and at the end manytimes you're more interested in pure firepower or rallys to finish the enemy or to save your bacon.

In our games steam plays and extractions/massacres were several times the stuff for great stories of the game; Heroic stands to dismal defeats. In our minds it could be any one of many problems, traps, mires, or predicaments that one's either gotten oneself into, or was wilely laid by the enemy. I remember one particullarly nasty "snow-covered ravine" (called by my brother, the Russki) as my Germans floundered in the snows of a wicked winter attempting to hunt the bear in his homeland. 

Course if you're the very fun challenging Italians, you might just want to call it a day and go for a swim. :D

There was a stream near where I lived when I was younger that we used to play in and around.  Some parts of the bank sloped down gently and other parts were dropoffs of about 5 or 6 feet.  Sometimes, part of the bank that had appeared easy to get up would be almost impossible and you'd have to move along the stream, maybe only a couple of feet, maybe quite a way.  I suspect attempting to do it whilst carrying a gun and backpack, possibly under fire, would make it harder.  The stream in Up Front doesn't necessarily mean you're moving as a unit across a stream. It could mean that one of your guys has slipped down a steep bank into a gully and can't get out easily, it could mean that you find yourselves exposed on the bank, it could be a nice shallow stream with gently sloping banks that hardly causes a problem at all.  You don't find out exactly how much of an obstacle it it until you try to ford.

I think that a lot of us who have grown up in the city have no idea what it is like going through wilderness.  You can't just go straight from point A to point B.  the terrain just wont let you.  Terrain features that you had no idea were there really do just appear in your way.  This can be anything from a waterway to a shear drop off that looked perfectly flat 30 meters back.

title: Transferring, what position is the man that's leaving the group?
question:
Here's the situation:

Group A has 1 man in it, Group B is a multi-man group.  I simultaneously transfer 1 man from A into B and from B into A.  I'm doing this to increase my firepower in group B while not having to reduce my hand capacity for having only one group not giving my opponent an extra card in his hand.

My attacker fires on group B.  I know both transferring men get attacked but I don't know which position they are in for the RNC draws.

According to the rules for the proposed new edition (I can't find them in the current edition) it says:
POSITION. When resolving attacks and Snipers while 
Individual Transfer is in progress, those Men undertaking 
Individual Transfer are considered to occupy position 1 
through the number of Individual Transfers, the temporary 
position numbers being allocated by the attacker. The Men 
in the receiving Group occupy the remaining higher 
number positions.

This rule tells me that if I had two men transferring into the same group they both are in position 1 and 2 for the attack and the attacker chooses which of the two is in the 1st position.  What this rule doesn't address, and I can't find it even in the new edition, is if 1 of the two transferring is leaving the group.

So my question is: When a group gets attacked that has one man transferring into it and one man transferring out of it, which position is the man that's transferring out for the RNC draw?
author: DiploGuy
consensus_answer:
Here's the situation:

Group A has 1 man in it, Group B is a multi-man group.  I simultaneously transfer 1 man from A into B and from B into A.  I'm doing this to increase my firepower in group B while not having to reduce my hand capacity for having only one group.

You do NOT have to worry about a reduced hand capacity if you are down to one group.  The penalty for having a single group is to increase your opponent's hand capacity.

Any time you are down to one group, you are in world of hurt.  The risk of transferring a man out seems much worse than allowing your opponent the extra card.

The rule you quote does not specify whether the transferring men are entering or leaving--so entering or leaving does not matter.  (The may be garbled in the wording.  If they mean that, it should read "The Men in the targeted Group occupy the remaining higher 
number positions.")

In the original game, the relevant ruling was in the errata--though it appears to apply only to men transferring into the group:
17.8 When a man is in the process of transferring and the receiving group is fired on, what position does the transferring man occupy for purposes of the fire resolution?
A. Transferring men are always attacked first.

replies.body: What makes you think it matters whether the individual is transferring in or out of the group in question? I'm not seeing that. It just says "undertaking individual transfers," which is the case whether you're entering or leaving.

Here's the situation:

Group A has 1 man in it, Group B is a multi-man group.  I simultaneously transfer 1 man from A into B and from B into A.  I'm doing this to increase my firepower in group B while not having to reduce my hand capacity for having only one group.

You do NOT have to worry about a reduced hand capacity if you are down to one group.  The penalty for having a single group is to increase your opponent's hand capacity.

Any time you are down to one group, you are in world of hurt.  The risk of transferring a man out seems much worse than allowing your opponent the extra card.

My attacker fires on group B.  I know both transferring men get attacked but I don't know which position they are in for the RNC draws.

According to the rules for the proposed new edition (I can't find them in the current edition) it says:
POSITION. When resolving attacks and Snipers while 
Individual Transfer is in progress, those Men undertaking 
Individual Transfer are considered to occupy position 1 
through the number of Individual Transfers, the temporary 
position numbers being allocated by the attacker. The Men 
in the receiving Group occupy the remaining higher 
number positions.

This rule tells me that if I had two men transferring into the same group they both are in position 1 and 2 for the attack and the attacker chooses which of the two is in the 1st position.  What this rule doesn't address, and I can't find it even in the new edition, is if 1 of the two transferring is leaving the group.

So my question is: When a group gets attacked that has one man transferring into it and one man transferring out of it, which position is the man that's transferring out for the RNC draw?

The rule you quote does not specify whether the transferring men are entering or leaving--so entering or leaving does not matter.  (The may be garbled in the wording.  If they mean that, it should read "The Men in the targeted Group occupy the remaining higher

17.8 When a man is in the process of transferring and the receiving group is fired on, what position does the transferring man occupy for purposes of the fire resolution?
A. Transferring men are always attacked first.

title: Close Combat Question
question:
I now have 4 sets of UF Rules to contend with — 
1. my Original 36 page printed rulebook from 1983 complete with Marmalade, Coffee and Wine stains.
2. a pdf copy of 1 with addenda added
3. a pdf Rules Rewrite (not sure of author, or completeness)
4. a pdf File recently made available from BGG (new Edition I think).

Question: CC — Defender has 3 men. I am the attacker and have 2 men who attack Defender N°2. Result is a mutual KIA. We each remove our killed man. I now still have my second man alive and kicking. Does he return to his group or does he directly enter another CC with one of the two remaining defenders? I ask this because he was designated as entering CC at the start of the turn.

Also, I've "adopted" the new ruling on CC entry — (no longer necessary to Infiltrate) - How do the rest of you play this at present? Old rules or new?
author: Masonstone
consensus_answer:
to tag onto this thread, cause the OP seems satisfied with it being answered;  Every turn in which your soldier wants to enter CC, regardless of whether he already had in the previous turn, still requires a morale check first?

I do think the CC process needed to be worked on only because you can burn through a ton of cards in the attempt.  

One way without allowing CC to skip INF first would be to not have the fighting match-ups random, therefore no need to draw RPCs for each man.  I know it wouldn't be fair cause the attacker would make sure he goes after the strongest weapon with multiple men most likely.  Well I'm sure there's something that could be done to guard against that.  

Perhaps like this; The attacker chooses his man's opponent on the even number attacker and the defender chooses the opponent on the odd number attacker. What?  If you attack with 3 men, the defender will choose the opponent for the 1st and 3rd guy and the attacker chooses for the 2nd.  If you attack with 1 guy the defender chooses.  So the only way the attacker could ensure a multi-man fight would be for 4 men entering CC.  And the attacker would need 2 men to ensure he goes after the strongest weapon.  Seems fair to me and eliminates burning through cards for the matchup.

In this situation, the second man attacks only if your first man lost his CC--because second man's target is otherwise eliminated.

Also, not mentioned, is your first man gets a +3 to his CCV because he had an extra man helping him.  The second man would not get this bonus.   

Also, I've "adopted" the new ruling on CC entry — (no longer necessary to Infiltrate) - How do the rest of you play this at present? Old rules or new?

At present, use the old rules--it is doubtful the draft rules recently posted will be the final version, especially in this area.

I am against this change. Besides feeling right to me (it should take some effort to get your guys to get up close and personal with the enemy), I think it served a game purpose by giving you something to do with movement cards once you got in real close to the enemy.

I'll admit to coming from a stodgy grognard point of view on any changes. I'm not crazy about the relative range change, but it doesn't really change anything. This, on the other hand, does impact how the game works, and I was not happy when I heard about it.

Thanks for the reply. I wasn't totally sure due to reading about the case where the defender has a weapon with an assistant crewman — seem to remember that if the Ist guy gets it, then the crewman immediately goes into CC with the attacker. But that's another question.

Regarding the possible revision to the CC rules — from the few plays I4ve had using the easier CC entry — that I'm in favor for this — but does it better represent what did actually happen on the ground back in the 1940s?

I'm not crazy about the relative range change, but it doesn't really change anything. This, on the other hand, does impact how the game works, and I was not happy when I heard about it.

Seconded. The rules of the original game have a bad reputation due to the way they are organized, but this is just a formal thing. The rules themselves (contentwise) make for a great game and I don't see why they should change.

Thinking about this a little more, I'm inclined to go back to the old ways — more problematic for the "player" but then "Life wasn't easy for the guy on the ground" — My Dad is 98 this year, a tank commander in the Ardennes — he never speaks about it — all I have are some tatty B&W photos of him and his buddies when relaxing by their vehicles. Thank God it wasn't me.

Close combat was not too common, especially squad vs. squad.  It's an edge case that the designers included for extra chrome.  And we love Up Front's chrome.  Making it easier is ahistorical and munchkin-y.  So much for the re-designers not monkeying with the game.

He has finished his CC for the turn.  Next turn he can have another go if he's up for it.

As far as the new rules go, I would wait until they are finalised - I believe the new CC rules are still undergoing revision.

OK — will do
Thanks for everyone's input.

title: Infantry Boxed firepower question
question:
Does a soldier that is currently crewing get the "1" boxed fire power? Or would I have to uncrew him to get this? It states that each soldier gets "1", but not sure if this applies to ones that are crewing other weapons. Thanks,
Mike
author: k9mike
consensus_answer:
Does a soldier that is currently crewing get the "1" boxed fire power? Or would I have to uncrew him to get this? It states that each soldier gets "1", but not sure if this applies to ones that are crewing other weapons. Thanks,
Mike

No, a crewman forfeits his own firepower:  boxed or unboxed.

Here is the full quote of the rule:

11.2 A man assigned as an assistant crewman forfeits his own firepower as long as he remains in that capacity, although he does keep possession of his own weapon for possible subsequent use ([18.21] does not apply).

title: Minefield Clarifications
question:
Last night my Ivans got caught up in a double Minefield sandwich with Wire as the dressing — When still in the Minefield my group contained several men including an unpinned Commissar and one Broken man, the MMG gunner.

I had no Rally cards so at the end of my turn I drew the RPC to check for execution. Bingo — the vodka-fueled Commissar drew his pistol and shot the bastard from under his MMG. 

Next turn, I used my Action for the Group to assign another man to 'man' the MMG — and assumed that the existing crew would continue to crew for the 'new' MMG gunner.

Was all this allowable even though I am still in the Minefield?

And secondly, is all normal Fire from Minefield terrain treated normally?
Can the MMG still fire with full FP when crewed?
author: Masonstone
consensus_answer:
Couple of points about your earlier question - if you play a Movement card to remove Wire while you're on the Minefield, there is a chance one of your men will find a mine the hard way:

24.4 ... Whenever a Movement card is played on a Minefield for any reason (including the removal of Wire), a RNC must be drawn. If that RNC is red and > the number specified on the second line of the Minefield card's notes, another man in the group must undergo Minefield attack as per [24.31].

And if you haven't Acquired the MMG before you remove the Wire, playing the Movement card loses the MMG for good!

And finally, firing the MMG fully crewed under Wire not only uses bracketed FP, it uses bracketed breakdown number.

On the topic of how the attacker wins Scenario C, one thing to realise is that you can shift your groups from side to side a lot more easily than the defender, who has to filter all his movements through the Pillbox via Individual Transfer.  You can move your groups to C & D and work to Flank his group C while his Group A flounder in the distance.  If he sets up heavily in Group C, in the other hand, you can advance against his Group A and again his big group is further away.  Since he can only have 3 men in the Pillbox he can't get serious FP from it.

replies.body:
Next turn, I used my Action for the Group to assign another man to 'man' the MMG — and assumed that the existing crew would continue to crew for the 'new' MMG gunner.
A crew-served weapon cannot be acquired by any man other than the assistant crewman unless the assistant crewman is pinned (18.22).

So, unless you left something out (I assume the assistant was unpinned, since you thought you might fire with full FP and had no Rally cards) the assistant crewman has to acquire the MMG, and then you can assign a new assistant crewman to fire at full FP. That's two actions for the group.

None of that has anything to do with the minefield, though.

And secondly, is all normal Fire from Minefield terrain treated normally?
Minefield is a form of Open Ground terrain except where stated otherwise. No modifiers to offense or defense (24.2).

That's not counting the fact that you were in Wire, of course.

Thanks — so I made an error by not assigning the crewman to take up the MMG. I understand that now. Makes sense.
Thanks again

title: LMG, Flanking Fire & Hero card
question:
Say I have an LMG and I play a Hero card on it.  The LMG gets to double its bracketed FP, even if uncrewed or if its crew is pinned.  It doesn't get to double its unbracketed FP.  Correct?

What happens if a Hero card were played on the crewman of the LMG?  Does it impact the FP?

Now, say I have a LMG in a group that has the flanking fire bonus.  As I understand it, the LMG gets to double its unbracketed firepower if it is fully crewed with an unpinned crewman.  If it is uncrewed or its crewman is pinned, I can only double its bracketed firepower.  Correct?

Lastly, say I play a Hero card on the LMG that already has the flanking fire bonus.  The Hero should triple the LMG FP, but what is tripled?  I guess the conservative answer is triple the bracketed FP.  Does anyone know if the rules make it clear how to handle this case?
author: arjisme
consensus_answer:
Say I have an LMG and I play a Hero card on it.  The LMG gets to double its bracketed FP, even if uncrewed or if its crew is pinned.  It doesn't get to double its unbracketed FP.  Correct?

What happens if a Hero card were played on the crewman of the LMG?  Does it impact the FP?

Lastly, say I play a Hero card on the LMG that already has the flanking fire bonus.  The Hero should triple the LMG FP, but what is tripled?  I guess the conservative answer is triple the bracketed FP.  Does anyone know if the rules make it clear how to handle this case?

1) Correct.
2) No - unless he were pinned, when the FP would increase from bracketed to unbracketed.
3) Correct.
4) Correct, triple the bracketed FP.  I can't find a reference in the rules or errata, but the principle is that the Hero only applies to the principal crewman, so his base FP is the bracketed value, which is then increased once for Flanking and once for the Hero.

Mike asked about reinforcements--I am posting this for everyone to see:

Hi.
I know that you are the go to guy for any questions in regard to Up Front... so, here goes.....
In the 501 in 4 games...When units are to come into play as "Reinforcements"...Do they need to play a movement and or movements cards into play to have them move into a Group...group A or D before they are to start being part of the game? Just confused as to how these forces are brought into play and what is needed to do so...
Any help would be greatly appreciated.
Thanks
Mike
aka "k9mike"

They come in as reinforcements using rules in section 35.0:
- The reinforcements enter as a group in E at RC0 in open ground be playing a movement card to the discard pile (Often an optional rule is to allow entry at Group Z using red RNC movement card and Group E using a Black RNC Movement card--from Banzai Random Reinforcements, 49.0)
- If the movement card used to enter is a Flank Movement cards, you may enter at any range chit up to the highest (or lowest) one in a current friendly group.
- If you discard a concealment card and play a terrain at the same time as the movement, you can in a different type of terrain than open ground.

Once in play, the reinforcement group is not moving as Group E (or Z) and can be transferred to D (or A) normally. Groups cannot be at E or Z except as entry as reinforcements (i.e. no transferring from D to E). A second reinforcement group cannot enter at E or Z if the space is occupied.

And the break level is adjusted after reinforcements enter. (so if 4 reinforcements join a 12 man original force, the break level goes from 7 (12/2 + 1) to 9 (16/2+1) for American, German, British, Russians.

As 501 City Fight in Four is a DYO scenario: PC cards entered as reinforcements get a discount:
- 80% of cost if entered after Deck 1
- 50% of cost if entered after Deck 2
- 20% of cost if entered after deck 3
At least half the total PC cards you plan on using must start the game.

Here's a new question that came up in my latest session about reinforcements.

If your reinforcement consists of one man and he's in Group E do you transfer him to adjacent empty groups with a group transfer or an individual transfer?  The IT carries a +2 modifier while the GT appears to have no modifier (besides the sideways movement card).

IT transfer men BETWEEN 2 groups (which can include the last man of a single man group.)  Other requirements:
-  either the sending or receiving group must have an unpinned SL or ASL.
-  The groups must be adjacent and at the same range.
-  1 or more men may be individually transferred with a movement card played to the discard pile for each.

While transferring the men have a +2 modifier and if pinned return to their own group.  The IT ends when the destination group on a later turn accepts any or all the transferring men.

Group creation uses IT rules to split men from an existing group to form a new group.  Two men must be transferred at the same time (each with their own movement card) and the group is created when it has terrain placed on the new group on a later turm.  Also any men are pinned in the act of group creation, all men are returned to to their own group.

GT transfers an ENTIRE group (even a one man group) to a different ID letter--the letter the group is moving to generally must be vacant.  The movement card is played sideways on the group (which applies the +1 modifier) and the transfer ends when the group receives a terrain card (or open ground).

Two simultaneous GT's can be used to swap places of two adjacent groups.  The movement cards must be played on the same turn and both groups must enter terrain on the same later turn.  

You can also transfer two groups simultaneously the same direction, such as A&B to B&C so long as the "Leading" group (in this case B to C) plays its movement card and its terrain on an earlier turn or the same turn as the trailing group, so both groups never have the same group ID.

title: Clarifications needed regarding OT AFVs
question:
I would like to confirm a few things regarding OT AFVs.  First, once Pinned, I see no way to attack the crew at RR < 5 as there is no defense value for the crew shown on the flipped side.  Is that correct?

Second, it looks like a non-CC attack by a group of rifles on an OT AFV crew is very simple to compute.  You take the Fire Strength of the card they are able to use, factor in the attacker's terrain if it applies, factor in attacker movement and then draw an RNC to resolve.  Correct?  So if infantry stationary in Open Ground attack a halftrack at, say, RR2, it is the strength of the Fire card plus the RNC draw compared against the AFV's Morale and CE values.  Yes?

I thought I read something in the rules about AFVs whose names are underlined, but I can't find it for the life of me.  I was playing Scenario E, with Germans on attack and realized I didn't know how the cards explicitly identify which AFVs are OT.  I think the answer is any AFV that does not say "Button Up" on the flip side are OT AFVs.  It makes sense, but I can't spot where in the rules they explicitly define what an OT AFV is.  Can someone point me to that if it is in there?

Edit:  One further question.  An OT AFV is moving when it suffers a Pinned result.  The Movement card stays in play, correct?
author: arjisme
consensus_answer:
I would like to confirm a few things regarding OT AFVs.  First, once Pinned, I see no way to attack the crew at RR < 5 as there is no defense value for the crew shown on the flipped side.  Is that correct?

Except for the Bren Carrier and WASP, no AFV has PANIC values and so cannot be attacked with non-AT weapons when they are pinned or buttoned up.  This apples to ALL AFV's, not just the open topped ones.

Note:  At RR5 vs. an OT AFV, using "inherent boxed FP of 1" does not attack the crew, it is an AT attack vs. the k,i,s AT defense values.  Against a non-OT AFV, this form of attack cannot be used.

Second, it looks like a non-CC attack by a group of rifles on an OT AFV crew is very simple to compute.  You take the Fire Strength of the card they are able to use, factor in the attacker's terrain if it applies, factor in attacker movement and then draw an RNC to resolve.  Correct?  So if infantry stationary in Open Ground attack a halftrack at, say, RR2, it is the strength of the Fire card plus the RNC draw compared against the AFV's Morale and CE values.  Yes?

Against ALL AFV's movement and defensive terrain do NOT affect an unboxed attack (ie. vs. Morale/CE defense values, see 28.32--Defensive TEM DOES apply vs. boxed AT attack.)  Attacker TEM/movement penalties do apply and an AFV cannot play a concealment card.  Actually this is how you conduct non-AT attacks vs. ALL AFV's

Specifically for OT AFV's at RR5:
-  If you play a fire card that requires less firepower than the inherent boxed FP, you may resolve a non-AT attack vs. the OT AFV's Morale (or Panic)/CE values.  Then using the same Fire card, draw another RNC vs. the k,i,s AT defense values.
-  If the OT AFV has an infantry group for its own side adjacent to it at the same RC, the Fire Strength is reduced by 1 on the inherent boxed FP attack.

I thought I read something in the rules about AFVs whose names are underlined, but I can't find it for the life of me. 

Underlined AFV are assault guns, and do not have a rotating turret.   (Rule 28.2)  They are -1TH against moving target, -2TH when bogged or immobilized, and cannot fire while moving. 

 I was playing Scenario E, with Germans on attack and realized I didn't know how the cards explicitly identify which AFVs are OT.  I think the answer is any AFV that does not say "Button Up" on the flip side are OT AFVs.  It makes sense, but I can't spot where in the rules they explicitly define what an OT AFV is.  Can someone point me to that if it is in there?

All OT AFV's have "PINNED: requires Rally 3" on the back.  28.42:  "A Pinned result only applies to an OT AFV or IG."

Edit:  One further question.  An OT AFV is moving when it suffers a Pinned result.  The Movement card stays in play, correct?

Correct.  If you want a justification, the driver is relatively protected and can still drive, but the gunner had to take cover.

title: How to perform Individual Transfer of an Infantry Gun?
question:
I'm reading over the rules for Individual Transfer(IT) and the related errata.  The errata says an IG can do an IT, but rule 34.3 applies.  Looking at rule 34.3, it says a group with an IG in non-Open Ground terrain must play two movement cards before moving to new terrain (details ommitted).

How does this apply to an IT though?  Do you have to discard two Movement cards (one per turn) to initiate IT for an IG?
author: arjisme
consensus_answer:
I believe that the exposure to adverse terrain and/or fire vulnerability are intentional. 

For example, here are the conditions for Transfer for a normal soldier in adverse terrain:

17.81 If the transferring man starts in an unforded Stream, his transfer is conditional on his successful
fording of that Stream. If the transferred man starts in a Marsh, he cannot transfer unless his group
already has a Movement card in play (in which case he need play only one).

So basically what it appears to me is that the soldier in question has to be 'eligble' to move. For a Stream, that means Ford, for a Marsh, that means having a sideways movement in play, and IMO, for an Infantry Gun not in Open Ground, it would also mean having a sideways movement in play since that is the trigger to make the IG 'eligible' for movement.

In addition, in Squad Leader, moving a gun is considered 'Hazardous Movement' and carries a pretty stiff penalty if attacked. Since much of UF stems from Squad Leader, it also follows that any form of movement (including Transfer which is a re-positioning laterally) would carry a similar penalty.

To me, it would be a loophole to allow the IG to Transfer using a method that would be easier than just plain moving. Requiring having a sideways movement card in play keeps the Transfer requirement consistent with the other movement options available to the IG.

Just my $.02 ;)

I would say the second movement card would be the transferring movement as it's the second movement that is changing the position of the IG.  However since technically you discard the movement card for each man transferring and a 2nd movement card is required for an IG to move then maybe it would take a 3rd movement, which is then discarded, to be the transferring action.  Question then is would that be a +4 modifier to that IG for fire attacks against it?  So I guess I didn't help you really. :)   

Though I can't see myself ever transferring a IG into a group.  It just massively slows that group down and makes that group an even bigger target.    Let the poor IG crew draw the enemies fire while you advance the other groups.  

Though knowing how to handle this situation is still prudent.

It seems like the goal is to simply make it 'harder' move the IGs and requiring that extra step appears to accomplish that goal.

So in summary, in Open Ground, you can transfer an IG just like a soldier. If you're in non-Open Ground, you have to play a sideways movement card and then on a following turn you play a movement card for the Transfer.

I was looking at that fording rule today as well.  How do you think that is applied?  Since it applies only to the man attempting to transfer, I think the rule is saying you must discard a ford card OR both discard a movement card and pass a ford attempt check for a man to initiate a transfer from a Stream.

The Marsh situation is clear in that it says the entire group needs to be already moving before he can try to transfer.

The trouble with the IG is that it could be just one PC of several in a group.  So if I have a group with an IG in a Woods terrain, do I have to get the entire group moving sideways first before I can initiate a transfer of the IG?  Or is the intent to apply the movement restrictions just on the IG?  So maybe it should be that you discard a movement card for the IG, then mark it with a chit or some such, then discard another movement card on the next turn (otherwise the chit is removed and the transfer is cancelled).  That creates enough difficulty and exposure for the IG.  It will suffer a +2 modifier for any attack against either group for two turns as well as tying up the transferring group for two turns with its actions.

title: Bazooka vs. AFV
question:
Hi all - just wanted a quick confirmation from one of the experts on high as to whether or not I got this right. Here's the situation:

Crewed U.S. bazooka at RR3 to German SdKfz231 (k=2). U.S. player draws a successful To Hit RNC (red 1) on AFV. The bazooka's boxed effect number is 2, so the final effect number is 2 + RR (3) = 5. This is greater than k=2, so the AFV is KIA.

Is this correct? 

That is the total strenght of the attack.  You still need to draw an RNC to resolve the attack.
consensus_answer:
Hi Peter:

The answer is in 30.5.  The To Hit number is used, not the RR as for IGs and vehicles.  The exception of 25.4 does not apply.

replies.body:
Hi Peter:

The answer is in 30.5.  The To Hit number is used, not the RR as for IGs and vehicles.  The exception of 25.4 does not apply.
You still draw an RNC.  You also have to factor in terrain modifiers or hull down status.  (28.32, 28.9)

Yes don't forget that the terrain the AFV is in does affect (effect whichever) the fire strength for attacks against its armor.  The morale/CE is not modified by the terrain.  If there is a choice you decide which one you're going after before drawing the RNC.

The justification for this (in case anyone's interested) is that a shaped-charge weapon doesn't rely on the kinetic energy of the round to penetrate, but rather on the explosive/combustive properties of the round.  Hence the range at which the hit is achieved is immaterial.  However, at closer ranges it's more likely that the hit is on a vulnerable part of the target - similar reasoning to the HE To Hit process.

For AP shot (ATR, AT boxed values), in contrast, the closer you are the higher the impact velocity - hence adding the RR to increase the effect.  [It will be interesting to see how the new version of UF reflects this - presumably by subtracting the Range or some slightly more complicated calculation such as adding 5 and subtracting the Range.]

In both cases, as has been said, the target's Terrain subtracts from the effect, presumably to allow for the chance of the shot being deflected or slowed by passing through foliage/brickwork etc.

Note also that a Hull Down target halves the chance of a hit, but if a hit is achieved there is no reduction for Terrain.

title: Second Story Buildings
question:
SCENARIO BB STALINGRAD - General Magazine Vol 22 No.3

This scenario has a number of special rules designed to simulate the street to street fighting at Stalingrad — rule BB3 uses a Buildings/Hill combo to represent Second Story Buildings.

Here is the rule as printed in the General.

BB3. Hill cards may only be used in conjunction with Buildings cards to represent Second Story Buildings. Both cards are played together as an Action (the Buildings card having been drawn as per BB1.2). Such action may be taken ONLY after a sideways Movement card has been previously played. The group does not receive the extra defense modifier of the Hill; but does receive the attack modifier. The combination is treated in all other respects as a Buildings card.

I recently played this scenario for the first time — I understand rule BB3 as it appears in the General. My Question is this:

1. Can you EXIT a Second Story Buildings directly by playing a MOVEMENT card ( in any of the three orientations) , subsequently playing another terrain on that Movement card,

2. OR should you be forced to play the Movement card SIDEWAYS to simulate MOVING BACK DOWNSTAIRS. 

Then EITHER playing another new Buildings card to remove the original Buildings/Hill combo, OR playing another Movement card (in any of the three orientations) . Phew, that was wordy - my apologies.

Has anyone else experience of this Scenario BB?  And how did you play it?

PS. All the Buildings cards are available as a separate draw pile, for use by both players (BB1.2).
author: Masonstone
consensus_answer:
The urban rules for scenario BB is a bit lacking. Matthew Ellison made a good attempt at expanding on these rules on a former Up Front website run by Andrew Maly. Ellison's take on this was that you needed to play a sideways movement card also to come down from the upper floor. After this movement had been played you could play terrain or movement as usual OR remove the hill (2nd floor) and take up position on the ground floor of the building again. Sounds good to me.

R.:)

title: Rally All as applied to non-adjacent groups
question:
Need some clarification on Rally All (rule 10.23)...

Given:  Group A at range chit 1 & Group C at range chit 0, both groups have pinned men; Group A has the SL & Group C has the ASL (both unpinned).

Will a Rally All card rally all the pinned men in these two groups?  The rule is not clear on whether non-adjacent groups have to be at the same range.

Well it certainly isn't easy writing rules because there are so many interpretations a person can take.  

Agreed! Writing rules is very difficult. As with any "legal" type writing, the goal is to write in such a way that NO interpretations are possible, let alone necessary -- the words succintly say exactly what the designer means, no more and no less, and cannot be read to mean something else.

Such perfection is unlikely, if not impossible, given the budgets and abilities of game publishers. But for every verb-noun disagreement, incorrect tense, or misplaced comma (as in the now-classic "eats, shoots and leaves"), the rules writer creates a potential for conflict and multiple interpretations. "Surely the designer can't mean that; it makes the game unplayable. He must mean this instead." -- leaving players to decide for themselves what this is.

A few inaccurately written rules can be clarified in errata, but if every rule in a game is written to allow interpretation, the authority of the rules is non-existent. You don't have a game then; at best you have a concept, and players can just make things up as they go.

So, yeah, it's tough -- but important!

title: What Weapon-Target combinations can gain the Flanking Fire bonus?
question:
Mostly agree!

A2: I think a flanking FT would attack the Flank defence value of the AFV, but at single FP (representing getting a shot at a more vulnerable target).  Similarly, I think inherent infantry boxed FP, when flanking, would attack the Flank factor (I've always been unsure whether this represents grenades, as you suggest, or limited penetration of thin armour by small arms at close range.  Probably both).  Not sure whether it would have doubled FP, but strictly 17.4 says "A group entitled to Flanking Fire doubles its firepower (EXC: flamethrowers) for all subsequent fire against the flanked defending group", so probably it does.

I take your implied point that 28.46 says "Anytime an AFV is the target of ordnance fire which enjoys a Flanking Fire advantage, that AFV defends with its FLANK defense values" - the question is whether it actually means "boxed" fire here (another term used is "anti-armor attacks" which also seems to be synonymous - or is it??)

A3: Here I think you give the small arms doubled FP, again representing an advantageous fire position, again based on 17.4 as above.  A CE AFV need not be a tank, it could be a half-track where you get a good position to fire into its interior, for example.

title: New Ordnance Attack vs an AFV Rules Question

Now that the Relative Range calculation is being flipped so that RR0 is closest are the AVF's having their boxed value increased by five and then subtracting RR?

2nd Edition Up Front (old RR Rules).

title: the range would be what?
question:
Group A is at RR5, opponent Group C is at RR1.  So would that mean they are at RR3 to each other?  

Edit:
Opps, yeah I meant Group A is at RC5 and opponent Group C is at RC1.
author: DiploGuy
consensus_answer:
Relative Range (RR) is the distance between two groups.  Range Chit (RC) is a measure of how far a group has advanced.

Assuming what you meant was Group A is at RC5 and opposing Group C is at RC1, then they are at RR3 (RR4, minus 1 for not being adjacent), Group A being in Group C's rear.

title: Artificial Terrain and Artillery Strikes
question:
The question was about effect of the attacker's terrain - and the answer is no:

40.21 

A Fire Mission is resolved in the same way as an ordnance attack except there is no To Hit process (other than the placement RNC described in [40.2]) and therefore no play of Concealed cards to aid the defender. In addition, there is no modification of the attack strength due to Relative Range or the non-existent To Hit RNC draw. The 5 Attack Strength is modified only by the defender's terrain (EXC: Woods) and movement status, and the individual RNC (subtracting red RNC's, adding black RNC's) drawn to resolve the attack on each man in the target group.

Bearing in mind the attacked group can be out of the attacker's LOS, the presence of Smoke/Wire on the attacking group is irrelevant.

title: Panic, Rout & KIA confusion
question:
Rule 6.53 confuses me a bit.  I understand how to apply the rule to achieve outcomes, but its language creates some confusion for me I want to clear up.  A pinned man can have three outcomes from a fire attack:  no effect, ROUT or KIA, correct?  There is no PANIC outcome, per se, but the Panic value is used to determine for a successful attack whether a man is routed or killed, except if he is outright killed by an attack meeting/exceeding his KIA value.  Correct?

If the above is right, then good.  It's just the wording makes it seem like there is a Panic result and then I start thinking what's the difference between Panic and Rout? So I just want to make sure I am understanding this.
author: arjisme
consensus_answer:
Rule 6.53 confuses me a bit.  I understand how to apply the rule to achieve outcomes, but its language creates some confusion for me I want to clear up.  A pinned man can have three outcomes from a fire attack:  no effect, ROUT or KIA, correct?  There is no PANIC outcome, per se, but the Panic value is used to determine for a successful attack whether a man is routed or killed, except if he is outright killed by an attack meeting/exceeding his KIA value.  Correct?

If the above is right, then good.  It's just the wording makes it seem like there is a Panic result and then I start thinking what's the difference between Panic and Rout? So I just want to make sure I am understanding this.

When firing at a pinned man:
-  If the fire number +/- RNC is less than Panic value:  Man survives.
-  If the fire number +/- RNC is greater then or Equal the Panic value, but less the KIA value:  Check for Or Rout/KIA (GT or =, KIA; LT, Rout)
-  If the fire number +/- RNC is greater than or equal to the KIA value:  Man dies, unless RPC 7w = his morale value on front in which case he is wounded.

Rout and KIA both eliminate the man, but:
-  Rout:  1 VP.  Man takes weapon with him (exc. crewed weapon)
-  KIA:  2 VP, weapon remains available for retrieval.

Two special cases:  
-  Japanese use determine rout/KIA on a number 2 higher than their their Panic value.
-  Wounds:  If the the man routs or if the fire value +/- RNC exactly equals  the KIA number, Check for wound.   If the Morale Value (on the front) = RPC 7w, then the man is wounded rather than the original result.
