A question about winning a scenario with a Gully.  My friend and I were playing Scenario F, where you have to get four or more cards to Range 4 in terrain that will reduce the Fire Strength of Fire on them.  I had group at Range 2 and played a Movement card and changed the range chit to range 3, then next turn placed a Gully on them.  A few turns later I pulled another Movement card and flipped my range chit to 4, and there we hit a wall.  According to the rules you cannot win with a group that is moving.  But if a group is in a gully they’re allowed to advance an additional move up the gully.  The group has moved, is in Gully Terrain, but the Movement card stays in place.  So the question is: after playing the second Movement card, allowing the group to advance up the gully, had they reached range 4, thus winning the game, or did the group have to play a subsequent Movement card and another Terrain at range 5 to win?

A)  Like all terrains except marsh, Gully does NOT require a second movement card to exit.  Only one movement card to exit a Gully and you could have won the game simply by placing any Terrain with negative defensive TEM on it.

B) You are ALWAYS to place a second movement card (on a later turn).  However only the last 2 movement/terrain cards in play are counted for the defensive TEM.  With a terrain (say, woods) & 1 movement card, the TEM is whatever the terrain was -2, with +1 for the movement for a total of -1.  If you have a Woods terrain and 2 movement cards in play, only the two movement cards count, so TEM would be +2. 

Gully DOES have special rules that affect a movement cards--The first movement card is considered to be "in the gully":  
-  So the opposing cannot fire on a group in a gully with one movement card--unless the firing group is on a Hill or is at RR5.
-  If s second movement card is play, enemy groups (except those on a Hill or at RR5) cannot see the first movement card only second one is visible--i.e.  Defensive TEM is +1.  (An enemy group on a Hill could see both the first and second movement card--therefore +2 TEM)

C)  Actually the victory condition rule is specific:  When when it says Range Chit 4, it does NOT mean range chit 4 or higher.

title: card required for open terrain? and what cards are required to be shuffled back into the deck?
question:
Got some questions that I don't want to hunt through the rule book to find answers for.

1a: During the terrain placement round if a group doesn't get a terrain placed are you then required to place an open ground card down?  And if so do you take that from your hand or the deck?

1b: if at anytime during the game a group moves into open terrain are they required then to place a card down to indicate that?

1c: assuming you are not required to place a card down for open terrain are you still allowed to entrench?  Or must you have an open terrain card placed first?

2: if during a fire mission say you're 3 cards into a 6 man group and the first deck runs out.  What cards currently not in the discard pile are required to be shuffled with the deck?  Example: say you fired an ordnance so you have the To Hit card (1), your opponent has a concealment card down (2), and you have the 3 fire resolution cards down (6) and you have 3 more to do.  So would any of those 6 cards that are part of the current fire mission be required to be shuffled back into the deck?

You could even have a situation where:
Hero and fire card are placed (2), then opponent puts down concealment (3), then you begin firing on the 6 man group, but half-way through (6) a gun malfunctions so you do an RPN (7) then you pin a guy (8) but your opponent immediately plays a hero card (9) and right before the last guy the deck runs out (10).  So can you keep all 10 cards out of the deck for the next pass?  Those are things to consider depending on if you want the deck to move along as fast as possible or not.
author: DiploGuy
consensus_answer:
Got some questions that I don't want to hunt through the rule book to find answers for.

1a: During the terrain placement round if a group doesn't get a terrain placed are you then required to place an open ground card down?  And if so do you take that from your hand or the deck?

1b: if at anytime during the game a group moves into open terrain are they required then to place a card down to indicate that?

1c: assuming you are not required to place a card down for open terrain are you still allowed to entrench?  Or must you have an open terrain card placed first?

At the start of the game, any groups that did not receive a terrain card are considered to be in open ground for all purposed:  0 TEM, can entrench, can receive wire from opponent, etc.

2: if during a fire mission say you're 3 cards into a 6 man group and the first deck runs out.  What cards currently not in the discard pile are required to be shuffled with the deck?

All cards are shuffled into the new deck--except for those terrain/movement/wire/smoke that are in play on a group and cards removed per the scenario conditions (First five buildings...):  The fire card, any heroes played to avoid pin or double FP of one man, any RNC's/RPC's drawn to resolve attacks/malfunctions, the entire discard pile etc.  All of them.

On a related note:  If the fire attack has started when the last card is drawn in the last deck, reshuffle the deck and conclude the attack before finishing the game.

On another note, close combat is handled slightly differently--the attack doesn't start until the RPC's are drawn to determine which man attacks which defender.  That means finish all morale checks before the deck runs out.

Following on from previous responses, if there are cards that you really don't want to see in play (such as Streams or Snipers when you can't use them, or Minefields in scenarios where they are in use by your opponent), use them as open ground just before the deck runs out.  Then they don't get reshuffled (since they're not discarded until the group completes its move away from the open ground).  This also applies to scenario-defined cower cards such as Buildings - as the defender you may want to reduce the number of Terrain cards that the attacker can use.

I think there are more cons with this tactic though.  I suppose if you got entrenched and were able to lay a smoke or two on yourself then staying in open ground wouldn't be so bad.  But minus 2 to your attack probably negates any benefit.

title: Weapon Malfunction
question:
I've played UF several times but I get the feeling I'm still handling the weapon malfunction wrong.

I used to think:

1) You draw a red 6 and stop the fire mission immediately.  Consult the RPC line on that card to find the malfunctioned weapon.  That's it.

After awhile I learnt that was wrong so then I played it:

2) You don't stop the fire mission you just reduce the fire strength by -1 and keep going.

After awhile I learnt I was still doing it wrong so then I played it:

3) You do all that but you must draw a seperate card only for the RPC immediately after you draw the red 6.

I played it that way for awhile but later learnt I still had it wrong.  So now I play it:

4) You do all of that but the weapon that malfunctions determines how much you reduce the fire strength by.  It's still -1 unless the weapon that malfunctions is contributing at least half of the firepower then you reduce it by half of what that weapon is contributing.  So a weapon that malf. with 4 firepower reduces the fire strength by -2.  And if it's a weapon that isn't contributing at all you still reduce the fire strength by -1 but that weapon doesn't actually malfunction.

I'm pretty sure I still have it wrong though.  Can someone clarify please.
author: DiploGuy
consensus_answer:
Malfunctions are pretty complicated topic:

Fire attacks:
If during a fire attack, a red 6 (or 5, if you have a weapon that breaks on that number) causes a malfunction.

-  First determine if you even need a RPC check:  If a firing flamethrower or enemy weapon that has been captured MUST malfunction OR if there is only one choice.  (This happens mostly with red 5 draw and uncrewed MG or Japanese/Italian MG, because only cards marked with X5-6 would be affected.  Note:  previously malfunctioned weapons are always X6--so a malfed Japanese MG would not break on a red 5.)

-  If group consist of one armed man (i.e. crewed MG has 2 armed men, the MG man and the crewman--even though the crewman is not using his weapon.):  the malf occurs on that man's weapon and the rest of the fire attack is canceled. 

-  If needed, draw an RPC to pick which man is affected.  (Include all men (except transferees) in the draw.

-  Based on which man is selected, apply the following results
*  Unarmed man, non-firing FT or infiltrator:  N/E
*  Crewman:  No malf, but continue attack with -1 FS.
*  Man with malfed weapons:  Eliminate weapon, no effect on FS.
*  Man with weapon (even if pinned):  malf weapon and reduce FS of attack by FP of the malfed weapon/2 (round up)

Ordnance Attacks:
If the group was only firing ordnance, check for malfunction ONLY on the To Hit draw.  If it comes up, the weapon malfs and the attack is canceled.  If a red 5 or 6 is drawn during the draw for each man after a successful To Hit draw, no malfunction will occur.  

Also demo charges, the malfunction can only occur on the first card drawn to resolve its attack.  Afterward, any red 6's are ignored.   A bit like ordnance.

Whew!

Also remember, all men with malfed weapons (or are unarmed) are -1 to both Morale and Panic values until they fix/acquire a working weapon.

Fixing weapons in Up Front is much easier:  Use an action for the group to fix one weapon.  Draw an RNC and check the waepon chit--If repair comes up, the weapon is fixed (remove/flip weapon chit).  If Remove comes up, remove the weapon chit and placed an unarmed chit.  Otherwise, N/E.

Weapon Malfunctions [Section 19]
* If a fire check reveals a red 6 [or 5 if using a bracketed
firepower on a crew weapon], then a weapon malfunctions.
* Draw an RPC to determine whose weapon malfunction.
This malfunctions unless the person is a crewman, or was
ordered not to fire. (Yes, their weapon malfunctions even if
they had zero firepower or were pinned. Many soldiers fired
uselessly in war).
* A man can only be ordered not to fire if he was infiltrating,
had ordnance or a flamethrower.
* Grab the appropriate malfunctioning weapon chit and place
it on the soldier.
* For every 1-2 points of firepower lost, the fire strength is
reduced by one (for the remaining targets).
* In the case of a weapon with 0 firepower, the fire strength
is still reduced.
* However, if the soldier was pinned, no fire strength is lost.
* The soldier suffers a morale and panic penalty while the
weapon is broken.
* The group can take it's action to attempt to fix the weapon,
draw a RNC and compare it to what is required on the
weapon chit. (This could fix the weapon, destroy it, or result
in no change).

title: Flanking Fire questions
question:
I’ve played several games of UF now, but the rules on Lateral Flanking Fire, or 'Flanking with a Move card' are causing me some trouble.  I understand Natural Flanking - easy to visualize - but the Lateral Flanking Fire leaves me a bit confused.  

17.1 says, "Flanking Fire can originate at any Relative Range from a group whose last placed "Flank" Movement card was played sideways and remains in play at the end of the turn in which it was played." 
 
Question #1: Does 17.1 mean by "at any Relative Range" that the flanking group can be at, say, Range 0, while the enemy group being flanked is at its Range 3, while the friendly group with the same letter ID as the group being flanked is at Range 2?  Or even if the enemy group is at Range 2 and the friendly directly opposite group is at range 1?  Like I say, I can visualize Natural Flanking, but this seems to say you can flank another group from quite a ways back.

Question #2: 17.2 seems to say that the two directly opposing groups can be at any relative range.  Am I correct that they don’t have to be at RR5?  Again, this allows flanking at long ranges.

My thanks ahead of time to all you Up Front veterans who humor those of us new to the game.
author: L4D2
consensus_answer:
I’ve played several games of UF now, but the rules on Lateral Flanking Fire, or 'Flanking with a Move card' are causing me some trouble.  I understand Natural Flanking - easy to visualize - but the Lateral Flanking Fire leaves me a bit confused.  

17.1 says, "Flanking Fire can originate at any Relative Range from a group whose last placed "Flank" Movement card was played sideways and remains in play at the end of the turn in which it was played." 
 
Question #1: Does 17.1 mean by "at any Relative Range"
Yes, it does mean at any range. 

that the flanking group can be at, say, Range 0, while the enemy group being flanked is at its Range 3, while the friendly group with the same letter ID as the group being flanked is at Range 2?  Or even if the enemy group is at Range 2 and the friendly directly opposite group is at range 1?  Like I say, I can visualize Natural Flanking, but this seems to say you can flank another group from quite a ways back.

"Quite a ways back" (RR3) is ~100 yds.  Not really that far.  After all all rifles have 2 FP at that range.  If you are able to get a group of 5 rifles (i.e. the maneuver group) in a flanking position at RR3, they'd have 20 FP.

Flanking doesn't anything to do the ranges but the being attacked at two different angles.  Flanking at long range, means you double a lower firepower.

Question #2: 17.2 seems to say that the two directly opposing groups can be at any relative range.  Am I correct that they don’t have to be at RR5?  Again, this allows flanking at long ranges.

Yes, the Front Group can be at any range. 

My thanks ahead of time to all you Up Front veterans who humor those of us new to the game.

Up Front often abstracts terms:  "Wire" doesn't mean necessarily the group is stuck in wire--the rules describe it as any "fate" that discomfits the group.  

Likewise, "Flank" is simply a shorter way to say "having a fortuitous clear firing lane at the enemy who cannot react because he has to defend his front.".  It is the effect the target group is being attacked from the front and the side simultaneously, making the position untenable.  Without the Front Group, the defending group could while staying in its terrain, "turn" to face the threat.

title: Pinned on the Move
question: Yes, they're still considered moving and still have the movement penalty.  You can still play a terrain card on them on a future turn, however.  I missed this rule the first time I played.
consensus_answer:
Not being the designer or developer I probably am going to miss a few details and it is likely that I cannot the question to your satisfaction, but here goes...

In all games time is a little bit flexible or is at least bent, rendered and twisted to fit the events being portrayed on the table (or floor, or screen, etc.). So the idea is that the Pin result happened in an instant of game play but placing that in the actual course of time being represented is tougher. That one soldier is pinned and cannot move, but the rest of the team might still be able to move (and drag the pinned soldier with them).

It was a tad rare for soldiers to not move from one position of cover to another so the idea is that they were heading towards something when they received fire.

I hope that conveys the ideas in a reasonable fashion. No it might not be the most realistic portrayal but what game is?

Now that you are pinned on the move, if you are fortunate enough to have a good location close to you (ie in hand), you can drag your pinned soldier into it for cover. Can someone explain the rationale behind this rule? It confuses me.

"Pinned" doesn't necessarily mean "cowering on the ground unable to do anything".  It could mean the soldier is shocked to the point where all he thinks about is getting into cover.  So it's reasonable for him to leap into the nearest ditch/building/woods, but he isn't going to do anything else until he's got into the safer position, and once there he's going to keep his head down until he recovers his composure, ie until you get and play a suitable Rally card.

Also you can always leave a guy behind rather than getting the whole group shot ta sh#t.Waiting for that ralley card.I,ll cut a pinned man loose in a New York second to get out of a potential squad break ,or to quick dash to victory.
Or play any card in your hand over the movement card to stop moving...open ground.that would remove the movement card.

title: New player -- couple questions
question:
I just started playing again (after a 20+ year layoff!), and had a couple questions. Really simple stuff, but I don't want to mess up any of the basic mechanics. 

1. If I play a movement card on a group after the first turn -- *without* a terrain card -- what happens on the second turn? Is that group still considered moving and the RR adjusted accordingly? Or is the group now considered stopped in open ground until I play a second movement card?

2. The rules mention the playing of two movement cards on a single group. Can two be played on one group in the same turn in the way two fire cards can be played? Or would it have to be two consecutive turns to stack movement cards?

3. I'm a little unclear on the removing of cards as specified by the scenarios. Take A, for example. "Remove the first five Buildings cards to be discarded unused or as a RPC/RNC draw." So does that mean all building cards are unusable as terrain until five have been removed? Are they treated as cower cards until then?

Thanks in advance, all. This board has been invaluable to getting back in the swing of things. Also, if anyone reading this is in or around the Twin Cities and wants to play UF, do let me know!

Thanks,
Jason
author: AlbertaClipper
consensus_answer:
It is subtle, but you can play terrain on a Flanking group and maintain the Flank bonus! It is not really useful for Flamrthrowers.

17.4: A group entitled to Flanking Fire doubles its firepower (EXC: flamethrowers) for all subsequent fire against the flanked defending group until one of the following actions occurs.

17.41: Flanking Fire is lost whenever another Movement card or a Wire card (not a Terrain card) is played on top of the flanking group.

17.42: Flanking Fire is lost whenever a Terrain card is played on the flanked group -- even if subsequently rejected.

17.43: Flanking Fire is lost whenever the defending group plays a Movement card (even to remove Wire ir unsuccessfully ford a Stream). Movement cards played by individuals within the flanked group directly into the Discard pile have no effect on Flanking Fire.

17.44: Flanking Fire is lost if either group is eliminated, or the group directly opposite the flanked group is eliminated or changes its group ID.

17.5: When Flanking Fire is lost, remove the Flank Fire chit. The Flank card itself need not be removed if still in place, although it cannot be used again for Flanking Fire until redrawn from the Draw Pile and replayed.

replies.body:
The group is considered moving. It does not get to advance the range chit again. You must play another movement card to get another range chit advance. Moving is bad though, as attackers get +1 for that.

You cannot play two movement cards on a group in the same turn.

Yes, they are cower cards. So you wait until five or whatever, have been discarded or revealed as RPC/fire attack results, and then the rest are in play and good.
Thanks for the quick response. Appreciate it.
IIRC, you can play a face down card on a moving group to represent open ground, which removes the movement danger. Useful if you don't have any other terrain to play on your moving group.
Yes, you can.

I just started playing again (after a 20+ year layoff!), and had a couple questions. Really simple stuff, but I don't want to mess up any of the basic mechanics. 

1. If I play a movement card on a group after the first turn -- *without* a terrain card -- what happens on the second turn? Is that group still considered moving and the RR adjusted accordingly? Or is the group now considered stopped in open ground until I play a second movement card?

There seems to be a misinterpretation here.  Movement in Up Front is at least a two turn process:
-  First you must play a movement card (changing the range chit if moving forwards or backward--not changing the range if played sideways--when you play the Movement card).  This group is considered moving and takes +1 TEM, has fire penalties, have an opponent play terrain on it, etc.  On later turns, another movement card can be played before entering terrain changing range chit again as appropriate, etc. (but this increases the danger, see below). 
-  On a later turn, you can play terrain (including any card face down as Open Ground) to stop moving.  The previous terrain card and any movements are discarded at this time.  Your group is no longer moving.

2. The rules mention the playing of two movement cards on a single group. Can two be played on one group in the same turn in the way two fire cards can be played? Or would it have to be two consecutive turns to stack movement cards?

Two or more movement cards can be played on a group.  This can be done accumulating over two (possibly nonconsecutive) turns.

Note:  Defensive TEM's are applied based on the last two movement OR terrain card on the group.  So with ONE movement card leaving say Woods terrain, the TEM would be -1 (-2 for Woods + 1 for Movement).  With a second Movement card, the TEM would be +2 (Only the two movement cards count--the Woods beneath both movements would be ignored)

Having a +2 TEM is hazardous to the health of you men. 

3. I'm a little unclear on the removing of cards as specified by the scenarios. Take A, for example. "Remove the first five Buildings cards to be discarded unused or as a RPC/RNC draw." So does that mean all building cards are unusable as terrain until five have been removed? Are they treated as cower cards until then?

Yes, exactly correct.  In Scenario A, any building cards in your hand before 5 can be removed from your hand through discarding them or playing them as open ground.  

When discarded, these buildings must be placed face up off to the side.  (When used as Open ground, the building card is not revealed or removed play when the group has moved and entered new terrain.)  Also any building drawn for RNC/RPC checks are also placed face up into the pile.  Once the required number of buildings are set aside, any remaining buildings become BUILDINGS.  

It often pays to hold onto a building when four are out in the hopes that a fifth will soon appear.

title: 13.5 - Open Ground beneath a Wire?
question:
Okay, I'm working through the first section of Up Front rules.  We've played a couple of games "meeting of patrols" and we've made are share of mistakes but we're getting better.  After rereading the rules, I'm stumped by 13.5 " Open Ground may be placed beneath a Wire or Smoke card and above a Movement card..."  

I get 13.34 that says you can't put a terrain or movement on top of a Wire until it's removed, but I don't get this one.  I guess the rule itself isn't ambiguous, just the rationale?
author: cfisher
consensus_answer:
Okay, I'm working through the first section of Up Front rules.  We've played a couple of games "meeting of patrols" and we've made are share of mistakes but we're getting better.  After rereading the rules, I'm stumped by 13.5 " Open Ground may be placed beneath a Wire or Smoke card and above a Movement card..."  

I get 13.34 that says you can't put a terrain or movement on top of a Wire until it's removed, but I don't get this one.  I guess the rule itself isn't ambiguous, just the rationale?

The rationale is kind of an desperation move after your plan disintegrated when encountered the enemy:  You are moving, your opponent plays wire on you, maybe he pins one or more men in the group.

To get to your intended target terrain, you need to:
-  Rally pinned in the group and/or use voluntary panic to all the men unpinned.
-  If the entire group is still unpinned (hopefully, your opponent hasn't fired in the meantime at a +2 disadvantage.), play a movement to remove the wire.
-  Then on your next turn play the terrain you originally intended.

But if you don't have movement to remove the wire or rally to unpin the men, you may be better off "stopping and reassessing the situation."  You stop moving, improving the TEM to only +1 and may be able to discard more cards (particularly if you playing the Russians) to get the movements and rally cards you need.

replies.body: The basic idea is that the wire (which could represent any significant problem the troops are having) prevents you from reaching the next "nice" piece of terrain you wanted to reach, e.g. the building you are holding in your hand.  So the troops just hit the dirt, simulated by the playing of an Open Ground card underneath the wire.  So they are still stuck by the wire, but slightly less vulnerable because they are no longer moving.  But once they get rid of the wire they will need to get up again to make it to the building.
When would it be appropriate in a game example?  I tried and can't seem to come up with one.

Let us suppose that you are in some Brush and would like to advance on your opponent. Happily, you have a Movement card and a Woods card, hooray!  You play the movement card above your Brush card. On your opponent's turn the lilly-livered, addlepated cad drops Wire on your moving group. 

Marvelous. 

Your -1 Brush, +1 Movement, +1 Wire for a net of +1 to be hit. You can't entrench (because you're moving), your LMG is using its bracketed firepower (because you're moving), your MMGs and mortars can't fire at all (because you're moving), your Fire cards are halved (because you're moving), firepower of bolt action rifles (which is most of the rifles) is halved, rounding down (because you're moving), and their are some other penalties.

But if you play an open terrain card "under" the wire you will lose the Movement and Brush cards and still be at +1 to hit. You still can't Entrench, but you lose all those fire and Infiltration penalties. If you think it might be awhile before you see another Movement card, or if you have another pressing need for the first movement card you see, or if you have a nice fire card you'd like to use immediately, you *might* want to lose the Movement card.

Additionally, if this group just arrived at the RR necessary to win you might want to clear the Wire with the next Movement card and then Entrench for the win. 

I'm not certain there's a time when it's clearly and unequivocally the best thing to do, but it's often a defensible choice.
Oh, I forgot, it also lets you get a card out of your hand without using a discard. Sometimes that's a nice extra.

It's a very handy move if you are stuck with a movement card covered by wire.  As long as the wire is on top of the movement card, there is +2 modifier going against you.  If your men are already pinned, you may have no chance at all to remove the wire until you can rally them.  Placing the open ground removes the movement card and could give you a chance to recover.  Of course you would lose the "lingering" benefit of the terrain you were leaving, but if you were already in open ground or coming out of a stream or second card out of a marsh there is nothing to lose anyway.

When would it be appropriate in a game example?  I tried and can't seem to come up with one. Well, maybe this isn't an example as much as it is a "reason".  That wire card is increasing all incoming attacks against you and the fact that you may have one or more Movement cards in play only makes it WORSE.  After you play enough Up Front, you'll come to appreciate EVERY single +1 modifier either for or against you.  By placing an Open Ground card beneath the wire, you negate your opponent's bonus to his Fire Strength due to your Movement status, which can make all the difference in the world.

Also, if you happen to have a Movement on your group when they have a Wire discarded on them and you also DO NOT have any Terrain cards or other Movement cards in hand to immediately get rid of the wire, it doesn't make sense to retain Movement status with the wire on your group.  By doing so, you are tactically forcing your group into the hopes you can draw a Movement card in order to remove the Wire (while your opponent's shots get that Fire Strength bonus against you) which could take awhile if you're unlucky.  Not to mention, if you do draw a Movement card all your group can do that turn is remove the Wire, so you're STILL in Movement status.

  Now, consider the fact that if you ALSO didn't have a Terrain card in hand even if you did manage to previously draw a Movement card to remove the Wire, now you're back to step one, hoping that you'll now draw a useful terrain card to get those men in some cover AND.....you're still in Movement status with an opponent getting bonuses to his shots.  

As a rule of thumb, if I'm Moving and have a Wire card discarded on me AND I don't have a Movement card (to remove the Wire) OR a Terrain card in hand (where I was just getting ready to go), I'll go to ground (Open Ground) to remove the Movement penalty.  Long story short, it's just too damn risky to flap out there with a Movement card on your group AND a Wire card giving +2 to my opponent's Fire Strength while my group is getting shot to pieces trying to both remove the Wire and find some good Terrain.

Hope this helps, Cheers.

title: Infiltration is kinda’ weird.
question:
In the last three days I’ve played my first four games of Up Front.  We’re really getting into it, and the rules aren’t too daunting.  But one speed bump we came across last night was Infiltration and Close Combat.  MAN!  Infiltration is HARD!  I was playing the Russians last night in Scenario B and trying to infiltrate a German-occupied house and take on the guys in CC.  One Russian chickened out, the other two got into the building to take on two unpinned Germans and one pinned.  I killed one German (who was pinned), but both my Russians were killed.  This was our first experience with Infiltration/Close Encounter, and my conclusion is that they’re pretty weird rules.  For example:

1. According to rule 20.5 and 20.73, "A man who has infiltrated the defender’s position is still part of his group, in his group’s terrain," and "A man who has successfully finished CC is still a member of his group, occupying the terrain of that group".  That seems pretty weird to me.  If they’ve infiltrated, aren’t they supposed to be IN the enemy’s position?  And especially so if they’re already locked in close combat - pretty long arms to reach from one terrain to the other.  And they still take fire from the enemy as though they’re still crouched with their squad.  I understand that the rules help streamline play, but if you have 36 pages of rules in fine print, it seems they could have come up with something a bit more realistic for CC.

2. You can ONLY infiltrate to engage in Close Combat.  No charging across the street to take on the enemy.  In Combat Commander you have Advance cards that let you move into the enemy hex and fight it out mano a mano.  In SL and ASL you can also rush into the enemy-occupied hex and fight it out.  I haven’t played any other games besides these at this scale, but it seems to be a rules issue easily resolved.

SO, I’m compelled to ask: Has anyone come up with additional rules to allow this in UF?  Anything in The General, or anyone have any well-tested house-rules they’d recommend?  It seems to me that it’d be pretty easy to allow a group at relative range 5 to play a Movement card and attempt to move into the enemy terrain, which allows the defenders a chance to fire on the charging attackers.  I’m open to all suggestions, and also steeling myself for those who will shout me down for even suggesting it.

For those of you who have pondered this rules question, my thanks for all your input.
author: L4D2
consensus_answer:
There are no alternate rule to infiltration and close, because they work really well.  Infiltration is used for at least four reasons:
-  Entering close combat on a later turn.
-  Doubling firepower (which will forfeit infiltration status)
-  Preventing victory conditions ("The first player to have at least four unpinned personality cards in one or more NON-INFILTRATED groups....")
-  Setting a demo charge.

RR5 in Up Front means basically within 50' of each other--multiple "terrains" do exist in each virtual hex:  defender in a building with attackers in the woods right outside.  Infiltration involves find an advantageous position either for a powerful fire attack (i.e. doubling FP) or a close combat.

Like Wire, infiltration abstracts details.

I looked at Banzai here on this site, but there is no file for the rules.  Can someone tell me how the Japanese are allowed to move into the enemy terrain?

The Japanese do not "enter enemy terrain".  

They have a special rule which allows them declare BANZAI any one enemy group with the use of Movement played in sideways mode with an unpinned (A)SL.  

After they declare Banzai:
-  The group can only move toward their targeted group (and no other Japanese group can move on a turn, unless the Banzai group has moved first.
-  All pinned men in the Banzai group are immediately rallied.
-  Banzai groups cannot play terrain (thus they often are taking +2 double movement TEM) --but they can have terrain played on them by their opponent.
-  If a banzai group reaches RR5 to their target  does not have to infiltrate to attempt close combat--they enter CC on the next turn after reaching RR5 and continue to do so until targeted group still exists.
-  However, and it's a big one, men under Banzai are never pinned.  Any pin result is a **immediate** KIA.

Also berserk Russians enter CC without infiltration.

The key to "getting" infiltration is thinking of it not as "among" but "extra close and *unobserved*.

With respect to #1, you kind of have to imagine that "Infiltration" means "on the verge", so they're still in their woods, but right next to the stone wall, unobserved, ready to pounce or shoot. So they're still in their group if fired at from a distance, but they can leap over the wall or through the window and start stabbing before anyone could do anything about it, and even jump back to their buddies if they wanted.

With respect to #2, iirc CC is not the only way to take advantage of Infiltration - you can also double the personality's firepower for one attack, which removes Infiltrated status. So you got up close, to the side, maybe a little behind, *unobserved* and you can spray with that SMG to marvelous effect before jumping back amongst your buddies. 

It all makes sense to me. If you think about it when the enemy has guns there's a big difference between being very close to them and being close enough to CC. It takes a lot of guts, but when it works it really works.

I like how SL handles it, too, but that is a different game.

Are we even sure CC necessarily means hand-to-hand?  I know the ability to use the gun as a bat is a factor in the PCs CC value but that doesn't mean he had to use it to smack his enemies head.  RR5 isn't point-blank range, so I like to think of CC as that.  Which makes more sense that he's still part of his group.

You didn't mention the oddest rule for infiltration though.  Your opponent can retreat to RR4 and any infiltrated men maintain that status.  That one is harder for me to rationalize.   

Until they play a terrain card or move again to RR3.

I can see that as, you have obtained a favourable fire position, and they hastily move out of the cover they are in to avoid your fire.  While they're doing this, they are still vulnerable to your enhanced fire.

The Banzai rules in the banzai expansion allow a similar effect but only for the Japanese.  No infiltration is needed once RR5 is reached.  So the rules could probably support charges into CC by other nations.

title: Infantyr Guns, infiltration and Close Combat
question:
Here's something I've been scratching my head about:

Under what number (basically) do you check for infiltration against a lone IG. Do you check under 1 because it is only one personality card in the group or do you check under 3 because the crew is regarded to consist of three crewmembers?

I believe you check under 1, but I'd like to see what others mean about it.

Somewhat the same problem occurs when entering CC. Do the crew defend together as three men or is the IG only considered one man for CC purposes?

I believe one should consider the IG to be three men and look at it as a three-man group/crew, but I'm not 100% sure about this. Anyway it will take some care when deciding the odds and CC-pairings in a multi-attacker CC versus an IG...

R.:)
author: stroar
consensus_answer:
Here's something I've been scratching my head about:

Under what number (basically) do you check for infiltration against a lone IG. Do you check under 1 because it is only one personality card in the group or do you check under 3 because the crew is regarded to consist of three crewmembers?  I believe you check under 1, but I'd like to see what others mean about it.

34.2 An IG may form its own group or combine with one or more personality cards to form a group.  In either case, the iG occupies ONE position in the group.  

So for both determining the number of "men" for entering infiltration and the RPC draw to determine which "man" is attacked in CC, the IG takes counts as 1.

Somewhat the same problem occurs when entering CC. Do the crew defend together as three men or is the IG only considered one man for CC purposes?

I believe one should consider the IG to be three men and look at it as a three-man group/crew, but I'm not 100% sure about this. Anyway it will take some care when deciding the odds and CC-pairings in a multi-attacker CC versus an IG...

Yes, the IG is considered crewed by a a 3 man crew.  In order to defeat the IG, 3 separate CC attacks must be won by the attacker under rule 20.71.

title: First game and a few questions.
question:
After Zerosum posted his review "Just Play It" I decided I had to buy this game.  Finally got it on ebay at an affordable price, though it was in worse condition than the guy listed it.  Anyway, a friend and I sat down to our first game of Up Front last night.   We were using the rewrite of the rules by David Muñoz de la Peña, with occasional reference to the original rules for some clarification. The Tutorial Scenario is pretty stripped, but still we had some questions come up.  Some of you old Up Front hands will know the answers to these.

1. The German player is allowed to discard one card after playing his Actions.  If he doesn't play any actions, is he still allowed to discard only one?

2. If player A plays a fire card on a group, and player B plays a Concelament card, does the Concelament card stay on that group if player A has another group fire on player B's group?

3. We really don't understand the movement rules for the terrain "Gully".  The rule reads, "A group in a Gully is still considered to be in the Gully after the group receives a Movement card. The group exits the Gully upon receiving a second Movement card OR a Terrain card on the first Movement card. The first Movement card used to exit a Gully does not modify attacks on that group, but does affect the group’s Range counter."  The "OR a Terrain card" obfuscates the reason to play TWO movement cards.  So can you play one movement and then a terrain or not?  Doesn't that amount to moving normally?

Thanks to all who can clear these up.
author: L4D2
consensus_answer:
Yes.  Unless the  Germans are playing with elite status (the only standard scenarios are K: Elite Troops On the Attack and R: Paratroop Drop feature elite troops), which allows a second discard is the Germans perform zero or one actions. 

2. If player A plays a fire card on a group, and player B plays a Concelament card, does the Concelament card stay on that group if player A has another group fire on player B's group?

Concealment cards last for one fire attack.  If your opponent fires on you again from another group on the same turn, you may play another concealment card, if you have one.  

That means if your opponent makes a small fire attack but could make a bigger one from his large firebase, it may be better to hoild onto your last conceal card.   

3. We really don't understand the movement rules for the terrain "Gully".  The rule reads, "A group in a Gully is still considered to be in the Gully after the group receives a Movement card. The group exits the Gully upon receiving a second Movement card OR a Terrain card on the first Movement card. The first Movement card used to exit a Gully does not modify attacks on that group, but does affect the group’s Range counter."  The "OR a Terrain card" obfuscates the reason to play TWO movement cards.  So can you play one movement and then a terrain or not?  Doesn't that amount to moving normally?

Yes.  It is just like moving normally--the rule is essentially (re)stating that visibility rules (only visible from  Hill or RR5) as well as the defensive TEM still apply even one movement card played on the group in a Gully.

Gully has a unique exception:  When playing 2 movement cards to exit a Gully, the first movement card is still considered to have taken place "in the Gully"  So if fired upon then the defensive TEM is +1 (The first movement was "hidden), unless they are fired upon by a group that could have seen them when they were "hidden" (i.e. on a Hill or at RR5 when the group only only had one movement card.)

Then last night another friend joined us and wanted to learn the game as well, so we printed off a three-player scenario here on the site.  It was like going from first grade to high school - we were really in over our heads.  Tank, anti-tank gun, bazooka, elite troops.  But we just referred to the rules a lot and got through it.  Well worth the effort.  Planning another three-player Tuesday evening.

title: Natural Flanking and Encirclement
question:
This is a question about Natural Flanking and Encirclement.

17.3 Flanking Fire occurs naturally without use of a Flank Movement card whenever a group moves forward to Relative Range 4 from Relative Range 5 thus placing it behind an adjacent enemy group which also has an opposing group directly in front of it (with the same group ID letter).

The example shows an adjacent group moving forward to flank the enemy.  So, for example:

(1) Red:  A1  B3
.....Blue:  A0  B1  C2

If Blue group C moves forward from R2 to R3:

(2) Red:  A1  B3
.....Blue:  A0  B1  C3

it moves with respect to Red group B from RR5 to RR4 and thus achieves Natural Flanking on B.  So far so good.  Now, what of this situation:

(3) Red:  A1  B3
.....Blue:  A0  B1  D2

Here there is no Blue group C and group D is not adjacent to Red group B.  So if it moves forward to R3, there is no question of flanking:

(4) Red:  A1  B3
.....Blue:  A0  B1  D3

But what if Blue group D then laterally transfers to C:

(5) Red:  A1  B3
.....Blue:  A0  B1  C3

It is now in the same relative position as in the successful natural flanking in (2).  Does it achieve flanking on B?

I would say not, because it is established that you can't flank a group using a Flank card while also performing a lateral transfer (because the would-be flanking group isn't adjacent to the "flanked" group when the Flank card is played).  

[This interpretation is a little contentious, however, because the original rules do say: "17.7 Lateral Group Transfer: A group capable of movement can change its group identity and thereby its position directly opposite an opposing group by announcing a Lateral Group Transfer and playing a Movement card in the sideways mode (including a Ford or Flank card thereby possibly fulfilling double purposes).", which does seem to imply quite strongly that you can both Flank and Lateral Transfer with one card.  I can't find anything in the Errata to cover this, but I believe it has been discussed and the consensus is as I said above.]

OK, that wasn't my main question (though as always impassioned discussion is eagerly welcomed.)  What I was wondering was this:

Once a group has achieved this position, encirclement becomes possible:

17.6 Encirclement. A group which is behind an adjacent enemy group (i.e. has reached Relative Range 5 with an adjacent group and then advanced past that group to Relative Range 4 again) may encircle it in a subsequent turn by playing a sideways Movement card (even if currently being flanked by that group) while still at Relative Range 4, and placing an Encircled chit on the opponent's group.

So our intrepid group C has got behind the flank of its victims:

(6) Red:  A1  B3
.....Blue:  A0  B1  C3

and now plays a sideways Movement card to Encircle them, causing alarm and despondency amongst their ranks.  But what if group C got to this position by the second route above, ie by advancing to R3 as group D and then laterally transferring?

My feeling is Yes it can (if only because remembering how a group got to a position would be unworkable).  But really I think the question is a little wider.  If group C has achieved Natural Flanking, it can lose it in the ordinary way (by the flanked group moving, or by group C receiving Wire, for example - this is clear in the Errata).  Once it has lost Natural Flanking, can it still Encircle?  I would say so, because 17.6 quoted above doesn't mention flanking, only the relative positions of the two groups.  But what does the team think?
author: Barbarossa
consensus_answer:
In this case, I think the errata and rules don't match:

Rules:
17.3 Flanking Fire occurs naturally without use of a Flank Movement card whenever a group ***moves forward*** to Relative Range 4 from Relative Range 5 thus placing it behind an adjacent enemy group which also has an opposing group directly in front of it (i.e.  with the same group ID letter).

Errata:
17.3 In the example below, if Red Group B moves up to Range Chit 2, does it have to choose whether to get natural flanking fire on A or C or does it get natural flanking fire on both?

BLACK   A   B  C
RED	A   B  C
	
Red Group B gets natural flanking fire on both Black groups A and C. 
***Black groups A and C get natural flanking fire on Red group B.*** 

***Emphasis Mine***

The rules clearly implies (forward) movement is required to gain flanking fire, the errata does not appear to.

Did the rules only intend to limit natural flanking fire to advancing an adjacent group to RR6 while simultaneously having a group in front?  Or did they intend to allow natural flanking by any method when they reached this relative position.  

There are many ways for this to occur:
-  lateral group transfer to reach an adjacent RR6 position (as Ed showed)
-  move group to adjacent RR6 first and then lateral group transfer the front group into position.
-  having groups an adjacent group at RR5 and a front group, then the OPPONENT moves his group forward (as int he errata example). 
-  If a group got somehow behind their opposing group, can natural flanking occur when you advance to RR4?  
Blue:  A
Red:   A  B
(All groups would be in the same relative position as in the "normal" method of natural flanking.  Most confusing situation is Scenario X: Surrounded, one player starts with groups in front and behind the enemy)

I don't know what intended.

One point of clarification, in the example above where Group D moves to position C through LGT and using a Flank card for the LGT, it would obtain a flanking position on B.  However it cannot achieve "natural" flanking fire without use of a Flank card.

To pull this a bit further I would actually also consider allowing group C to use LGT to become the nation's second group B. This will probably have to be considered house rules, but I can see no good justification for this not to be allowed. After all we have that exact situation in scenario X. So the designers have obviously thought of that as a posibility. 

Why this option hasn't been explored further by more detailed rules, I guess might be because this situation would very rarely occur. And, after all, encirclement is acheived by C playing another sideways movement card. C just doesn't have to change its group ID to complete the encirclement. title: Do you still draw a card for a RPC check on a one man group?

title: Doubling BAR with Hero card
question:
I have a very clear memory of a rule which only allowed doubling the firepower of a BAR using a hero with a black RNC.  I have found references to the rule but no existing copy of the official errata from which I recall it.  It is listed in 45.52 in the Banzai rules for the Japanese LMG but nowhere for the American BAR.  The "unoffical errata" contains the following statement:

"44.9 In the Official errata the American BAR and all LMG’s in the game are listed as to which Hero Cards they may use to double their firepower. What about the LMG’s of the Minor Powers listed in Jim Burnett’s article “Cold Front” and any new LMG’s that are introduced in other variant articles?

A.     As a rule a Minor Power’s LMG’s in Jim Burnett’s article would have the same capability as the Major Power whose Personality Cards they are using. However since many new variant Personality Cards are being created for just about every Minor Power in the Second World War I would have to say this:

a.       Any new LMG with both regular and bracketed Firepower numbers on its card may use both Hero Cards to double its bracketed Firepower.

b.      Any new LMG with only regular Firepower numbers on its card may only use the Hero Card with the black RNC to double its Firepower."

Does anyone have a copy of the original errata?  Is this rule still used in most play?
author: mcszarka
consensus_answer:
I have a very clear memory of a rule which only allowed doubling the firepower of a BAR using a hero with a black RNC.  

...

Does anyone have a copy of the original errata?  Is this rule still used in most play? 

The FAQ (consolidated errata - available in the files section) has this:

44.9  This rule states that the British and (via exception) Japanese non-crew served LMGs can only double its firepower with the black RNC Hero card, thus implying that the American BAR can use either Hero card.  Specifically "This rule cannot be used for other nationalities 
(EXC:Japanese)."  However, rule 50.6 (DESERT WAR) states "Like all LMGs in the game which are not considered a crew-served weapon, a Hero card can be used to double the LMG's firepower only if the Hero card is also a black RNC."  Which rule is correct (as they contradict each other), and how is the BAR handled?  
A.  Both are; nor do they contradict.  The BAR is not considered to be an LMG.  Either hero card may be used to double its fire.

title: Multiple guns to acquire = multiple turns? and gun malf. twice?
question:
I had a group that got ripped apart by a MMG.  So there were 3 guns I wanted the surviving men in that group to acquire.  I couldn't see any reason why each man would have to take turns attempting to acquire different guns.  So as the sole action for that group I drew 3 cards for each man attempting to acquire the 3 separate guns.  

Does anyone object to doing it this way?

Also, in this game while drawing for the fire resolution I drew two red sixes.  It didn't happen in this case but it got me wondering what happens if the same weapon malfunctions twice on the same turn?  Does anyone know?
author: DiploGuy

but again a sole action for a group can include multiple men doing something, 6 men rally, 5 men shoot, 4 men entrench... there are many examples of your soldiers doing an action simultaneously.  There's even a rule that specifically permits this: 3.3 Men (plural) may switch positions within a group during their player turn...

In fact the rules allow a soldier in, say, position 1 to get up and move to, say, position 9 and also then crew for a weapon as a sole action. 11.12

Therefore is seems completely consistent to say more than one soldier may attempt to acquire different weapons in the same group as their sole action.  Sole action doesn't mean 1 soldier doing something.  It means a group can't attempt to acquire a gun and also fire.  Or rally and also entrench..

title: Accepting individual transfer from multiple groups
question:
We had a slightly unusual situation last night. My opponent had groups A, B & C, all at range 2.

In his turn, group A played a Movement card to send one man into group B by Individual Transfer. In the same turn, group C played a Movement card to send one his men into group B.

The following turn, group B accepted these men. The rules talk about one group sending men by individual transfer, and the receiving group accepting them in a subsequent turn as their sole action.

We presumed that the group could accept men from both groups as their sole action that turn. I presume this is correct - the rulebook doesn't specifically prohibit or allow this.

Is there an errata or FAQ answering this question?

Any opinions?

Cheers,

Marty.

17.8 If Groups A & C each transfer a man to Group B simultaneously, can B receive both of them with one action?

title: AFV and terrain
question:
Gully: immediately you must check for a bog.  But whether you're bogged or not are you considered in the gully and therefore unable to fire out of it or be attacked in it (ex. RR5 enemy, hill or mortar)?  And subject to the same movement requirements as infantry to get out?

Does the terrain modifier effect attacks against AFVs?  Same answer for ordnance weapons?

Attacks from an ordnance weapon into terrain has its fire strength modified only, not its To Hit number?
author: DiploGuy
consensus_answer:
Gully: immediately you must check for a bog.

Yes.

But whether you're bogged or not are you considered in the gully and therefore unable to fire out of it or be attacked in it (ex. RR5 enemy, hill or mortar)?  

Yes

And subject to the same movement requirements as infantry to get out?

Gully has no restrictions for exiting--only limits on firing at or receiving fire from with only one movement card on it.

The restrictions on AFFV that are not in infantry:
-  AFV cannot enter Marshes, so they must reject them when an opponent plays one on an AFV.
-  An AFV must exit a Woods with a sideways movement card.

Does the terrain modifier effect attacks against AFVs?  Same answer for ordnance weapons?

Yes--with one exception:  Woods does has no Defensive TEM vs. Mortars or artillery ordnance attacks.

Attacks from an ordnance weapon into terrain has its fire strength modified only, not its To Hit number?  

Yes.

title: Firing to a pinned M3 Halftrack
question:
Hi

I don't know if I'm right but it seems to be impossible to "kill" a pinned halftrack with non boxed firepower weapons.

Am I right?

Cheers
author: bonzillou
consensus_answer:
Infantry have an inherent boxed FP of 1 against AFVs at RR 5:-

28.7 INFANTRY Vs OPEN TOPPED AFV:
All Personality cards have an inherent boxed firepower of 1 at Relative Range 5 which can be used against an Open Topped AFV's boxed defense value in addition to using their normal firepower at that range against the AFV's unboxed defense value using a second RNC for the combat resolution.
[EX: If three riflemen are at Relative Range 5 to a CE German halftrack, they would have a total of 9 unboxed firepower factors to use in playing a Fire card(s) vs the exposed crew of the halftrack. Although they could Pin the halftrack, and perhaps kill the commander, this would not immediately destroy the AFV. However, they also have an inherent boxed 6 firepower of 3 vs an Open Topped AFV at Relative Range 5, so if the Fire card they play does not require more than three firepower factors, the same Fire Strength card can be used to attack the halftrack a second time with another RNC, but this time against its armor defense. Therefore, if the three riflemen play a "Fire 2" card requiring 3 or less firepower factors against the halftrack and draw a black RNC of 2 or less, they have no effect vs the crew. However, regardless of the first RNC drawn, they may draw another RNC to use against the AFV itself; if they draw a 0 or any black RNC they will destroy the halftrack; a red 1 RNC would stun it, or immobilize it (depending on the color of the next RNC drawn). This is the only way a Pinned AFV can be affected by infantry attacks without boxed firepower weapons outside CC. Note that had the infantry played a higher strength Fire card, no second attack against the AFV itself could have been made by that group during that turn because they would have lacked the necessary boxed firepower factors.]

Also, it can be attacked by CC:-

28.8 CLOSE COMBAT Vs AN AFV:
An AFV may not attempt to infiltrate, but may be attacked in CC by any armed man (including Secondary Weapons) which has infiltrated the AFV group during that turn. The "group" column of the AFV used to determine the RPC draw is not 1. The group column checked is "2b" for a Buttoned Up or Pinned AFV, "4c" for a CE AFV, and "5o" for a CE Open Topped AFV. Column shifts to the left or right on the RPC due to vision or terrain [20.31]-[20.39] are handled normally. In addition, there is a one column shift to the left on the RPC for each Commander Killed result previously suffered by the AFV. The actual resolution of CC against an AFV is much different from that against infantry. The defender (i.e. the AFV) does not draw a RNC. The attack is resolved solely on the basis of the infiltrating attacker's RNC and modifications to the attacker's strength.

title: Things I Didn't Get Quite Right the First Time, and Other Easily Forgotten Rules (Scenario A Edition)
question:
You ran into all that the first time you played?

Just kidding, I'm guessing you mean the first time you ran into each of those situations.

This is a great list for new players and a great set of reminders for when we get rusty. I didn't know some of that...
consensus_answer:
S
(Section numbering refers to the Up Front 2nd Edition rulebook)
The numbering is the same as first edition.

3. During initial terrain placement, a terrain card can be played on an opponent's group. This terrain cannot be rejected. (3.6)

Each player can only play terrain cards only in their first turns until they pass.  Then both players refill their hand to their hand limit.

4. A movement card can be placed on a group sideways for lateral movement. (5.4)  Comment: We were usually only playing cards in the Advance mode, and occasionally in the Retreat mode. I now see that playing a lateral move can be useful if one wants to enter new terrain without changing Relative Range.

Lateral movement MUST be used to exit a stream and as the first card when exiting a marsh.  Lateral movement is also required for using a FLANK movement to  game Doubled FP, and transferring to another Group ID.  Also exiting in sideways mode is useful in exiting Minfields (but those do not appear in scenario A)

8. A Pinned personality that panics is only counted as a KIA for victory points only if the Random Position Number under '0r' of the panic-causing RNC is less than or equal to his Panic value. Otherwise, the personality has safely routed. I think this also will affect whether or not they leave their weapon behind -- will need to verify that. (6.53)  Correct.  Rout they take the weapon with them (Exc. crewed weapons) .  KIA will leave it behind

9. Any terrain other than Open Ground can be played on an opponent's group in lieu of a discard, pending possible rejection. (7.3) Comment: This may seem obvious, but we've been tending to only play streams on each other. Also, this kind of cardplay can be important for aggressive VP considerations in Urban scenarios, for example, where Personalities must be occupying buildings -- slap a Brush card on them after they move to increase their Range chit! Then they have to make a decision..

In Scenario the Stream is the most popular terrain discard.  In other scenarios (like B or N) where player need to occupy buildings/jungle to score VP, player will discard brush on their opponent.  

11. Groups on hills *cannot* fire on groups in gullies at RR 5. (8.3)

NO!  It is an "exclusive or".  Groups in gullies may be fired upon from any opposing group on a hill or any opposing group at RR5.

12. A group can also potentially gain the benefit of flanking fire if a Flank movement card is played to ford a stream. (8.531)
Yes, but you have to drae a black RNC on the ford check, otherwise the Flank chit is not placed.

13. In Urban scenarios, Brush terrain is considered Hedges. (8.8) Comment: At this point I'm not sure if this has any impact on the game, or is just chrome.
Nope.  Brush is brush is brush.  

14. A 'RALLY ALL' card can be used to rally all Personalities in *two adjacent groups* if an unpinned SL, ASL, or Commissar is present in each group. Otherwise, the card can rally all personalities in a single group. (10.23)
Better read that again!  

Rally All can rally 2 groups if:
-  They are adjacent, AT THE SAME RANGE and one had an unpinned SL/ASL.
-  Any two groups if both groups have unpinned SL/ASL's.
This counts as an action for both groups.

27. If a player is reduced to one group, the other player's hand size increases by one. (15.6)

The more commonly missed rule is when a SL (or ASL acting as SL) is pinned, play with hand limit reduced by one.  Also reduce hand limit the turn the SL is killed and permanently once both leaders are killed.

29. For victory purposes, a terrain modified by wire may no longer be considered to reduce the Fire Strength of an attack. (16.42) Comment: I've just discovered a deliciously evil use for wire!  :devil:

Not quite, 

Wire reduces the defensive of terrain.  So a group at RC4 in Brush/Hill and wire would not count for victory because their net Def TEM =0, but Woods/Buildings/Wall/Gully and a single wire still has a -1 Def TEM and still would be OK.

replies.body:
8. A Pinned personality that panics is only counted as a KIA for victory points only if the Random Position Number under '0r' of the panic-causing RNC is less than or equal to his Panic value. Otherwise, the personality has safely routed. I think this also will affect whether or not they leave their weapon behind -- will need to verify that. (6.53)
Yes, a KIA'd personality leaves behind his weapon (unless moving, IIRC). A Panicked personality takes his weapon with him, usually the DC you need to win the game (in my personal experience).
Iirc, in certain terrain you always lose the weapon, even if not moving. This is usually the MG in the stream.

5. A group can retreat to a Relative Range (RR) of less than 0 if the movement card has a red RNC. A group at RR 0 will thus change to -1. This is called retrograde movement. Further movement cards can be played in Retreat mode if they contain a red RNC (i.e. to go from RR -1 to -2). (5.51)

What you mean is that a group can retreat to a range chit less than 0 if the RNC is red. Also bear in mind that a group must be at Relative Range 1 to at least one enemy group before it can move back to -1. An easier way to put it is that a group can never retreat to a Relative Range of less that 0 to the closest enemy group.

This list is a very good idea! So I fully encourage you to keep on. It will be of great benefit to newbies. And I'm pretty sure experienced players will find points they have missed here too. I'm sure I will.

R.:)

S
(Section numbering refers to the Up Front 2nd Edition rulebook)
The numbering is the same as first edition.

3. During initial terrain placement, a terrain card can be played on an opponent's group. This terrain cannot be rejected. (3.6)

Each player can only play terrain cards only in their first turns until they pass.  Then both players refill their hand to their hand limit.

I now see that playing a lateral move can be useful if one wants to enter new terrain without changing Relative Range.

Lateral movement MUST be used to exit a stream and as the first card when exiting a marsh.  Lateral movement is also required for using a FLANK movement to  game Doubled FP, and transferring to another Group ID.  Also exiting in sideways mode is useful in exiting Minfields (but those do not appear in scenario A)

Rout they take the weapon with them (Exc. crewed weapons) .  KIA will leave it behind

(7.3) Comment: This may seem obvious, but we've been tending to only play streams on each other. Also, this kind of cardplay can be important for aggressive VP considerations in Urban scenarios, for example, where Personalities must be occupying buildings -- slap a Brush card on them after they move to increase their Range chit! Then they have to make a decision..

In Scenario the Stream is the most popular terrain discard.  In other scenarios (like B or N) where player need to occupy buildings/jungle to score VP, player will discard brush on their opponent.

NO!  It is an "exclusive or".  Groups in gullies may be fired upon from any opposing group on a hill or any opposing group at RR5.

12. A group can also potentially gain the benefit of flanking fire if a Flank movement card is played to ford a stream. (8.531)
Yes, but you have to drae a black RNC on the ford check, otherwise the Flank chit is not placed.

Nope.  Brush is brush is brush.

Better read that again!  

Rally All can rally 2 groups if:
-  They are adjacent, AT THE SAME RANGE and one had an unpinned SL/ASL.
-  Any two groups if both groups have unpinned SL/ASL's.
This counts as an action for both groups.

title: Removing Terrain Cards
question:
I was curious how many of you played this particular nuance. If I have a Woods terrain card in play and place a movement card on top if it but then play another movement card on top of the first movement card, I'm no longer in the woods. Since this is the case, do you pick up the woods card and put it in the discard pile or wait until another terrain card is played before discarding the woods card? 

Yes, the woods card is now irrelevant for that moving group but it could make a difference if it gets thrown into the discard pile to be reshuffled, especially if a new deck is about to begin.

My gut feeling tells me that the woods card should stay in play until a new terrain is placed. Looking at 7.34, it says "Whenever a Terrain card is played (and accepted) on a group all Action cards beneath that Terrain card are placed in the Discard pile."

This is further reinforced by example E of 7.2, where there is a Brush--Movement--Smoke--Movement. It mentions the Brush card is effectively canceled because the second Movement card cancels any effect it might have, but it doesn't mention going ahead and discarding the Brush.
author: Keesvanloomacklin
consensus_answer: This is important because if you have two move cards and the opponent discards a terrain card on you that you reject(if you are allowed to) you remove the last move card if it was played sideways, in which case the effect of the terrain would be relevant again.......correct?

replies.body: This is important because if you have two move cards and the opponent discards a terrain card on you that you reject(if you are allowed to) you remove the last move card if it was played sideways, in which case the effect of the terrain would be relevant again.......correct?
Although it is important to remember that there are no terrain benefits/detriments from the original terrain card applied once the second movement card is played.
Personally, I wait until a new terrain card is in play, so as to keep track of Fire modifiers...
Keep it in play, you might lose that second Movement from having to reject two terrains.
Correct!

title: Wounds
question:
I'm having some confusion over when wound checks occur, specifically when a PC is pinned. For example take the American Sgt Allen. Unpinned, he will make a wound check on a final attack roll of 8 (his KIA number). I get that. 

But if Sgt Allen is pinned does he make a wound check:

1. When a final attack roll of 9 is rolled? (his pinned KIA number)

2. When a final attack roll equal to or greater than 7 (his Panic number) is rolled, ONLY if it makes him ROUT?

Rule 33.1 specifically says "Wounds lacking in the severity required to be considered an outright KIA may possibly occur anytime an infantryman ROUTS, or would otherwise be eliminated by a KIA result which occurred as a result of a RNC generating a final attack strength exactly equal to the lowest number required for a KIA."

Well, that tells me that a wound check is made if the KIA number is rolled EXACTLY when in either Pinned or Unpinned status, and if in Pinned status ONLY if the PC routes. The problem I have with that is the example after the rule makes it sound like ANY result that equals or exceeds the Panic number will ALWAYS cause a wound check, whereas the rule specifically states "anytime an infantryman routes". The point is, Panic can either result in either a successful route or unsurvivable panic (KIA).

title: Flanking question from a old guy trying to get the rules down again.
question:
Here's the layout looking from my side of the table (German, black) to my son's (Yanks, green) showing group ID and relative range ...

     
 2       4

 1       -
     

He'd just finished eliminating my cowardly group B and on his next turn moved his B forward to RR 5 to flank my A group setting this up ...

     
 2       5

 1       -
     

I played a -1 movement on my A group (abandoning the buildings they were nicely holed up in) to avoid the flank therefore with this result ...

     
 2       5

 0       -
     

Does this position now mean he can never flank me with his B group since he can't proceed to move forward to a RR of 6? Or is the mere fact that he's not opposed on the B group mean he automatically flanks my A group?

Thanks for help. (This was a scenario B btw.)
author: DaveyJJ
consensus_answer:
Here's the layout looking from my side of the table (German, black) to my son's (Yanks, green) showing group ID and relative range ...

No you are showing the range chits--relative range is the total of 2 range chits (modified by progressing beyond RR5 or lateral position A vs, C or D).  Granted the syntax of the rules of the rules is confusing, but most of your questions seem to stem from this confusion.

I am going to delete the next two positions--how you got to your situation doesn't matter.

     
 2       5

 0       -
     

Does this position now mean he can never flank me with his B group since he can't proceed to move forward to a RR of 6? 

I think I see the problem here--Why do you think his Group B cannot move forward?  Range Chit 5 is not a limit--the rules specify using multiple range chits as needed and Range Chits to 9 were supplied in Desert War. (See 5.6)

Also there are two forms of flanking: 
-  Natural Flanking:  i.e. reaching "RR6"
-  Lateral Flanking:  i.e. using a Flank Movement card.  (Which is FAR more common because it can be performed at any range.)

Even if he couldn't advance further (which he can), he could still Laterally Flank.

Or is the mere fact that he's not opposed on the B group mean he automatically flanks my A group?

Nope, not directly.  A group can't advance past an opposing group (i.e. same letter) from RR5 (e.g RC2 + RC3). (Another reason not to confuse RC and RR.)  Being unopposed, as in your example, means a group won't be blocked. 

Another rule you probably missed--since you are down to one group, your opponent will get an extra card.  

Thanks for help. (This was a scenario B btw.)

As to strategy, why would he even consider moving forward?  He almost certainly leads handily in victory points (assuming either of his groups are in a building.)  By retreating from a building, you gave up a number of VP's.

I guess I was getting confused in the first of three sets mixing up firing between my A and his B (which would be at -1 for diagonal firing) and relative range, which as you pointed out is already RR5. RR is always done by the chits.

Thanks for the clarification, makes sense now.

I guess I was getting confused in the first of three sets mixing up firing between my A and his B (which would be at -1 for diagonal firing)

There would not be a -1 RR penalty for 'diagonal fire' in this example. Group A firing to C or D would suffer the -1 RR penalty, as per 5.61

5.61 LATERAL DISTANCE: 

The Relative Range is further decreased by one (to a minimum of 0) if the groups in question are neither directly opposite (same lettered groups) or adjacent (B is adjacent to A and C; A is not adjacent to C, D, or E).

title: Group Formation Questions
question:
During setup:

Can the SL and ASL be put in any position in their group?

Can the SL and ASL be put in the same group?

Can the SL and ASL be used to crew a weapon?

Again these questions are just for the setup phase.
author: DiploGuy
consensus_answer:
During setup:

Can the SL and ASL be put in any position in their group?

Sure, but generally they are placed near the back because if the enemy has a weapon malfunction, that lowers the final fire strength for the remaining men of your group during this fire attack.

Can the SL and ASL be put in the same group?

Yes, though that would be more limiting on individual transfers which need an SL/ASL in either the leaving or receiving group.  Or for laying smoke which can only be done by SL or ASL.

Can the SL and ASL be used to crew a weapon?

Sure, most of the time, the SL is carrying a machine pistol, meaning he provides no FP until RR3.  Crewing with the SL is often most efficient way to maximize firepower at long ranges.

title: Firing against moving groups? Is the -1 move penalty cumulative?
question:
OK, one more question from this old guy trying to get back up to speed ...

1. When you fire against a group with one movement card and terrain under it, the terrain still modifies the firing; i.e., +1 when the opponent is moving out of a -3 building terrain = -2 overall firepower against that group.

And if you have two movement cards played, the last terrain bonus doesn't factor into it (logical). Are the -1 moving penalties against that group cumulative? -2 if they play a second movement card in the above example, and -3 if you had three cards (dashing forward as it were)?

Thanks.
author: DaveyJJ
consensus_answer:
You total up all the cards. So if a group is moving out of -3 Buildings, the 1st Movement card would make fire vs. that group -2. (-3 Buildings, +1 Movement). If you play the 2nd Movement card, that would make fire vs. that group -1. (-3 Buldings, +1 Movement, +1 Movement) Thus, the Movement cards are cumulative.

This is incorrect. Placement of a Terrain card effectively removes the influence of previously placed movement cards and 'wipes the slate clean' with regard to previous Movement card modifiers:-

5.41 

Once a Terrain card is played and accepted on a group, it removes all cards beneath it from further consideration until redrawn and played again later in the game [16.2]. Even if a group uses a Movement card to retreat, the terrain he retreats to will be determined by the next Terrain card played on top of that Movement card. All cards beneath an accepted, played Terrain card are removed and placed in the Discard pile.

If one Movement card is played on top of a Terrain card, the group is still in that Terrain, and receives cumulative modifiers for the Terrain card and the Movement card.

However, if a second Movement card is played, the group has now left that terrain and is considered to be in open ground - it would receive 2 x +1 modifiers for the two Movement cards, but would not receive the previously placed Terrain card's modifier.

In the above example, the Fire Attack Modifier would be +2, rather than -1.

Note that a third Movement card would still result in a +2 modifier, not a +3 modifier, as per rule 7.2:-

7.2 
The Fire Strength modifier of the last Terrain or Movement card placed on a defending group is used when resolving any fire attacks against that group. A couple of points about the position you may not have realized:
-  If the Russian group C advanced to RC 3 after the German B did, Russian C has achieved a natural flanking on German B.  (German B laterally transferring or moving at all, would remove any such Flanking chit,)
-  The Russian Group C, if they move sideways, would have an encircled position on German Group B.  All firepower from any group is doubled--very nasty.
-  On "devastated" Russian Group B, so long as Russian B exists BOTH of the above situations are still in play.  You really need to eliminate the entirety of Russian B to prevent both flanking and encirclement. 
-  Transferring from German B to C does nothing to increase your firepower against Russian group C.  Effective relative range when firing is only decreased when firing against group that are neither directly opposing or adjacent (i.e. A firing on C or D) 

Actually RR6 is an easier to understand than "RR4 behind the opposing group".  When firing, RR6 uses the same firepower/To Hit # as RR4.

On the bright side, you could use an action the group to have the unpinned crewman to acquire the crewed weapon and become the new principle weapon operator.  No RNC draw would be required in this situation.
