First off, relative range refers to the distance between two groups, derived by adding the range chits together.  When referring the specific positions (i.e. what number is on the range chit), the rulebook (confusingly) uses the term "range".  Players often use the term "range chit" to avoid confusion.

The designer's notes give the following distances for each range:
0 = over 400 yds.
1 =  400-200 yds.
2 =  100-200 yds.
3 =   50-100 yds.
4 =   25-50  yds.
5 =   under 25 yds (i.e. essentially the same area) 

Note the distances are not linear.

Any relative range less than 0 is simply treated in game terms as being "over 400 yds."  400 yds. is picked not because WW2 rifles were incapable of firing bullets that far.  It was that the average soldier did not have the marksmanship to be effective beyond 400 yds (or 200 yds in with the less well trained Russians, Japanese and Italians)

Also the rules prevent most situations where RR-1 (or more negative relative ranges) from occurring by:
-  Any retreating moves to a negative range chit must be done with a movement card with a red RNC printed on it (making about 1/2 of the movement cards useless for retreating--though they can be used for sideways or forward movement, removing wire, transferring, etc.)
-  You cannot make  a retreating move if the closest enemy group is at RR0.  Another group could be further away, so RR-1 or lower is possible--but this prevent all of the opposing groups from having negative RR's

You just don't get too many situations where you are firing at RR-1 (or more negative RR's).  Think of being at RR0 or negative RR as being "too far away to really hit them."

title: Group Transfer questions
question:
I wanna see if I have the rules about group transfer correct.

1. A group may only transfer if there are no other PCs occupying the group space they are trying to transfer into?

2. A group may only transfer to 1 of the 4 possible groups (A-D)?

3. Do groups have to transfer in subsequent order?  i.e. may group A transfer immediately to group C or D?  Or B to D...

4.  Does the whole group have to transfer together?  May you take 3 men out of your 5 man group and transfer them at the same time?

5. If you have a vehicle in group B and you want it to move to group D but there are PCs in group C can this transfer even happen?
author: DiploGuy
consensus_answer:
1. A group may only transfer if there are no other PCs occupying the group space they are trying to transfer into? 

Yes. The exception to this would be if two adjacent groups both played a movement card to exchange places (A becomes B, and vice versa). 

17.7 LATERAL GROUP TRANSFER:
 ......adjacent groups which are both capable of movement may each play a sideways Movement card simultaneously so as to exchange positions on the table and group ID's. 

 2. A group may only transfer to 1 of the 4 possible groups (A-D)?

Yes.

17.7 LATERAL GROUP TRANSFER:
Group ID transfers are limited to A through D (except when reinforcements enter play as Group E or Z;

3. Do groups have to transfer in subsequent order?  i.e. may group A transfer immediately to group C or D?  Or B to D...

Yes, they have to transfer to an immediately adjacent group id. Therefore it would take at least two turns for a group to move from position A to C.

17.7 LATERAL GROUP TRANSFER:
A group capable of movement can change its group identity and thereby its position directly opposite an opposing group by announcing a Lateral Group Transfer.........In doing so, it attempts to assume the identity of an adjacent, previously non-existant group.

4.  Does the whole group have to transfer together?  May you take 3 men out of your 5 man group and transfer them at the same time?

You can move less than the whole group, but only by performing Individual Transfer, playing one movement card per PC.

17.9 GROUP CREATION: 
Once play begins, a new group can be created only by the arrival of reinforcements [35.0] or splitting an existing group by individual transfer.

17.91
Individual transfer can be used to create a new group only if one of the positions next to the creating group (A through D) is not already occupied by a friendly group. To create a new group in that position, the creating group must qualify for Individual tranfer and simultaneously attempt to transfer at least two men to the new group.
17.92 
The Group Creation is completed when the new group plays a Terrain card. If any transferring man is pinned prior to the play of a Terrain card on its group -- the transfer fails and the entire group is returned to the creating group. Otherwise, all rules for Individual Transfer apply.

5. If you have a vehicle in group B and you want it to move to group D but there are PCs in group C can this transfer even happen?

The vehicle could 'swap positions' with the PCs in group C on the first turn (as above), and could then lateral group transfer to position D on a subsequent turn. Vehicles can never combine with other cards to form a group, however.

title: movement and infiltration question
question:
Movement:

M1)Whenever you place a movement card in the forward position on a terrain that doesn't require 2 movement cards you immediately increase your range chit, right?

M2) If a terrain requires two movement cards to exit only on the 2nd card is the range chit increased?

M3) If on, say, 3 consecutive turns you lay down a movement card on the same group then after those 3 turns the group would be at RR3 provided they began at RR0?  Or do you have to establish the terrain they are in before moving again?

Infiltration:

I1) the rules make it pretty clear that an infiltrator is subjected to any fire received by the group he came from.  As well as benefiting from any terrain that group is in.  The rules also seem to indicate that the infiltrated group could move back to RR4 and the infiltrator still maintains his status.  How then can he still receive the benefit of the terrain the group is in?  And if he loses his infiltration status how does he immediately jump back to his own group?

20.53 An infiltrator loses his infiltrator status only if... the infiltrated group plays a Terrain card at RR4

This implies the group could have moved back from RR5 to RR4 and the infiltrator is still there.
author: DiploGuy
consensus_answer:
I'm not so sure we're correct on "range chit increases after the 2nd movement card on a 2 movement card terrain."

Listen to the rules for Gully: 8.22, A group in a Gully is still considered in that Gully even after placing a movement card... Only by placing yet another movement card or a Terrain card... does the group leave the gully... However, each Movement card played in an Advanced or Retreat mode does affect the group's range chit...

Actually, after the first movement card is played on a group, the terrain card ALWAYS still applies for that group.  Only the last 2 movement or terrain cards are ever applied.

It says each so it has to be referring to the first one as well as the second one because there is no 3rd movement card needed for a Gully.  I guess it's no different than single movement terrain then.  The only reason this must be in the rules is to explain that because you still receive the benefits of the terrain your movement card is on being in the gully still means you can't fire out of or fire into (except for the few exceptions).

True, but a gullies have a special rule--even after playing 2 consecutive movement cards on a group leaving the gully, the first movement card is not counted for a defensive TEM--because when first movement card was played, the group was still "hidden" in the gully.  

It does NOT require 2 movement cards to exit a gully.

So Marsh and Stream I think are the only 2 movement card terrains where your range chit only increases after the 2 movement.  The difference from the Gully being that these two require the 1st movement card to be placed sideways.

Stream does NOT require 2 movement cards to exit.  You must move sideways to exit (and ford the stream using a special card or passing an RNC draw), but then you can place them into another terrain (or have one placed for you) on the next turn.

Marsh is the ONLY card that requires 2 movement cards to exit.

You seem to be missing a very important point, you can move sideways with movement card and change terrain without changing the range chit of the group or "transferring" to another letter.

title: Pinned Transfering man and hero card
question:
Hi

I have a man which is transfering to an adjacent group. This guy has just been fired at and becomes pinned.

If I play immediatly a hero card on him (cancelling the pin), is he still considered transfering?

author: bonzillou
consensus_answer:
Per section 10.4, the hero card isn't a "this didn't happen" card, it just immediately rallies the pinned man. It doesn't prevent the pin from happening. Thus, as per rule 17.84, the transfer status is lost.

Hi

I have a man which is transfering to an adjacent group. This guy has just been fired at and becomes pinned.

If I play immediatly a hero card on him (cancelling the pin), is he still considered transfering?
:what:

A bit of a munchkin play, there.  A Hero card doesn't "cancel" anything.  The man still gets pinned, even if someone rallies him immediately with a Hero card.

Despite what the rules might suggest (I don't think the rules on this is clear as glass anyway): I find it dowright rediculous that a Hero cannot be played on a man to allow him to complete his transfer, when a Hero card can indeed be played to allow a man pinned while trying to enter CC, to rally and try again the same turn.

As I've stated before with regard to Up Front, I think it is important to not loose sight of the fact that Up Front tries to simulate real life situations. Trying to enter close combat is probably one of the most nerve-wracking situations a soldier can encounter. Being fired at while trying to get from one foxhole to another sure can't be much fun either, but I bet trying to kill an enemy with cold steel or the butt of one's rifle beats the foxhole-switching in terms of psychological strain.

Probably the rules try to simualate fire on a transferring man the moment he gets up to start the transfer, but what if the case was that he was already well on his way?
Think for your self: If you are out in the open between two foxholes, you might be just as safe diving into the next foxhole as you'd be returning to you starting point if you're fired on while under way. I guess in many cases a soldier would chose to return rather than complete the transfer out of the logics of "you know what you've got, but not what you'll get". However I'm pretty sure many would chose to continue the transfer too. It could be as simple as you beeing closer to the next foxhole than to the place you came from when the burst is fired. Another thing to bear in mind is that a large group probably feels safer than a small group. With this I mean that a man transfering from a group with two soldiers probably might easier choose to complete the transfer if the group he's going to consists of more soldiers.

Anyway, what I mean is that one should not dissmiss entirely the possibility of a man completing transfer despite being pinned on the way. And playing a hero card to allow him to complete the transfer, I think is a good solution. So I suggest that as a house-rule. At least I always play it that way. And I feel that there are few arguments against it apart from what is written (or not written) in the rules.

R.:)

The difference between being pinned while in transfer and being pinned while infiltrating or entering Close Combat is that during transfer the pin was caused by enemy fire. The other pins are the result of failed morale checks. A Hero card offers a second opportunity to be brave while closing with the enemy, not to avoid bullets. So there is logic in its application to one circumstance and not the other.

I can't see that the way a man got pinned shoud make any difference. A pin is a pshycological condition. As is being heroic. What causes it shoudn't matter.

Another way to solve it would of course be that a man heroed after being pinned in transfer could continue the transfer provided the player had another movement card on his hand. That would make it even more similar to try again to enter CC.

R.:)

In game terms you are right, Roar, it doesn't matter how a man gets pinned. I was only trying to offer a rationalization for the difference in the two circumstances in question. A pin from fire is more than a psychological condition -- it's hugging the ground to avoid getting hit by very fast-moving metal. Failing a morale check, by itself, entails no particular danger, and the resulting pin can reasonably be said to represent a psychological condition that a heroic effort might overcome.

In any case, the rules and "official" understanding in tournament play are that a Hero card cannot be used to avoid a pin during Transfer and that the Transfer is cancelled. Any other "solution" would be, as you suggest, a house rule, which agreeable players are certainly free to employ in friendly games. The one you proposed sounds like another good use of the Hero card -- a reasonable variant worth giving a try!

title: Playing Terrain on an opponent - part of discarding?

title: Placing terrain on R0 opponent's group during game
question:
Hi

is it possible to place a marsh on an opponent's group which is at R0 during the game (not in the initial terrain placement phase)?

thanks
author: bonzillou
consensus_answer:
is it possible to place a marsh on an opponent's group which is at R0 during the game (not in the initial terrain placement phase)?

Except at the beginning of the game, during initial terrain placement, NO terrain card be placed on ANY group, friend or foe, unless that group has a Movement card previously played on it. (BTW, There can pinned men in moving group.)  Range makes no difference.

(Wire and Smoke are NOT terrain cards--they modify existing terrain cards and thus can be played on non-moving groups.)

BTW, playing any card on your opponent:  Terrain, Wire, Smoke (though this requires a US or German AFV with ordnance effect of 4+) or Sniper is accomplished with a discard.

title: CC procedure
question:
Hi
I have two infiltrated (previous turn) guys that successfully enter CC against a group of 2 ennemy soldiers.

While drawing RPC to see who they will assault, they both draw a 1 under the column 2. 

I'm not sure here, do they both assault the 1st ennemy soldier or do I have to create pairs?

thanks
author: bonzillou
consensus_answer:
Hi
I have two infiltrated (previous turn) guys that successfully enter CC against a group of 2 ennemy soldiers.

I assume that means they have passed their morale check or you played a Movement card to bypass this.

While drawing RPC to see who they will assault, they both draw a 1 under the column 2. 

I'm not sure here, do they both assault the 1st ennemy soldier or do I have to create pairs?

thanks

The point of drawing the RPC is determine which man they attack--you don't get a choice.  

If two or more men attack the same man, the attacker then picks which of those men attacks the poor b@st@rd first--he'd get +3 added to the CCV for each additional man attacking on that attack.  If the defender manages to survive, the attacker chooses the next man for close combat, but would have one less helper.  

If the defender is killed, any other men have no one to attack and thus remain infiltrated.

title: To Hit Frequency and Concealed cards
question:
Hi
I don't understand how the concealed cards work against the To Hit frequency according to 25.6.

If a mortar has a THF of 3 and i play a -2 Concealed card, its THF is downed to 1?

Another mortar has a THF of 1 and I play -3 concealed card, what will be the new THF?

Thanks

pascal
author: bonzillou
consensus_answer:
Hi
I don't understand how the concealed cards work against the To Hit frequency according to 25.6.

If a mortar has a THF of 3 and i play a -2 Concealed card, its THF is downed to 1?

Another mortar has a THF of 1 and I play -3 concealed card, what will be the new THF?

To Hit #'s work on spectrum like this:

Easier  0-5,  0-4,  0-3,  0-2,  0-1,   0,   1,  2,  3,  4,  5,   6  Harder

A Concealment card moves the To Hit# that many steps to the right in this spectrum:  So in your example:  To Hit  3  become To Hit of 5 when an Conceal -2 is played.

If the To Hit  0-1, a -2 Conceal would make it To Hit 1.  

Two other important Ordnance rules:
-  Malfunctions are ONLY checked on the To Hit Draw.  These are marked with a lower case x.  Once a hit is obtained, any red 6 that comes up does not malfunction the weapon.
-  For non AT ordnance weapons (i.e. unboxed effect #'s), the RNC # of the To Hit draw is added (color does not matter) is added to the Effect # of the weapon, ONLY if a 0 would have been a hit.  (i.e. The To Hit # is 0-N.)  

So if you had a 0-2 To hit with mortar and draw a red 1 to get a hit, the Effect number is 2 + 1 = 3.

However if your opponent played a -3 concealment, making your To Hit # 1, the same 1 would still cause a hit, but it is no longer added, so the effect remains 2.

This accounts for the increased chance of a direct hit at closer ranges. It also means you see most conceal cards played vs. ordnance when the To Hit # is 0-1 or higher, it decreases the chance and possibly the final effect.  Whereas in your examples, concealing only makes a low chance of hit even lower.  (And it's very annoying when you play a concealment card to turn a miss into a hit!)Yes, Richard is probably one of the best Up Front experts on the Geek. One thing that helped me understand your conundrum was to look at all the RNC's like it was an integer line with RED 0 through RED 6 starting in the middle and going to the left and BLACK 0 through BLACK 6 going to the right. Effectively, that makes 14 possible placements (or pips on a die if you prefer that analogy) for RNC's. Once you realize that the RNC number distribution is NOT evenly dispersed but that zero (both colors) is the most common RNC and that 6 (both colors) is the least common RNC, the integer line visualization makes more sense. If I'm not mistaken, the closer to the center of the integer line you get (zero), the more likely the RNC. I believe Banzai has a section in the rules that breaks down the exact frequency of all the possible RNC's, among other statistical analysis.

Welcome to the confusion that can be Up Front, but an otherwise awesome game!!

replies.body:
When you say THF of 3, do you mean 0-3?  If that's the case, than the to hit range drops to 0-1.

A THF of 0-1 which has a -3 concealment played on it would go as so:

0-1   unmodified
0  -1 concealment
1  -2 concealment
2  -3 concealment

You would need to than draw a 2 to get a hit, or a black 2 against a moving target.

Concealment first decreases the range of numbers you need to draw down to one number (0, the most common single random number in the deck) and each successive concealment makes it more difficult to hit, so you "raise" the number needed to hit to numbers less common in the deck.

title: Infiltration with flamethrower/secondary weapon
question: Rule 20.23 states you can abandon a flamethrower or secondary weapon as a hindrance when attempting to infiltrate. I can't find anything to say that these items cause a hindrance whilst infiltrating, only whilst in close combat. Is this the only malus they confer, or do they also affect infiltration attempts?
author: Badgeroonie
consensus_answer:
No, it does not affect the infiltration, but secondary weapons and flame throwers have negative affects on CCV, hence you might want to abandon the flame thrower or secondary weapon in preparation for an attack in close combat on a later turn after successfully infiltrating.

If you don't want the CCV penalty get rid of it when you infiltrate.

I should point out generally you won't want to get rid of a useful secondary weapon (ATMM, demo charge) when infiltrating.  

Panzerfaust, flamethrower have no additional benefit while infiltrating, why even try to infiltrate with these weapons?  

As for the radio, why even advance forward?   The man carrying it and SL should stay back,

What I'm getting at it is the situation shouldn't come up often.

title: RR and Lateral Group Transfer
question:
OK, I don't know how I didn't notice how awful this rulebook is the first time I read it, but I've gone back through it recently, and I've run into a huge problem.  First, we've got this quote from the rules.

"A group may not move forward if, in so doing, the Relative Range between it and its like-named (directly opposite) opposing group would exceed 5."

OK, well, this isn't even possible according to the rules for calculating Relative Range.  Any total of two range chits > 5 is subtracted from 10 to get the actual distance between groups.  Since you can never subtract 6 or more from 10 and end up with a number greater than 5, this has to be a mistake.

Now, it doesn't take a genius to figure out the intent of the rule is to disallow directly opposite units to move through each other, so I think it's safe to say that the rule is supposed to reference the sum of the range chits, not the actual RR.

Here's where the problem comes in; nowhere in the entire section on Lateral Group Transfers are the groups' RR or range chits mentioned.  If there are not range-based restrictions on who gets to transfer, and no adjustments made to the chits after the move is completed, it's possible to have a group both directly behind and directly opposite an enemy group.

So, does anyone know if this is a legal play, and if it is, am I correct in assuming the two groups aren't really considered to be behind each other for flanking and encirclement purposes?
author: mattlaclair
consensus_answer:
Try these rules

http://www.canyonpointstudios.com/UpFront.pdf

If not clearer, post to the ongoing new rules thread.

title: Panic and VPs
question:
Hi
I first have to say that I'm still not playing with the wounds rules.

is a panicing soldier considered KIA, and hence gives 2VPqs to opponent?

thanks
author: bonzillou
consensus_answer:
The rules use the word "panic" for two different ways:
-  When drawing RNC for a fire attack vs. and pinned man and the final fire strength >= the Panic value, but less than KIA value.
-  After the Panic value is exceeded, Rout is checked for.  If the unit does not rout, the man is said to "Panic"

To my way of thinking, call the first case, "Panic" and  the second case as "KIA"  

For all purposes, scoring, weapon now available for acquisition, elimination of the man, etc., the second case and straight KIA are exactly the same.  Why not call them the same thing.

So it's just easier to to think:
Final FS >= Panic, then the man Panics
Now check of whether he is Routed or KIA.

title: Ordinance
question:
Hi Greg,

Yes, in this example you would score a hit by drawing 0-2, so your draw of 1 would result in a hit. The colour of the number would not matter, unless either yourself or your target were moving, in which case a red 0-2 would be a miss.

Your hit strength when using boxed effect numbers against AFVs is equal to the boxed effect number, plus a number equal to the relative range between firer & target (in this case 2). This would result in a hit strength of 7 + 2 = 9 in your example.

25.4 HIT STRENGTH: 
Once a hit has been obtained, the strength of that hit is determined by adding the To Hit Random Number on the RNC just drawn to the Effect Number listed on the ordnance card. (EXC: IG/AFV ordnance firing at an AFV target does not add the To Hit Random Number just drawn; instead it adds a number equal to the Relative Range between the firer and the target.) The color of the RNC has no effect; all numbers are added. Having now determined the total strength of the attack (after modification for terrain and/or movement), it is resolved separately for each target in the defending group by drawing a new RNC and adding any black number or subtracting any red number drawn as per a normal fire attack [6.5].

If you are new to Up Front, I would advise starting with scenario 1 - a meeting of patrols, and wouldn't even think of attempting ordnance, let alone AFVs until you are familiar & comfortable with the rules for infantry, fire attacks, terrain effects, lateral group & individual transfer, infiltration, close combat, etc, etc. 

Take your time & learn to walk before you try to run - it will be worth it.

PS - the firepower adjacent to the range is used when the AFV fires its machine gun at a target rather than using its main ordnance weapon.
consensus_answer:
The ordnance rules do make sense once you understand what they are trying to represent.  There are two distinct cases: firing high explosive (HE) and armour piercing (AP) – solid shot.  In both cases, whether or not you hit uses the same process – you have to draw less than or equal to the To Hit number.

1) With HE, the important thing is how close to the target the hit is.  This is represented by getting a higher draw (but still within the to Hit number).  So if you are hitting on “0-3”, a 2 is a “closer” hit than a 0.  To represent this, the 2 is added to the HE (unboxed) effect against each target.  If your To Hit is low enough that it’s less than “0”, for example a “1”, you’re never going to get a really close hit, so you don’t get to add the 1 if you do hit.  On the other hand, if you have a high To Hit, eg “0-4”, you are fairly certain to hit, and have decent chance of getting a better hit by drawing a positive number – which increases your effect.

2) With AP, which is only used against AFVs, it’s different.  By making a successful To Hit draw, you’ve already hit the vehicle, and the question is whether you penetrate it – where you hit is comparatively unimportant (it’s assumed you hit on the front of the target – if you get a flank/rear shot the target usually has lower defence values to represent this).  What affects the likelihood of penetration is how close the firing ordnance is to the target.  So in this case you add the relative range to the AP (boxed) effect number of the ordnance.  For example, if you are both at Range 0, the RR is 0, so you add nothing.  If you’ve moved forward to Range 1 and he is at Range 2, the RR is 3, so you add 3.

In both cases, having evaluated the final Hit Strength, you check the final effect for each target (eg each man in a group targeted by HE) by drawing an RNC and use the red/black number, subtracting or adding the value to give the final effect.  For an AP shot there will never be more than one target, but you still do this final check by turning a single card.

Bear in mind that when firing ordnance against a AFV which is not buttoned up or pinned (open-topped AFVs are pinned rather than buttoning-up) you can choose whether to fire HE or AP – with HE you are trying to hit the exposed crew and force them to close down, or if you’re lucky, get a Commander Killed result.  In this case you use the normal HE procedure as above.

There are some ordnance weapons which don’t have a choice between HE and AP – they only ever fire one or the other.  So mortars only ever fire HE.  ATRs only ever fire AP, although they have an alternative use as a kind of infantry rifle with 1 FP.  Bazookas, panzerfausts, panzerschrecks and PIATs are firing a shaped charge whose effect is less predictable than solid shot, so there is a random element in calculating their effect, and they do use the HE procedure when firing against an AFV, even though the final result is compared to the AFV’s armour defence value.

And finally, just for completeness, some early war British AFVs didn’t carry HE ammunition, so they are confined to firing solid shot against infantry targets.  This is represented by using the HE procedure, but never adding a bonus to their unboxed Hit Strength of 0 even when they get a “close” hit.  So you can land a 6-pdr (57mm) solid shot among an infantry group and maybe scare them, but you’re unlikely to kill anyone!

Up Front really isn't a tank game, most of the standard AFV scenarios involve a halftrack or bren carrier or armored car or early war tank. 

The big boys, even detuned as they are, overwhelm any scenario in Up Front in which they appear.

Glenn Oberhauser (manhattandoctor here on BGG) is carrying out a rewrite of the rules, available here http://www.canyonpointstudios.com/UpFront.pdf.

The BGG page discussing the rewrite can be found here. It looks pretty good to me, and should be helpful.

Again, I would advise you to start with scenario A & work your way forwards slowly from there.

title: Questions
question:
Terrain cards might stop movement. If you play a terrain card on your own moving group, the group stops moving. If your opponent discards a terrain card on your group, you can choose to accept the terrain (and thus stop moving) or you can change the movement card you have in play to sideways (reducing your current range-chit again). If the movement card was already played sideways and you choose to reject it, the movement card is instead removed.

A wire-discard on your moving group doesn't stop movement, but you cannot enter terrain (except open ground) or play another movement card to change range until you have played a movement card to remove the wire.

R.:)
consensus_answer:
Don't forget that playing any card face down on the moving group also counts as terrain (open ground) and similarly stops movement and removes the movement card.

Not generally recommended unless in dire peril!

It depends--if you don't have any good terrain cards, it is often better to at least stop moving, even if it is open ground.  That removes the -1 Defensive TEM and allows you to fire at full fire strength

title: scenario C  /Pillbox/ GroupTransfers
question:
Can you transfer groups to and from the Pillbox in scenario C
For example you have 3 groups A / B in pillbox / C ...
if group A is ELIM may B (pillbox) transfer  into the A position While C moves into the pillbox at B.
group B plays sideways move card waits for terrain to move into A
group C plays sideways move card ........and moves into pillbox ?

OR is this a {pillbox vacated} action and therefore attacking player wins ?
ManyThanksToner
author: toner
consensus_answer:
Can you transfer groups to and from the Pillbox in scenario C
For example you have 3 groups A / B in pillbox / C ...
if group A is ELIM may B (pillbox) transfer  into the A position While C moves into the pillbox at B.
group B plays sideways move card waits for terrain to move into A
group C plays sideways move card ........and moves into pillbox ?

No, because once you place a terrain card on the group leaving B--the pillbox, like any other terrain card, would then be discarded.

You can move men into/out of the pillbox only by individual transfer.

title: lateral group transfer/fire attacks
question:
If a group wishes to move and form a new group ID it has to play a movement card sideways And wait until a new terrain card is placed on the movement card....if attacked while taking this action (before the new terrain card ) is it resolved as a normal movement ie Terrain(less fireStrength) and movement(plus F/S) 
Are there any additional modifers/chits for the lateral transfer? excluding wire hero flank ....
ManyThanksToner
author: toner
consensus_answer:
Instead of a new thread I'll trying getting my question answered here...

Can you place wire on an individual transfer?  The rules say wire is placed on a moving group.  It doesn't specifically mention an individual moving though.

Yes, wire can be placed. It would be placed on either the transferring or receiving group. It would affect fire against that group, including the transferring man (who is subject to fire against both groups until transfer is complete), but would not hinder or disrupt the transfer. 

This situation is dealt with specifically in the official errata:-

17.8 Before an Individual Transfer is completed, the opponent places wire on the "sending" group. Since the Transfer was begun when the sending group had no wire, can the transfer still be completed?
A. Yes.

17.8 Can an individual transfer INTO a group in wire?
A. Yes.

The rules say wire is placed on a moving group.

The rules don't say this. Wire can be placed on a moving or stationary group. 'Artificial terrain', such as wire and smoke, can be placed directly on a terrain card.

-  All attacks against it are +1
-  It cannot be entrenched

-  If the transferring group fire, it pays FS and FP penalties.

title: Rejecting Terrain Causes Relative Range To Be Less Than 0?
question:
Let's say I have two groups. 

Group A is at Range 0, and Group B is at Range 0, for a total Relative Range of 0.

Group A plays a Movement +2 Card, so Relative Range is now at 2 (2/0).

Group B plays a Movement -1 Card (with red RNC), so Relative Range is now at 1 (2/-1).

During B's discard phase, they play terrain on Group A. If Group A rejects the terrain, they will be forced to turn their Movement +2 Card into a Sideways Move, and move their range chit back to 0, which would result in a Relative Range of -1 (0/-1).

Is Group A allowed to reject the terrain? The rules state that a group may not place a movement card if the relative range between it and the closest enemy group would be less than 0. But what about rejecting terrain? Are they forced to accept the terrain?
author: mjacobsca
consensus_answer:
If I understand your scenario, the play is perfectly legal. There is no restriction based on RR against discarding terrain on an opposing group. And there is no limitation based on RR on accepting or rejecting terrain discarded on one of your groups.

1. Russian a0 moves up to a1(move fwd).
2. German A0 moves back to A-1(move retro) and discards Marsh on a1(move fwd).
3. Russian may now accept the Marsh and stop in a1(marsh) OR reject Marsh and change to a0(move side).
4. Russian rejects Marsh, changes to a0(move side). a0 plays a Wall and becomes a0(Wall).
5. German plays Woods and becomes A-1(Woods).

a0 and A-1 are at RR-1, but for all fire/TH purposes, they are considered to be at RR0.

Neither a0 nor A-1 can now play a retro Move card because of 5.51 which says a unit may not RETREAT if it will DECREASE the RR between it and the CLOSEST group TO < 0. The RR is already < 0 due to other legal plays, including a legal retreat played when the groups were AT RR1 after the Russian's advance.

If there were a Russian group in b3 now, German A-1 could retreat again to A-2, because the closest group (b3) is currently at RR2, regardless of whether Russian a is at 0 or -10.

If A rejects terrain, then the Relative Range would go to -1 when the previously played Movement Card was discarded.

What happens there?

title: Weapon Exchange
question:
There is a situation regarding Weapon Exchange that occurs from time to time that I have never been clear on.  The rules governing this are 18.21 and 33.3:

18.21: A man may not keep possession of, nor fire, more than one weapon. In acquiring a weapon, he automatically exchanges his previous weapon (EXC: [20.74], SW; [21.1]) for the weapon chit just gained by leaving a proper weapon chit in its place. Primary weapons of pinned and unwounded men cannot be voluntarily exchanged. However, a secondary weapon of an unpinned or wounded man may be given to another unpinned man in the same group automatically as the sole action of that group for that turn.

33.3 concerns crewed weapons and is clear.

The Errata clarify the situation somewhat, as follows:

 18.21 May an armed man give his primary and only weapon to an unarmed man?  
A. No, unless the armed man is wounded.  

 18.21 & 33.3 To clarify these two rules:  
A pinned man can never be involved in a weapon exchange.  
Weapon exchanges of primary weapons must involve at least one wounded man.  
Weapon exchanges of secondary weapons need not involve a wounded man.

So it's clear that an unpinned wounded man can exchange his primary weapon with another man.  My question is, how is this done?  :
a) Is it an automatic action by the group, as in the last sentence of 18.21?  Or,
b) Does it require a Weapon Acquisition draw?  Or,
c) Does the wounded man have to drop the weapon before requiring a Weapon Acquisition as a separate action in a later turn?

So, to make it crystal clear, say the US BAR gunner is wounded.  The player wants one of the riflemen to take over the BAR to use its full firepower.  Can this be done as an automatic action, or does the rifleman have to Acquire the weapon directly from the gunner, or does the BAR gunner have to drop the weapon, and then the rifleman have to acquire it in a later turn?

I have been playing c) but am inclining towards b) - I would appreciate other players' views.
author: Barbarossa
consensus_answer:
I would probably lean towards A)  A weapon exchange is an automatic action between the wounded BAR man and an unpinned unwounded rifleman.  

But the rules and errata don't precisely clarify the point.

title: Flanking and firing : is FS halved?
question:
Hi
I'm not sure about that:
A)a flanking group (per the play of a sideways movement card) is firing on the flanked group :
its FP is X2 but the FS card is halved (because it's considered moving).
Am I right?

B)If it was "naturally flanking" and not moving, FS would not be halved.
Am I right?

thanks
author: bonzillou
consensus_answer:
Hi

A)a flanking group (per the play of a sideways movement card) is firing on the flanked group :

Am I right

B)If it was "naturally flanking" and not moving, FS would not be halved.
Am I right?

Correct, but there is a little detail you missed.

You lose the the flank chit is 4 ways:
-  Flanked grouped group moves (even to remove wire) or enters terrain.
-  Flanking group moves or a wire card is played on the Flanking group
-  Flanking group rejects FLANK terrain card when opponent plays terrain on the group.
-  The group "in front" of the flanked group is eliminated or transfers to a different letter.

Note there is ONE action which stops the Flanking group from moving AND does NOT remove the Flank Chit:  The Flanking group enters terrain.  THAT is when you x2 FP but do not have to pay any FP penalty for movement, (Note movement 1/2's FP of Bolt action riifles (not semi automatics used by the US, and also reduces fire strength by 1/2 of all firing groups.)

The chit is what doubles firepower:  That is placed when a FLANK movement card or a movement card that moves the Flanking group to (effectively) RR6 AND there is a group in Front of the Flanked group.

question:
Hi,

here some questions after the first try:

what do the letters 4c and so on on the charakter cards mean. Do i have a choice beetween the differt "4" cards in the scenarions with the 4?

What exactly does 5.7 mean? In order to move further forawrd, the opposite group whose Range chit blocks a further advance would have to retreat or be eliminated. Does this mean you just can not move until the group opposite is eleminated or moves back? 

Concealed: Does this mean you have to remember who already shot and this group can never be concealed again?

FP of Americans is not halved when they move (on the card it is only mentioned on the german cards) just the FS

and another question: are there really enough moving cards in the deck? it seems i can not do anything in some rounds....
author: evil_puck
consensus_answer:
Hi,

just got my artcow order and now trying to learn this mess of a rulebook :-)

here some questions after the first try:

what do the letters 4c and so on on the charakter cards mean. Do i have a choice beetween the differt "4" cards in the scenarions with the 4?

Assuming you mean the RPC (Random Position Card) and generally used to select 1 man out of X men in the group for event like Sniper or weapon malfunction & infiltration.  So if there are 7 men in the group, you look at the number 7.

Some RPC numbers are used in specific situation which are marked by letters;  
-  7w is to check for wounds 
-  0r to check for rout during combat.
-  Cclose combat vs.AFV's:  2b if used to attack a "buttoned up AFV", 4c to attack "Commander Exposed AFV", 5o for "Open Topped AFV's"  (This menas it easier to attack a buttoned up AFV.

  What exactly does 5.7 mean? In order to move further forawrd, the opposite group whose Range chit blocks a further advance would have to retreat or be eliminated. Does this mean you just can not move until the group opposite is eleminated or moves back? 

When two groups are at RR5 to each other, they are are in the same area within about 15m each other.  Two groups with the same ID letter  (i.e. in the same column) cannot pass through each other.  So in order to advance further in the same column, the opposing group in the same column must either move back to allow you to move forward or the opposing group must be eliminated.  

Concealed: Does this mean you have to remember who already shot and this group can never be concealed again?

Nope.  Concealment lasts for single fire attack.  So if I fire at you from group A and you play a Concealment--the both the Fire cards, Concelment card and all RNC cards used to resolve the attack are immediately discarded.   If I then fire from Group B on the same group on the same turn or a later turn, the previous Concealment card has no effect.  You would have to play another Concealment card (if you had one), to reduce the fire.

A common tactic is fire is to fire from two groups on the same turn, hoping the first smaller attack will draw out a concealment card so the larger second attack can done at maximum strength.

FP of Americans is not halved when they move (on the card it is only mentioned on the german cards) just the FS

Whenever you mmove FS is always halved.

Firepower of bolt action rifles is also halved.  Only the Americans are using semi automatic rifles.  All other nationalities in UP Front use bolt action rifles.

In any case, it is usually a BAD IDEA to ever fire when you are moving.  

and another question: are there really enough moving cards in the deck? it seems i can not do anything in some rounds....

That is the point of the game--sometimes your troops cannot follow orders.  Maybe they can't hear them over the din of the battlefield.  Maybe that last bullet was too close and they won't break cover.  

Moving is the dangerous thing that can be done on a battlefield.  You generally do not want to move unless you have to or if you some sort of cover:  the enemy group mostly pinned or stuck in wire, a good conceal card or terrain card in hand.  

You have to spend many turns discarding, getting rid of cards you have no use for at the moment to hope getting ones you can use now.

Up Front is written in some heavy duty English that is more suited for a lawyer.

1. Not sure what you mean by '4c', however the list of character cards in a scenario is quite strict.  You must use the character cards listed exactly in the scenario.  This is for balance issues.

2.  What 5.7 means is that you can move forward and close range until you reach a Relative Range of 5 with the opposite group.  ex.  German Group B and American Group B are opposite Groups.  Once at RR5 neither can move forward in Range until either the Opposite Group is eliminated or move back in Range (thus changing Relative Range to 4)

Player A "My group B can satisfy the 12 firepower needed to use this card for a 5 strength attack vs your Group B.  5 FP, +1 I am on a hill, -1 You put me in Wire two turns ago and I have not burnt a Movement Card yet to get rid of it, -2 your Gr B is in a wooden building, +1 you also have a wire card that I discarded on your group some time ago that you still have not used a Movement Card to get rid of.  So my attack is 4 fire power, time to start drawing a RNC for each character in your group B to get the final attack vs each soldier."

Firepower is what you need to have to play a fire card. It is only modified by a few things, like moving for bolt action rifles or flanking.

Fire Strength represents the amount of accurate fire near the defenders. It is the main number on the fire card, and is modified by moving, terrain, concealment, smoke, wire, etc.
The higher the Fire Strength of an attack, the more likely the attack is to pin or kill enemy soldiers.

title: Terrain Capture /Relative Range
question:
RedGroup at RR1, BlueGroup at RR4 
Total RR is 5
Redgroup has infiltrated and engaged in CloseCombat and eliminated all
of BlueGroup
Redgroup can now take Bluegroups TerrainCard if desired
ExBluegroups RR4 chit is removed from play..
Redgroup remains at RR1 (with whichever terrain card prefered)
Is this correct ?
ManyThanksToner
author: toner
consensus_answer:
RedGroup at RR1, BlueGroup at RR4 
Total RR is 5

Assuming two things:
-  Red and Blue are opposing sides--which you never say.  Who the hell are "red" and "blue"?
-  That they are directly opposite (i.e. both have the same Group letter) or adjacent groups (one letter's difference).  If one was Group A and the other Group C or D or E, then the RR is adjusted by -1 to RR4.

For less confusion, express a group's position "Range 1" or "Range Chit 4" or RC4.  Use RR only to express the relative position between two groups. Red is at RC1 and Blue is at RC4.

Also any two directly opposite or adjacent enemy groups whose range chit total equals 5 are at RR5:  1 vs. 4, 2 vs. 3, 5 vs. 0, -1 vs. 6, etc.

Redgroup has infiltrated and engaged in CloseCombat and eliminated all
of BlueGroup
The groups must be at RR5 to each other in order to engage in CC at all.  

You must be at RR5 to establish infiltration and keep it if the opposing group moves to RR4 until that group places terrain, but you cannot enter CC unless the groups are at RR5.

Redgroup can now take Bluegroups TerrainCard if desired
Yes, they can now capture the opposing groups terrain if they wish.  In fact during each close combat, the winning man (if any) can capture any of the losing man weapons.  

ExBluegroups RR4 chit is removed from play..
Redgroup remains at RR1 (with whichever terrain card prefered)

The eliminated group no longer exists so their so their range chit is removed from play.  The eliminating group, even if they choose top capture terrain, remains at whatever range chit they are at.

title: infiltration+flanking+hero
question:
If a PC infiltrates successfully from a group which already has Flank firepower bonus and next turn draws a Hero card what is his total Firepower bonus 
Flank+Inf+Hero
 x3....?
ManyThanksToner
author: toner
consensus_answer:
Hmmm, I'm not sure about that. I tend to take the original stance from the ASL game which always said "Don't focus on what the rules DON"T say, but what they do say." In this case, I might tend to cap the F.P. off at x3.

Where in the rules can this be justified?  You say one thing, yet doing another.

There is no rule anywhere that says FP is limited to x3. 

 Nevertheless, a very good question and your logic seems completely sound to me Bob. I must admit though, your second statement made me laugh about "deserving what happens" :)

There are rules that say that FP is doubled when infiltrating, flanking and having a Hero card played on a man and a note saying that in the case of a Hero only that "If the man is already entitled to double firepower, triple it instead."  (For argument's sake, the Hero doubles the uncrewed FP of crewed weapon, but neither flanking nor infiltration have this restriction, so you can't argue consistency.)

Clearly there are several reasonable interpretations (which may be covered in the errata--but I can't check since the website is down):
-  Each FP doubling could be implied to add one to the multiplier in each case, therefore x4.
-  FP is doubled for flanking and then doubled again for infiltration, the the Hero clause is interpreted as adding one multiplier to the final modifier, therefore x5.
-  FP is doubled for flanking and then doubled again for infiltration, the the Hero clause is interpreted as converting one of these doublings to a tripling, therefore x6.
-  FP is doubled for flanking and then doubled again for infiltration, the the Hero clause doesn't say anything anything about already quadrupled FP, so it doubles FP again:  therefore x8.
-  FP is doubled for flanking and then doubled again for infiltration, the the Hero clause is interpreted as converting each of these doublings to a tripling, therefore x9
-  FP is doubled for flanking and then doubled again for infiltration, the the Hero clause is interpreted as not applying at all (It says doubled FP is tripled, but does not say anything about higher multipliers.) therefore x4 (Yes, it is same result as the first case, but a completely different reasoning.)

I think the first 3 and the last are reasonable interpretations given what the rules actually say.

As for realism, you are talking about having M1 rifle (with an 8 round clip) multiplied at x4 generating more FP than a crewed heavy machine gun even with no multipliers.  Clearly that doesn't make sense.

In the absence of actual errata and the fact that I have never seen this situation come up in actual play of 100's of games, I think the "each doubling results in increasing the FP multiplier by 1" is the best interpretation.

I just read the relevant rules:
Flanking doubles the firepower of the group that is flanking (rule 17.4)
Infiltration doubles the firepower of the individual that has infiltrated (rule 20.51)
A hero card doubles the firepower of an individual or triples it if it is already doubled. (rule 10.45)
This specific situation is not mentioned in the errata.

I see several possibilities.
1. Infiltration and Flanking double firepower for the same reason (fire coming from an advantageous direction). Because of this, they do not stack. (net x3 FP from the infiltrator).
2. Infiltration doubles individaual firepower, Hero increases individual FP to triple, group FP is then doubled (net x6 FP for the infiltrator).

I lean towards #1 - neither infiltration nor flanking say that they do anything when the firepower is already doubled.  They also both have the same exclusion (flamethrowers). To me, this tends to indicate that infiltration is merely individual flanking, and thus shouldn't be doubled again. Even if the infiltrator is firing from a different advantageous direction, he then isn't firing from the same direction as the flanking group, and shouldn't get the flanking bonus.

title: Close Combat vs. Infantry Guns

author: Keesvanloomacklin

The IG will add +3 twice (once for each additional crew member - unless it has a commander killed chit).

title: Rally All card--Design Flaw?
question:
Regarding rule 10.23 (Rally All)---I find it odd that two adjacent groups at the same range with a leader in EITHER group may utilize the Rally All card as well as two groups NOT adjacent to each other but with leaders in BOTH groups. I'm assuming the reason only one leader is needed to utilize the Rally All card with adjacent groups is because they are: 
A.) Adjacent and B.) At the same range. In the case of non-adjacent groups using Rally All, I can understand why each group must have a leader. 

Here is my question. What happens when you have two groups, BOTH with unpinned leaders and adjacent, but not at the same range? This situation satisfies the requirements of being adjacent (as per the first use of the card) and the requirements of having leaders in both groups (as per the second use of the card), but because they are not at the same range it seems only one group could be rallied. This seems a bit penalizing to me that two adjacent groups both with unpinned leaders but not at the same range can NOT use the Rally All card to full effect. Comments?
author: Keesvanloomacklin
consensus_answer:
No it is NOT an interesting question, but an overly silly misreading of the rule.

One unpinned leader can use Rally All for two groups IF AND ONLY IF the two groups are adjacent and at the same range.   Unpinned leaders are required in both groups when the groups are not adjacent AND at the same range.In the instance of using Rally All for non-adjacent groups both with unpinned leaders, I don't see any stipulation about them "having to be at the same range". If they had added your second sentence "Unpinned leaders are required in both groups when the groups are not adjacent AND at the same range", that would have made WAAAAY more sense. The fact that you see this and I don't maybe speaks to the fact that I have indeed overlooked or "misread the rule."

Then again, Yiannis, Rob, and Jeff before you all seem to have noticed what I have although I'm beginning to lean towards your interpretation for simplicity's sake. Gotta love those barracks-room-lawyer-Avalon Hill  style of rules....especially for a game with no board :shake:

Thank you for answering.

title: Russian Discards
question:
If a Russian player takes these 3 actions 
Fire, Rally, Movement ...and he has a terrain card Stream in his hand May he play the terrain on his opponent?   And refill his hand to 4 cards ? Or must he hold the stream in his hand and refill only 3 cards

If a Russian player has 4 terrain cards in his hand 3 Marsh 1 Stream could he play all 4 onto the opponents [(4)groups with move cards ] and Refill his hand ?
OR
must he discard  the terrain into the discard pile and refill at the end of his turn?
ManyThanksToner
author: toner
consensus_answer:
If a Russian player takes these 3 actions 
Fire, Rally, Movement ...and he has a terrain card Stream in his hand May he play the terrain on his opponent?   

A) Fire, Movement, Rally are all actions.  A Russian player CANNOT discard any cards if they do any actions (With two exceptions:  Elite 
troops, Entrenchment)

B)  Playing ANY CARD on an opponent (terrain, wire, sniper) is ALWAYS done with a discard.

Because of A & B, the answer is no.

And refill his hand to 4 cards ? Or must he hold the stream in his hand and refill only 3 cards

Refilling your hand to 4 cards means to draw as many AS NECESSARY until you have 4 cards.  If you no cards in hand at the end of the turn, you draw 4.  If you have 1 card left in your hand, you draw 3.  2 cards left, draw 2.  3 cards left, draw 1.  Or 4 cards left  (If you only performed entrenchments, weapon repair, etc.), draw 0.
 

If a Russian player has 4 terrain cards in his hand 3 Marsh 1 Stream could he play all 4 onto the opponents [(4)groups with move cards ] and Refill his hand ?
OR
must he discard  the terrain into the discard pile and refill at the end of his turn?
ManyThanksToner

Since playing terrain on an opponent *****IS***** a discard.  So yes, you can play as many terrain cards on your opponent, so long as it legal to discard (i.e. no actions, except entrenchment.)

You ALWAYS refill your hand at the end of your turn, whether you played cards for actions or discarded.

OR
must he discard  the terrain into the discard pile and refill at the end of his turn?
ManyThanksToner

Since playing terrain on an opponent *****IS***** a discard.  So yes, you can play as many terrain cards on your opponent, so long as it legal to discard (i.e. no actions, except entrenchment.)

You ALWAYS refill your hand at the end of your turn, whether you played cards for actions or discarded.

A Russian player may discard UP TO four cards if he takes NO card action.

He does not need to discard four cards, he can discard one, two or three cards - the choice is his.

There is one action he can take while discarding - entrenchment. However, for each group that attempts entrencment, his discard capacity is reduced by one.  So, if two groups attempt to entrench, the Russian player could only discard up to two cards on that turn.

So, for your example:

If he plays Fire, Rally, Movement - he cannot discard any cards as he has taken at least one card action.

If he has 3 March and 1 Stream - and the opponent had four moving groups - he could play all of them on the opponent's groups.

Hope this helps.

title: Campaign Game Promotions
question:
After years of using the Campaign rules for Up Front, I noticed something which made me wonder whether I've been playing them wrong all this time.  This has to do with marking slashes in the "Promotion" column.

What I've been doing is putting a slash in the Promotion column every time a man increases his Morale or Panic value by accumulating 5 Elan points (42.44), and putting a slash in the "Survival" column each time he survives a scenario (42.45).  Then, a man increases his rank (eg from PFC to CPL) when he has 10 slashes in the Survival and Promotion columns combined (erasing those slashes).  So, for example, a CPL who has survived 6 scenarios and has increased his M3P4 to M5P6 (ie 4 increments) is promoted to SGT. Fine.  

However, I noticed for the first time that, in the notes at the bottom of the US and Russian rosters, it says for column 9 (Promotion): "Enter / if in play at game end; enter / whenever man improves rating".  This would mean that a man who survives a scenario always gets two slashes (one in Survival, one in Promotion) and may get a second in Promotion if he gains an M/P increment.  Thus, accumulating 10 slashes in the two columns taken together will obviously be much quicker - taking about half the number of scenarios.

So, I can see three possibilities:

1) Take this as read, such that any man who participates in and survives every scenario of a 10-game campaign is guaranteed two promotions even if he gains no M/P increments.

2) This is a misprint: when preparing the rosters, someone did a copy and paste and accidentally included the "Enter / if in play at game end;" phrase under the "Promotion" column when it should only have been against the "Survival" column.

3) This is an editing mistake: the original idea was to enter survival slashes only under "Survival" and aggregate the "Survival" and "Promotion" columns to determine promotion.  Then it occurred to someone that, if you noted survival in both columns, you need not add them together, so they put the note under the "Promotion" column - but they forgot to amend the rules in sections 42.44-45 to match.

Anyone got any comments or ideas?
author: Barbarossa
consensus_answer:
Thanks Andy.  That's how I read it (and have always played) and it makes good sense.  

I suspect option 3 in my mail - the editing mistake in the rules - was the origin of this.

author: cedar
consensus_answer:
Hi, just a quick question about encirclement. Does encirclement prevent the encircled group from retreating? 

No.  You may still retreat.  One way to break encirclement is get bother encircling groups in front of the encircled group, that is done by retreating at least twice.
 
[17.62]    An encircled group remains encircled until either opposing group which comprises the encirclement is eliminated, or infiltrated by the encircled group, or changes its group ID chit [17.7], or is at Relative Range 1 or less from the encircled group, or both encircling groups find themselves "in front of" the encircled group.

Nope.  The "encircling" group is adjacent to (and does not have the same letter as) the opponent's group it is encircling.   Only groups with the same ID chit letter block each other.

title: Infiltration + wire + capture
question:
Lets say that my moving group in a forest succesfully inflitrates an enemy group positioned in a building.

On his turn my opponent plays wire on my group.

I CC him and kill all of his men.

I decide to capture his building.

According to rules when a moving group captures an opponent's terrain  the move card is discarted.

What about the wire? Does it stay or it also discarted?
author: Emil 109
consensus_answer:
If you infiltrate and then are thrown in wire, you may attempt CC.  In that you are correct. 

But, you can't take the opposing terrain after eliminating the last man while infiltrating--You are in wire and the only terrain that can be placed while you are in wire is Open Ground, which goes underneath the wire..  

 13.34   Neither Terrain nor Movement cards can be placed on top of a Wire card by either player; the Wire card must first be removed by play of a temporary Movement card. Note that a group on Wire may not play a Movement card to remove the Wire as long as that group contains a pinned man.

13.5   Open Ground may be placed beneath a Wire or Smoke card and above a Movement card by the moving player so as to eliminate his group's Moving status, yet leave the Wire and/or Smoke in play.

The rule makes no distinction between playing of a card (from either hand) or terrain capture.  I see no reason why that would make a difference.

Terrain Capture rules make clear that its use is completely optional:

20.8 TERRAIN CAPTURE:   
    Whenever the last man in a group is eliminated while his group is infiltrated, the Terrain card his group occupied (including entrenchments) is subject to capture by any group currently infiltrating that group regardless of the movement status of either group. The captor has the choice of replacing his own Terrain card with that of the eliminated defender's, or simply removing the eliminated group's cards to the Discard pile. Note that if two different groups can claim capture of the defender's Terrain card, it cannot be given to both groups, but that player can choose which of his groups to give it to. He could also transfer any man currently infiltrating that group during that turn into the group which receives the captured Terrain card. Any Movement cards in play on either the captor or the eliminated group are removed when the Terrain card is placed on its new group.

The mandatory rule 13.34 has precedence over rule 20.8 which merely gives you the opportunity to capture opposing terrain--subject to other rules.

title: Question about movement effects on infiltration attempts
question:
Hi,

I'm sorry, I don't have the rulebook with me, so I can't quote the rules, but I think I can be clear enough to get an answer to this question.

On my turn, I attempted infitration with four men in a five man group (one man was pinned), in Brush, at RR5 from an enemy group that was moving in woods. I used a movement card for two of the four men, and the other two took morale checks. One passed, so three men were attempting to infiltrate the group. When calculating the column to use for the resolution of each attempt, we had to factor in that infiltrating a group which is moving creates a column shift to the righ (two columns, I believe). However, in the rules it states that an infiltration attempt taken by a man in a non-moving group, who uses a movement card rather than a morale check to enable the infiltration attempt, does not suffer the movement penalty. 

We differed in our interpretation. My opponent thought that meant if both groups are not moving, you don't use the column shift. I thought that any man whose group was not moving, and used a movement card to allow the infiltration attempt, did not suffer the column shift for infiltrating a moving group. Who got it right?

If need be, I'll get the rulebook out when I get home and post the relevant paragraph, I believe it was 20.4 or so? I want to make sure I've got that right if it happens again.

Thanks,

Chris
author: fatgreta
consensus_answer:
Rulebook can be found online here: http://www.iufl.org/Rulebook/

Regarding your question:

The exception is noted in the rules to let you know that the movement cards you play into the discard pile in lieu of a morale check for infiltration do not count as "moving" status for purposes of calculating the column shift.  I.e. Playing a Movement card to get infiltration status does not satisfy the conditions of getting a column shift for movement.

So that means:

Whether or not a movement card was used to gain infiltrator status,
Both groups not moving = no shift
Either group moving = shift (2 to the right for either group)

Your opponent was correct.

(EDIT: Trying to make it a little clearer.)

Thanks for such a quick reply, and definitely thanks for the link to the rules. Still, after reading your post and rereading the rule I still disagree. Here's the rule:

20.39 MOVING & INFILTRATION:  

    If the attacker is attempting to infiltrate from a Moving group, there is a two column shift to the right to determine infiltration status. If the defending group is currently moving, there is a two column shift to the right to determine infiltration status. The number of Movement cards in play by each side do not further alter this shift. If the attacker is attempting to infiltrate from a group which has already been infiltrated, there is a two column shift to the right to determine infiltration status. NOTE: This Movement penalty is not applied to a man attempting infiltration whose group is not moving, but who has played a Movement card into the Discard pile to avoid the need to make a Morale Check.

The section after NOTE: is what I'm referring to. That paragraph is referring to a situation where the infiltrating is not moving. If the use of a movement card for a man "whose group is not moving" cancels the movement penalty, what movement penalty could it be canceling? The infiltrator's group is not moving, so the only column shift would be that caused by infiltrating into a moving group. In other words, if the movement penalty always applies to infiltrate a moving group, why have that final paragraph at all?

Thanks,

Chris

title: Flanking
question:
Hi all, we are trying to learn ho to play this incredible game, but there are some rules which we are not sure if we understand. In particular, in order to play a Flank card, it has to be played sideways. What does this mean exactly?

a) Does this mean that the group is doing a side movement? In this case, can the group receive a terrain card? Do they suffer the +1 attack strength modifier?

b) Are the soldiers of the group moving, i.e., bolt rifles multiply by 0.5 their FP, MMG cannot fire, attack strength is dvided by 2 and so on.

c) Can you use a FLANK movement card to ford a stream? And to exit a marsh?

Thanks!

David
author: davidmps
consensus_answer:
Hi all, we are trying to learn how to play this incredible game, but there are some rules which we are not sure if we understand. In particular, in order to play a Flank card, it has to be played sideways. What does this mean exactly?

a) Does this mean that the group is doing a side movement? In this case, can the group receive a terrain card? Do they suffer the +1 attack strength modifier?

b) Are the soldiers of the group moving, i.e., bolt rifles multiply by 0.5 their FP, MMG cannot fire, attack strength is divided by 2 and so on.

c) Can you use a FLANK movement card to ford a stream? And to exit a marsh?

Thanks!

David

In general, a Flank Movement card does everything a normal Movement card does, including when played sideways to obtain Flanking.  So yes, all the above effects occur: the group is moving sideways and can receive a Terrain card (either from its owner or by enemy discard), incoming Fire attacks are +1, and they suffer the Moving Fire disadvantages.  However, the group is Flanking while the Movement card is in play, so Bolt-Action rifles are halved and doubled (ie retain their normal FP).  Semi-auto rifles double their FP like other weapons.  Fire Strength is still halved and rounded down.

It can also be used to Ford or while in a Marsh, with some special but logical effects:
- if you use it to Ford, and fail (red RNC), the Movement card goes away and you don't get the Flanking advantage.
- if you use it for the first Marsh exit card, you can't play a Terrain card until you've played a second Movement card - which removes the Flanking, unless the second card is also a Flank card and is played sideways.

The group retains Flanking when it plays or receives a Terrain card, so you can Flank, then play a Hill for maximum effect.  You lose the Flank by moving or receiving a Wire card, or if the Flanked group plays a Movement card (even to remove Wire - so think hard before discarding Wire on a Flanked group).

One thing often forgotten is that, in order to Flank, the Flanking group has to be adjacent but not opposite to the Flanked group, and there has to be a friendly group opposite to the Flanked group.  So if you have groups A, B, C and the enemy has groups A & B, your A can Flank his B, your B can flank his A, your C can Flank his B; his A can Flank your B, his B can Flank your A; but his B can't Flank your C because he has no group opposite your C.

And finally, you can't combine Flanking with Lateral Group Transfer (eg moving group B to group C) because of the above rule that an opposite group must exist before you Flank.  This again is logical if you think about it.

There are some other details about Natural Flanking and (Heaven help us) Encircled, but read section 17 carefully and it should come clear.

Good luck!

replies.body:
Hi all, we are trying to learn how to play this incredible game, but there are some rules which we are not sure if we understand. In particular, in order to play a Flank card, it has to be played sideways. What does this mean exactly?

a) Does this mean that the group is doing a side movement? In this case, can the group receive a terrain card? Do they suffer the +1 attack strength modifier?

b) Are the soldiers of the group moving, i.e., bolt rifles multiply by 0.5 their FP, MMG cannot fire, attack strength is divided by 2 and so on.

c) Can you use a FLANK movement card to ford a stream? And to exit a marsh?

Thanks!

David

In general, a Flank Movement card does everything a normal Movement card does, including when played sideways to obtain Flanking.  So yes, all the above effects occur: the group is moving sideways and can receive a Terrain card (either from its owner or by enemy discard), incoming Fire attacks are +1, and they suffer the Moving Fire disadvantages.  However, the group is Flanking while the Movement card is in play, so Bolt-Action rifles are halved and doubled (ie retain their normal FP).  Semi-auto rifles double their FP like other weapons.  Fire Strength is still halved and rounded down.

It can also be used to Ford or while in a Marsh, with some special but logical effects:
- if you use it to Ford, and fail (red RNC), the Movement card goes away and you don't get the Flanking advantage.
- if you use it for the first Marsh exit card, you can't play a Terrain card until you've played a second Movement card - which removes the Flanking, unless the second card is also a Flank card and is played sideways.

The group retains Flanking when it plays or receives a Terrain card, so you can Flank, then play a Hill for maximum effect.  You lose the Flank by moving or receiving a Wire card, or if the Flanked group plays a Movement card (even to remove Wire - so think hard before discarding Wire on a Flanked group).

One thing often forgotten is that, in order to Flank, the Flanking group has to be adjacent but not opposite to the Flanked group, and there has to be a friendly group opposite to the Flanked group.  So if you have groups A, B, C and the enemy has groups A & B, your A can Flank his B, your B can flank his A, your C can Flank his B; his A can Flank your B, his B can Flank your A; but his B can't Flank your C because he has no group opposite your C.

And finally, you can't combine Flanking with Lateral Group Transfer (eg moving group B to group C) because of the above rule that an opposite group must exist before you Flank.  This again is logical if you think about it.

There are some other details about Natural Flanking and (Heaven help us) Encircled, but read section 17 carefully and it should come clear.

Good luck!

You lose the Flank by moving or receiving a Wire card, or if the Flanked group plays a Movement card (even to remove Wire - so think hard before discarding Wire on a Flanked group).

There are three other situations that remove the FLANK FIRE chit:
-  Flanking group rejecting terrain played by his opponent (Since any sideways movement card is removed when terrain is rejected, this would remove a flank movement card.)
-  If the Front group is eliminated/transferred to another letter  (BOTH groups are important.)
-  The flanked group has a terrain card (including open ground) played (so don't flank a group that is already moving.)
Well, maybe - but there are times when a quick answer is better than a full one!

I am impressed! Lighting replies!

Thank you both!

David

title: Scenario X "Surrounded". How does this actually work???
question:
Scenario X is a scenario I suspect is not played very much. And that's due to its rather blurry special rules regarding encirclement. It states that "the defender does not start the game technically encircled as per 17.6. Such encirclement status is incurred only per 17.6" and then some other half-clear mumbo-jumbo about groups both in front and behind are at RR5 (yeah, right, as if that's very likely to happen before the defending squad is either shredded or have made short work of the attackers trying to close in).

What I'd like to have a clearer understanding of, is how do you go about to encircle the defender in this scenario apart from getting to RR5 with at least half your force?

Here is how I interpret the rules.

The usual startup will look something like this:

A(0)    A(0)     A(10)

B(0)    B(0)     B(10)

The basic rule 17.6 states that encirclement is only acheived whan a group advances past an enemy group to RR4 and then play a subsecquent movement card. The encircled group must also have an enemy group directly in front of it who merely have to exist If you follow this rule literally, an encirclement of red group A is not possible until the situation is something like this:

A(0)     A(0)     A(10)

B(4)     B(0)     B(10) 

However, rule 17.62 further down states that the encirclement is broken if "either encircling group is ar RR1 or less to the encircled group". According to that, to encircle red A, the situation must be like this:

A(0)     A(0)     A(8)

B(4)     B(0)     B(10)

Then comes my clue: Since in scenario X, the defender starts with enemy groups already on both sides of it, there will be no passing it by as that has actually happened already. Since an encirclement is kept until the enemy groups get to RR2 to the encircled group, in my opinion the incirclemet would also be effective from the point the neccessary enemy groups reach RR2 to the group they intend to encircle and then play a subsequent sideways move. In other words, encirclement of red A would happen already at this point:

A(0)     A(0)     A(8)

B(2)     B(0)     B(10)

Please enlighten me!

R.:)
author: stroar
consensus_answer:
Surrounded is a very confusing set up the way it is described in the rule book.  Bruce Wigdor's IUF program implements it is the surrounding player sets groups at both RC0 and RC10, the defender is its RC0.  For game purposes, the groups at RC10 are designated Group I, J, K, etc.

The attacking groups at RC0 advance towards the defender normally, by increasing their RC number.  The attacking groups at RC10 advance towards the defender by LOWERING their RC number.

The defender advances towards the RC0 groups by increasing their RC into the positive numbers, and towards the RC10 groups by DECREASING  (-2 < -1) their RC into the negative numbers.

The standard relative range rules including the correction for RR over 5 (if sum of RC > 5 then RR = 10 - (sum of RC's)) always work out in this system:

Attacker at RC 2 fires at defender at RC 1 => RR = 2+1 = 3
Attacker at RC 2 fires at defender at RC-1 => RR = 2-1 = 1
Attacker at RC 8 fires at defender at RC 1 => RR = 8+1 = 9 converts to 10-9 = 1
Attacker at RC 8 fires at defender at RC-1 => RR = 8-1 = 7 converts to 10-7 = 3

(All of these assume firing is at groups with same ID letter or one letter off (i,e, directly opposite or adjacent opposite groups)

If everything is laid out on a board:

Att RC   Def RC    
0          5       Attacker starts here
1          4
2          3
3          2
4          1
5          0       Defender starts here
6         -1
7         -2
8         -3
9         -4
10        -5        Attacker starts here
 

Now onto encirclement:

Essentially, Encirclement has to be done from groups that start on the SAME side but otherwise happens per normal rules:  

An encircling group B that started at RR0 must reach "RR6" (i.e. RR4 behind the defender group A they are encircling) and then play the sideways movement card (while also having their own group A) to create the encirclement.  (This is the normal encirclement rule) 

An encircling group J that started at RR10 must reach RR4 (thus passing the defending group A they are encircling) and then play a sideways movement card (while having their own group I) to create the encirclement.

Groups that started on opposite sides cannot combine for an encirclement.   

So:  Attacker group B may encircle Defending group A below:
AF1:  A(0)  B(6)
DF:   A(0)  B(-2)
AF2:  I(0)  J(0)

Likewise Attacker group J may encircle Defending group A below:
AF1:  A(0)  B(0)
DF:   A(0)  B(2)
AF2:  I(0)  J(4)

It actually works out reasonably well after a game or two on IUF.  

And it is an interesting scenario of both sides.  
-  The attacker can't put too much strength in one of the two sides, the defender will move towards the smaller/safer force.  He can't lose too much in one force, because the defender will crush that side and run.
-  If the defender can't weaken one of the sides and advance towards it, he is usually picked apart.

Actually X is a pretty balanced scenario--except Japanese defense (75% break is the killer.)  One of my favorites and worth the effort.

title: Infiltration counter question
question:
The back of the 'infiltrator' counter says:

2xFP
+2 Right
Keep +3

author: Avalon Polo
consensus_answer:
NRBH, but IIRC (how's that for more obfuscation...)

+2 right, means that the infiltrated group will have a harder time to counter-infiltrate other groups - signified by a 2 column shift to the right if any member of the infiltrated group tries to infiltrate another group
